carousel.body: Look for a decision you make over and over and rarely improve on. Repetition without learning is the signature of something that should be a rule instead.

carousel.title: Set the bar, not the best
carousel.body: Write what good enough looks like, in specifics. A standard you can check against beats an aspiration to find the optimum you will never confirm.

carousel.title: Write the rule down
carousel.body: An unwritten rule is a preference, and preferences get renegotiated whenever you are tired. Written ones have to be formally overturned, which is harder.

carousel.title: Set a review date
carousel.body: Pick a date months away to reconsider the rule. That is what keeps it from becoming a cage, and it stops you reopening the question every week.

sparks.hook: Expectations are the one thing you can raise for free and pay for forever.
sparks.insight: Satisfaction is roughly the gap between what happened and what you expected. Abundance quietly inflates the second number: if a hundred options exist, the one you get should surely be excellent. So genuinely improving conditions can still produce falling satisfaction, because the standard rises faster than the reality. Lowering expectations sounds like a defeat and is closer to arithmetic. The alternative is being permanently disappointed by outcomes that are objectively good.
sparks.why: This follows directly from comparison-based accounts of satisfaction, and it explains why people in wealthier settings with more options do not report proportionally higher contentment.
sparks.apply: Pick one area where you are chronically disappointed and write down what you are implicitly expecting. Then ask where that expectation came from.

sparks.hook: Choice matters enormously up to a point, then it starts charging you.
sparks.insight: None of this is an argument against choice. Going from no options to some options transforms a life, which is why autonomy is a basic human need rather than a consumer preference. The curve simply is not a straight line. It rises steeply, flattens, and then bends down as effort, regret and expectation start costing more than the additional quality is worth. The useful skill is knowing roughly where you are on that curve in any given area.
sparks.why: Framing this as a curve rather than a rule resolves most of the argument the book has generated, since critics and supporters are usually describing different regions of it.
sparks.apply: Name one area of your life with too few options and one with too many. Spend this month adding to the first and pruning the second.

carousel.title: Check where the pain is
carousel.body: Ask whether a given area frustrates you because there is nothing available or because there is too much. The two problems feel similar and need opposite treatment.

carousel.title: Expand where it is thin
carousel.body: Where options are genuinely scarce, more choice helps a great deal. This is the steep part of the curve and it is worth real effort to climb.

carousel.title: Prune where it is thick
carousel.body: Where options are abundant, cut the field to a handful before you start comparing. Filtering first is cheaper than evaluating everything and regretting later.

carousel.title: Delegate the rest
carousel.body: For decisions that do not repay attention, take a trusted recommendation and stop. Outsourcing a choice is a legitimate way to spend your attention elsewhere.

actions: Write a good-enough standard for three recurring decisions, then buy or choose the first option that clears the bar without checking any further.
Unsubscribe from the three sources that most often show you options you were not looking for, and delete the shopping apps you browse rather than use.
Take one reversible decision from the past month and close it deliberately: no returns, no revisiting, no comparison shopping after the fact.
Identify one area where you genuinely have too few options and spend an hour widening it, so you are not treating abundance as a universal problem.
books.not_for_you_if: You want current evidence rather than a 2004 argument, or you already decide quickly and are looking for help with something other than overthinking.

verification.notes: First published 2004 by Ecco. The choice-overload effect has been substantially qualified since: a 2010 meta-analysis found a near-zero average effect, and the phenomenon is now understood as conditional. The link to rising depression rates is disputed. Both are flagged in the sparks. All prose original.

books.title: The Righteous Mind
books.subtitle: Why Good People Are Divided by Politics and Religion
books.author: Jonathan Haidt
books.why_it_matters: It offered a testable explanation for why decent people find each other's politics incomprehensible, and made moral psychology a public conversation. It is the standard reference for explaining division without calling half a country stupid.

crux.headline: Judgement comes first, and the reasons are assembled after
crux.body: You do not reach moral conclusions by weighing arguments. You react, fast and physically, and your reasoning then goes to work building a case for the verdict you already reached. That is why moral arguments so rarely move anybody: you are presenting evidence to a lawyer rather than to a judge. It also means your political opponents are not failing to think. They are reacting from a different set of moral concerns and then reasoning about as well as you do.

sparks.hook: You reach the verdict in a second, then spend an hour justifying it.
sparks.insight: Moral judgement arrives fast, as a reaction rather than a conclusion. Reasoning turns up afterwards to produce a case, and it is very good at that job — which is why an argument that defeats your stated reasons rarely changes your view. Haidt's image is a small rider on a large elephant: the rider looks articulate and in charge, while the elephant decides the direction. Persuasion aimed only at the rider gets you a better argument and no change of mind.
sparks.why: Judgements are made faster than the reasons for them can be generated, and people readily produce fresh justifications when the original ones are refuted. The strong claim that reasoning never matters goes further than the evidence.
sparks.apply: In your next disagreement, notice how quickly your verdict arrived. Then ask what would have to be true for the other position to be reasonable.

sparks.hook: People hold moral views they cannot defend, and keep holding them.
sparks.insight: Presented with a scenario engineered so that nobody is harmed and every objection is blocked in advance, people still judge some acts wrong and then discover they have run out of reasons. What happens next is the instructive part: they do not change the verdict. They say they cannot explain it but they know it anyway. That is strong evidence the judgement never rested on the reasons, and that the reasons were recruited to defend something already decided.
sparks.why: Moral dumbfounding has been demonstrated in several studies, though critics argue some scenarios are contrived enough that participants reasonably distrust the setup. The core observation that conviction outlives its justification is not seriously disputed.
sparks.apply: Take one strong moral view of yours and write the best case against it. Notice whether losing that argument makes any difference to what you believe.

sparks.hook: Your reasoning works for you the way a lawyer works for a client.
sparks.insight: Reasoning is usually assumed to be a truth-finding instrument that occasionally fails. It behaves more like an advocate that occasionally succeeds. Given a conclusion you want, you search for supporting evidence and stop as soon as you find some. Given one you dislike, you search for a flaw and stop as soon as you find one. Both searches feel identical from the inside, and the difference in how hard you looked is where most motivated reasoning actually lives.
sparks.why: The asymmetry between must-I-believe and can-I-believe searching is well documented, and reasoning improves markedly in groups with genuine disagreement. That is the practical implication: use other people as the correction.
sparks.apply: For your next firm opinion, deliberately search for the strongest opposing evidence, with a rule that you read three sources before you stop looking.

sparks.hook: Different people run on different moral concerns, not fewer of them.
sparks.insight: Moral reactions appear to draw on several distinct concerns: protecting people from harm, fairness and proportionality, loyalty to your group, respect for legitimate authority, and a sense of purity or degradation. People differ in how heavily they weight each. Somebody whose objection is rooted in loyalty or sanctity is not making a mistake about harm; they are responding to a concern you may barely register, and the conversation fails because neither side hears the other's real grounds.
sparks.why: Moral foundations theory is influential and useful, but the exact number of foundations is contested and the questionnaire's structure has not always replicated cleanly. Treat it as a working map rather than a settled taxonomy.
sparks.apply: In your next political disagreement, work out which concern is really driving the other person, then address that one instead of the one you would have used.

sparks.hook: The moral world you find obvious is a minority position globally.
sparks.insight: Educated, wealthy, individualist Western populations are unusual on many psychological measures, morality included. They tend to build ethics almost entirely out of harm and fairness, treating everything else as personal taste. Most people in most places also moralise loyalty, hierarchy and sanctity, and regard a society without them as one that is coming apart. Reading the rest of the world as morally underdeveloped is a description of your own sample being strange rather than theirs.
sparks.why: The finding that Western educated samples are outliers across many psychological measures is robust and has forced a rethink of what counts as a human universal. Most published psychology still draws on those samples.
sparks.apply: Read one serious argument from a moral tradition you find alien, with the aim of stating its case well enough that a member of it would agree.

sparks.hook: People are mostly self-interested and occasionally something else.
sparks.insight: Human beings compete hard with each other and then, under the right conditions, dissolve into a group and work for it at real personal cost. Marching, singing, drilling, worshipping and playing team sport all trigger it. The point is not that groups are good — the same machinery produces armies and mobs — but that a picture of people as purely self-interested fails to explain the behaviour most in need of explanation, including your own at a concert or a protest.
sparks.why: The evolutionary account here relies on group-level selection, which remains contested among biologists. The psychological observation — that synchronous group activity produces strong shared identity — is well supported independently of that argument.
sparks.apply: Notice one group you dissolve into and what it makes easy. Then ask what it would take for that same feeling to make you cruel to outsiders.

sparks.hook: Religion works less as a set of beliefs than as a way of binding people.
sparks.insight: Arguing about whether religious claims are true misses most of what religion does. Ritual, restriction and shared worship build groups that trust each other, cooperate and stay together, and the demanding parts are often exactly what makes the trust credible. That is a functional account rather than an endorsement, and it explains why religious communities keep appearing in research on social support and cohesion regardless of what anyone believes about the metaphysics.
sparks.why: Religious participation is associated with social support, in-group cooperation and some health benefits, largely through community rather than belief. The evolutionary story about how this arose is more speculative than the correlations are.
sparks.apply: If you have no religious community, identify which secular structure supplies the same things: regular attendance, shared ritual, and duties to specific people.

sparks.hook: The team that gives you meaning also decides what you cannot see.
sparks.insight: Belonging to a moral community delivers real goods: purpose, trust, people who will help you. It also installs a set of things that become unthinkable rather than merely wrong, plus a strong incentive not to notice evidence that would embarrass your own side. This is not a failing peculiar to the other team. The better you are at reasoning, the more effectively you can defend whatever your group already believes, which is why education does not reliably reduce partisanship.
sparks.why: Politically motivated reasoning is often stronger in more numerate and better informed people, because they have more tools for reaching the conclusion they want. Group identity predicts belief better than knowledge does.
sparks.apply: Name one fact that would embarrass your own side. Check whether you know it as precisely as you know the equivalent fact about the other side.

sparks.hook: If you want to change a mind, do not start with the argument.
sparks.insight: Because the verdict arrives before the reasoning, an argument aimed at somebody's stated reasons hits the part that was never doing the deciding. What moves people is a shift in the intuition underneath, and intuitions shift through relationship, respect and being genuinely heard rather than through evidence. That is slower and much less satisfying than winning, and it is the only route that reliably works. Warmth first, then a specific claim, is the order that succeeds.
sparks.why: Persuasion research consistently finds that perceived respect and shared identity condition whether evidence gets accepted at all. Approaches built on listening and personal narrative outperform argument in field experiments on contested issues.
sparks.apply: In your next hard conversation, state the other person's view until they agree you have it right, before you say a single word of your own.

carousel.title: Lower the threat
carousel.body: Warmth, curiosity, no audience. Somebody defending their standing in a group cannot weigh evidence, and being watched makes the defending compulsory.

carousel.title: State their view back
carousel.body: Summarise their position until they say you have got it right. Nobody listens to a person who has clearly not understood what they are arguing against.

carousel.title: Find the shared concern
carousel.body: Locate a value you both hold, then show your position serving it. Arguments land when they are made in the other person's moral currency.

carousel.title: Make one small claim
carousel.body: Ask for a shift in a single specific belief rather than a change of side. Whole conversions are threatening, and threatened people stop listening.

sparks.hook: You cannot see your own bias, but you can build a check for it.
sparks.insight: Individual reasoning is poor at correcting individual bias, because the reasoner and the bias are the same person. What works is external: people who disagree with you and whose good faith you accept, a rule that you must state the opposing case first, a habit of noticing when a conclusion arrived faster than the evidence could possibly allow. None of this feels like insight. It feels like admin, which is exactly why almost nobody does it.
sparks.why: Reasoning improves substantially in groups where genuine disagreement exists and where members share a goal of getting it right. Solo debiasing efforts have a poor track record by comparison.
sparks.apply: Recruit one person who reliably disagrees with you and ask them to review your next significant decision before you commit to anything.

carousel.title: Time the verdict
carousel.body: Notice how long the judgement took. Anything that arrived instantly on a complex question was an intuition, whatever reasons you produced afterwards.

carousel.title: Write the other case
carousel.body: Put the strongest opposing argument in writing, in its own terms. If you cannot make it convincing, you do not yet understand what you disagree with.

carousel.title: Find a real dissenter
carousel.body: Ask someone who genuinely disagrees and whose good faith you accept. Groups with real disagreement reason better than any individual does alone.

carousel.title: Name the cost of being wrong
carousel.body: Say what you would lose socially by changing your mind. That answer explains more of your certainty than the evidence does.

actions: Write the strongest version of a political position you reject, then show it to somebody who holds it and revise until they say it is fair.
Identify which moral concerns drive your own reactions most strongly, and which ones you barely register when other people raise them.
Recruit one thoughtful person who disagrees with you and set up a standing arrangement to review each other's significant decisions.
In your next argument, spend the first five minutes only listening and summarising, then see whether the conversation goes differently.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a settled scientific account rather than a synthesis. The foundations framework is contested, and the evolutionary argument leans on ideas many biologists reject.

verification.notes: First published 2012. Moral foundations theory remains influential and contested; its questionnaire's factor structure has not always replicated, and the group selection argument is disputed among biologists. The claim that conservatives predict liberal answers better than the reverse has weakened in later work. All prose here is original.

books.title: The Selfish Gene
books.author: Richard Dawkins
books.why_it_matters: It replaced a fuzzy idea of animals striving for the good of the species with a sharper question: which copies get made. That shift reorganised how biologists explain altruism, family, conflict and cooperation, and it gave the culture the word meme.

crux.headline: You are the vehicle, not the passenger
crux.body: Natural selection does not care about you, your group or your species. It only tracks which stretches of code get copied into the next round. Bodies are temporary machines built by those copies to make more copies. Once you look at behaviour from the gene's point of view, things that seemed puzzling snap into place: why parents sacrifice, why siblings fight, why cooperation is common and unlimited generosity is rare.

sparks.hook: Evolution has no interest in you. It is keeping score of copies.
sparks.insight: The usual picture has individuals struggling to survive and pass on their traits. Flip it. What actually persists across millions of years is not any animal but the information that builds animals. A body lasts decades; a gene lineage can last for millions of years, moving through bodies the way a message moves through couriers. Once you take that view, the striking question is not why organisms die but why they exist at all — and the answer is that they are useful machinery for the copying.
sparks.why: The framing is not a separate theory of evolution but a change of accounting unit. Explanations that were awkward at the level of the individual become straightforward at the level of the replicator.
sparks.apply: Take one animal behaviour you find baffling, such as a bird feeding a chick that is not its own, and ask which copies benefit rather than which individual benefits.

sparks.hook: Selfish genes routinely build generous animals. The title fools people.
sparks.insight: The word selfish here describes an outcome, not a motive. Genes want nothing; they have no inner life at all. The shorthand simply says that the versions which end up common are the versions that got copied more, whatever their effect on anyone's happiness. And it turns out that a very effective way to get copied is to build an animal that shares food, defends a nest and cooperates for years. Selfishness at the level of code produces devotion at the level of behaviour with no contradiction.
sparks.why: This is the most common misreading of the whole framework: people take it as a claim that humans are fundamentally selfish. The argument is about which genes spread, and it makes no claim at all about what an animal feels.
sparks.apply: Whenever you meet a claim that biology proves people are naturally selfish, check which level it is talking about, code or creature, and ask whether it has silently swapped them.

sparks.hook: Helping your sister carries copies of you into the future too.
sparks.insight: You share about half your variable genetic material with a sibling and a quarter with a niece or nephew. So a gene that makes an animal help close relatives can spread even if the helper pays a real cost, because the copies it is protecting sit inside those relatives. The maths is blunt: the benefit to the relative, discounted by how closely related they are, has to exceed the cost to you. That single inequality explains sterile worker bees, alarm calls, and why families cooperate in ways strangers rarely do.
sparks.why: Hamilton formalised this in the 1960s and it holds up well across social insects and vertebrates. It also predicts the friction: kin cooperate strongly but never perfectly, because relatedness is a fraction rather than one.
sparks.apply: Map who in your life you help without keeping score. Notice how sharply the effort drops as the relationship gets more distant, and ask what actually earns exceptions.

sparks.hook: The winning strategy is not the nastiest one. It is nice with a memory.
sparks.insight: When strangers deal with each other repeatedly, pure exploitation stops paying, because the other side stops dealing. Computer tournaments that pitted strategies against each other found the durable ones shared a shape: never defect first, punish defection immediately, then return to cooperating rather than nursing the grudge, and stay simple enough that your partner can read you. Being predictable is not naive here. It is what lets the other side learn that cooperating with you is safe.
sparks.why: Axelrod's tournaments produced this result, and the logic depends on repetition. If a relationship is genuinely one-shot with no reputation attached, cooperation is much harder to sustain and defection often does pay.
sparks.apply: In your next ongoing negotiation, state your rule out loud: how you will respond to good faith and how you will respond to bad faith. Then follow it exactly.

carousel.title: Open cooperatively
carousel.body: Never be the first to defect. Starting with good faith costs little in a repeated game and it opens the whole space of mutual gains that pure caution never reaches.

carousel.title: Retaliate immediately
carousel.body: Respond to a defection at once and in proportion. Delayed punishment teaches nothing, and a strategy that never punishes is stripped for parts by anyone who notices.

carousel.title: Forgive fast
carousel.body: Go straight back to cooperating once they do. Holding the grudge locks both sides into a spiral that costs you far more than the original defection did.

carousel.title: Stay readable
carousel.body: Keep your rule simple enough that the other side can work it out from your behaviour. Cleverness that looks like randomness destroys the trust it was meant to exploit.

sparks.hook: Populations settle on strategies nobody would have chosen for them.
sparks.insight: Imagine a species where fights can be settled by bluffing or by real violence. If everyone bluffs, one genuinely aggressive individual cleans up. If everyone is violent, injuries pile up and a cautious individual does better. So the population drifts to a mix that cannot be invaded by any newcomer playing something different. That balance point is not the arrangement that would be best for the species, and no one negotiated it. It is simply the only mix that is stable against defectors.
sparks.why: This is what an evolutionarily stable strategy means: a state defined by what cannot successfully invade it, not by what would produce the most collective good. Stability and optimality are different things.
sparks.apply: Look at an unpleasant norm in your industry, such as inflated job titles. Ask who would lose by unilaterally stopping, and you will usually see why it persists.

sparks.hook: Nothing evolves for the good of the species. Cheats would eat it.
sparks.insight: It feels natural to say animals limit their breeding to avoid exhausting the food supply, or that a herd sacrifices for the herd. The problem is invasion. Put one individual in that restrained population who breeds at full speed, and its descendants inherit the same disregard while everyone else's restraint feeds them. Within a few generations the noble version is gone. Self-sacrificing arrangements only survive when something protects them, such as relatedness or repeated dealings with a memory attached.
sparks.why: This is the standard objection to naive group selection, and it is a matter of arithmetic rather than cynicism. Later work does allow selection above the individual under specific and demanding conditions.
sparks.apply: When someone explains a behaviour as being for the good of the group, ask what stops a free rider. If there is no answer, the explanation is probably incomplete.

sparks.hook: Ideas obey the same rules as genes, and they do not care if they are true.
sparks.insight: Anything that gets copied with variation, and where some variants get copied more, will evolve. Culture qualifies. A tune, a phrase, a rumour, a ritual: each spreads according to how catchy and transmissible it is, not according to how much it benefits the person carrying it. That is why a false and frightening story travels faster than a careful correction, and why the most successful ideas in your head arrived because they were good at arriving, not because you assessed them.
sparks.why: The analogy is deliberately loose and has been argued over ever since, since cultural copying is far less faithful than genetic copying. It still gives you the right first question about any viral idea: who benefits from the spread.
sparks.apply: Take the last thing you shared online and ask what made it spreadable. If the answer is outrage or novelty rather than usefulness, do not share the next one.

sparks.hook: Parents and children are not on the same side. Not entirely.
sparks.insight: A parent's interests are spread across all their offspring, present and future. Any single child is far more interested in itself than in its siblings. So the amount of food, attention and care a child would ideally extract is more than the amount a parent would ideally give, and the gap is not a failure of family life but a structural feature of it. Weaning conflicts, tantrums, sibling rivalry and the exhausting negotiations of adolescence all sit in that gap.
sparks.why: Trivers set out the logic of parent-offspring conflict in the 1970s. It predicts that the disagreement is permanent and bounded rather than resolvable, because the underlying interests genuinely differ without being opposed.
sparks.apply: Next time a family negotiation feels irrational, ask what each side is optimising for. Expect a settlement rather than agreement, and stop trying to win the argument outright.

sparks.hook: Selection stops watching once you have reproduced.
sparks.insight: A gene with a nasty effect that appears in your twenties gets removed from the population quickly, because its carriers leave fewer descendants. A gene with an equally nasty effect that only shows up at seventy is almost invisible to selection, since its carriers have already had their children. Over time that asymmetry lets late-acting harms accumulate in the genome. It is a bleak but clarifying way to think about ageing: not a design flaw, but the region where the design pressure runs out.
sparks.why: This is the standard evolutionary account of senescence, and it fits the observation that species with high adult mortality tend to age faster. It explains the shape of the problem, not any particular disease.
sparks.apply: Treat the parts of your health that only matter after fifty as things biology will not maintain for you, and put them on a deliberate schedule now.

sparks.hook: You are the one machine that can refuse its own instructions.
sparks.insight: The bleak reading of all this is that you are a puppet of your chemistry, and that ending is explicitly refused. Humans model the future, argue with each other, and build institutions, and those capacities let us do things that make no sense in copying terms at all: use contraception, adopt strangers' children, give blood, give money to people on the other side of the planet we will never meet. Understanding the machinery is what makes the refusal possible, because you cannot deliberately override a rule you have never seen.
sparks.why: Nothing in the framework says gene interests should be your interests. Confusing an explanation of where an urge came from with a justification for obeying it is the naturalistic fallacy, and it is the most common mistake made in this territory.
sparks.apply: Pick one urge you can trace to an old incentive, such as hoarding status or sugar, and design a specific rule that overrides it this month.

carousel.title: Name the old incentive
carousel.body: Work out what the urge would have been useful for in a world of scarcity and small groups. Craving, hoarding and status anxiety all made sense somewhere.

carousel.title: Check the current payoff
carousel.body: Ask what the same urge produces now, in an environment of abundance and strangers. Usually the machinery is intact and the environment it was built for has gone.

carousel.title: Separate origin from permission
carousel.body: An explanation of where a drive came from tells you nothing about whether to obey it. Natural is a description, never an argument for anything.

carousel.title: Write the override
carousel.body: Set one concrete rule that beats the urge without needing willpower in the moment, and put it somewhere you will meet it before the urge does.

actions: Take one human behaviour you find puzzling and write two explanations: one at the level of the individual, one at the level of the gene. Compare which fits better.
Audit your own generosity for a fortnight. Note who received it and how closely related or how frequently encountered they were, and see the shape that emerges.
Track one idea you hold strongly back to how it reached you, and ask whether you adopted it on evidence or because it was unusually easy to catch.
Choose a single urge with an obvious ancient logic and write an explicit rule that overrides it, then test the rule for thirty days.
books.not_for_you_if: You want warmth and lived human experience rather than argument, or you bounce off books that make you rebuild your intuitions from the arithmetic upward.

verification.notes: First published 1976 by Oxford University Press; later editions added chapters, including material on reciprocal cooperation and the extended phenotype. All prose here is original.

books.title: The Social Animal
books.author: Elliot Aronson
books.why_it_matters: It is the book that taught social psychology to several generations of students and made the field readable without making it silly. Its central claim, that ordinary situations produce extraordinary behaviour in ordinary people, is one of the discipline's genuine contributions.

crux.headline: The situation explains more than the person does
crux.body: When somebody behaves badly the instinct is to reach for their character. Decades of experiments suggest you would usually do better asking what position they were standing in: who was watching, what everyone else appeared to think, what the authority in the room expected, how the choice was framed. This is not an excuse for anything. It is a far more accurate predictor of behaviour, and it means changing situations is usually more effective than changing people.

sparks.hook: You will doubt your own eyes if enough people say otherwise.
sparks.insight: In the classic experiments, participants judged which of several lines matched a reference. The task was trivially easy alone. With a group of confederates confidently giving the wrong answer, a substantial share of people went along with it at least once, and some did so consistently. What makes it unsettling is not that people lied to fit in, which is expected, but that some genuinely began to doubt what they could plainly see.
sparks.why: Asch's conformity studies are among the most replicated in psychology, though conformity rates vary with culture, era and group composition. A single dissenting voice in the group cuts conformity dramatically.
sparks.apply: In your next meeting, state your view before hearing the room, or ask the most junior person first. Order of speaking determines much of the outcome.

sparks.hook: Ordinary people did terrible things because a man in a coat asked calmly.
sparks.insight: Milgram's obedience studies found that a majority of ordinary volunteers continued delivering what they believed were dangerous shocks when instructed by an unremarkable authority in a plain setting. No coercion, no threat, no ideology. Later examination of the archives complicated the picture: the experimenter improvised prods beyond the script, many participants suspected the setup, and compliance was pushed harder than the published account suggested. The core finding survives, in a more qualified form.
sparks.why: Archival work by Gina Perry and others documented deviations from protocol and variable participant belief. Partial replications under modern ethics have found substantial obedience, so the phenomenon is real but the original framing was too clean.
sparks.apply: Decide in advance what instruction you would refuse and say it out loud to a colleague. Deciding in the moment is exactly what the situation is designed to prevent.

sparks.hook: The mind does not tolerate holding a belief that its own behaviour contradicts.
sparks.insight: When what you did clashes with what you believe about yourself, something has to move, and it is almost never the behaviour, which has already happened. So the belief adjusts. You conclude the tedious task was interesting, that the person you were unkind to had it coming, that the choice you made was obviously the better one. This is not lying. The revision happens below awareness and feels exactly like ordinary reasoning, which is precisely what makes it so difficult to catch.
sparks.why: Cognitive dissonance is one of the most productive theories in the field, with a large experimental literature. Some individual studies have not replicated well, and the size of the effect depends heavily on how free the person felt in choosing.
sparks.apply: After a decision you defended strongly, write the strongest case against it. If that is hard to do, the defence was probably doing work for you.

sparks.hook: The harder it was to get in, the more you will insist it was worth it.
sparks.insight: People who go through an unpleasant process to join a group rate the group more highly afterwards than people admitted easily. The mechanism is dissonance: having suffered for something worthless is intolerable, so the value goes up. This explains initiations, gruelling training programmes and the fierce loyalty of people who endured a difficult onboarding. It is also why an ordeal is a cheap way to manufacture commitment, and why organisations reach for it so often.
sparks.why: Aronson and Mills's initiation study is a classic and the effect has replicated, though effect sizes vary. The general principle, that effort raises perceived value, is well supported across several literatures.
sparks.apply: Ask whether your loyalty to something tracks what it delivers or what it cost you to join. Value the outcome, not the entry fee you already paid.

sparks.hook: Competent people become more likeable the moment they spill something.
sparks.insight: A person seen as highly capable is rated more likeable after a small clumsy mistake, while the same mistake makes an average performer look worse. Competence at a distance creates a gap that a visible flaw closes. The practical version is not to stage clumsiness, which reads as false, but to notice that admitting an error rarely costs you what you fear, provided your competence is already established. The mistake usually makes you easier to be around.
sparks.why: The pratfall effect is a real finding, though it is moderated by the observer's own self-esteem and by gender in ways later studies have documented. The magnitude is modest and the conditions matter.
sparks.apply: Admit one small mistake out loud this week without over-explaining or apologising twice. Watch what happens to the temperature of the room.

sparks.hook: The praise that means most comes from someone who did not like you at first.
sparks.insight: Approval that has always been there is background noise. Approval that increases over time carries far more weight, because it registers as something earned and as evidence you actually changed somebody's mind. The unfortunate corollary is that the reverse hurts disproportionately: warmth that cools is far more painful than coolness that was always there. Constant unwavering praise from a partner or a manager will simply stop being heard, whatever its content.
sparks.why: This is the gain-loss account of interpersonal attraction from Aronson and Linder. It is an elegant finding from the 1960s that has not been extensively re-tested, so treat it as suggestive rather than settled.
sparks.apply: If you praise somebody constantly, make it specific and occasional instead. Undifferentiated approval carries no information and eventually reads as politeness.

sparks.hook: Putting hostile groups in one room does nothing. Giving them one job does.
sparks.insight: Contact between groups in conflict does not reduce prejudice by itself, and can make things worse when the groups arrive with different status and no shared purpose. What works is interdependence: a goal neither group can reach without the other, on roughly equal footing, with some institutional backing. This is why forced integration of a classroom without restructuring the work usually disappoints, and why a genuinely shared task can change attitudes that argument never touches.
sparks.why: The contact hypothesis has substantial meta-analytic support, and the conditions matter: equal status, common goals, cooperation and institutional support. Contact without those conditions produces much weaker effects.
sparks.apply: To reduce friction between two teams, design one deliverable neither can produce alone. Shared work outperforms any amount of joint training on empathy.

carousel.title: Build real dependence
carousel.body: Structure the task so each side holds something the other genuinely needs. Contact without interdependence is just proximity, and proximity alone can sharpen hostility.

carousel.title: Level the standing
carousel.body: Give both groups comparable status inside the task. Unequal footing reproduces the original hierarchy and confirms whatever each side already believed.

carousel.title: Set a shared goal
carousel.body: Define one outcome both are judged on together. A common target does more to redraw group boundaries than any appeal to fairness or good intentions.

carousel.title: Back it from above
carousel.body: Have the institution visibly support the arrangement. Without that, the first setback gets read as proof the whole exercise was naive from the start.

sparks.hook: Persuasion works best when nobody is aware of being persuaded.
sparks.insight: A message from someone who appears to have nothing to gain lands far harder than the identical message from an obvious advocate. Overheard arguments outperform directed ones. A communicator arguing against their own apparent interest is unusually convincing. None of this is about the quality of the argument, which is uncomfortable if you believe people are persuaded by evidence. It also means the most effective persuasion in your life was probably invisible at the time.
sparks.why: Source credibility, perceived intent and overheard communication effects are long-standing findings in persuasion research, though many specific studies date from the mid twentieth century and the effect sizes vary considerably.
sparks.apply: Before being persuaded, ask what the speaker gains if you agree. Before persuading, remove whatever makes you look like an interested party.

sparks.hook: Reduce a child's reason for obeying and the obedience lasts longer.
sparks.insight: Children given a severe threat not to play with a toy avoided it while the threat stood and returned to it later. Children given a mild reason, just enough to stop them, tended to conclude on their own that they did not want the toy much, and that conclusion persisted. Insufficient external justification pushes people to supply an internal one, and internal reasons outlast the enforcement. This is the same mechanism that makes large incentives produce compliance that evaporates.
sparks.why: The forbidden toy studies are a well-known demonstration of insufficient justification, consistent with the wider dissonance literature. They are old studies and modern replications are limited.
sparks.apply: Use the smallest pressure that actually works. If you need a large threat or a large reward, the behaviour will stop the moment either is withdrawn.

sparks.hook: This field checked its own homework and did not like the marks.
sparks.insight: Social psychology has been at the centre of the replication crisis. Several textbook studies did not survive scrutiny: the prison experiment turned out to involve heavy coaching of participants, the priming results that filled the 2000s largely failed to replicate, and several prominent researchers were found to have fabricated data. What survived is still substantial, including conformity, dissonance and contact effects. Read older editions of any social psychology text knowing which chapters have since thinned.
sparks.why: Large-scale replication projects found that a substantial share of published social psychology effects did not reproduce at the original size. Later editions of this book address the crisis; the early ones necessarily do not.
sparks.apply: Before repeating a famous psychology study, search for its replication record. Two minutes of checking will prevent most of the confident errors people make.

carousel.title: Check for a replication
carousel.body: Search the study name together with the word replication before you cite it. The most quotable findings are disproportionately the ones that later failed.

carousel.title: Look at the sample size
carousel.body: Many classics ran on a few dozen undergraduates. Small samples produce large, unstable effects, which is exactly the kind of result that gets famous.

carousel.title: Ask how big the effect is
carousel.body: A real effect can still be too small to matter for any decision you are making. Statistical significance is not the same as practical relevance.

carousel.title: Keep what survived
carousel.body: Conformity, dissonance and contact effects have held up reasonably well. Scepticism is a filter to apply, not a reason to discard the whole field.

actions: Change the order of speaking in one recurring meeting so the most junior person goes first, and record whether the conclusions change.
Write down in advance the instruction you would refuse to follow at work, and tell one colleague what it is.
Take two teams that dislike each other and design one deliverable neither can complete alone, with equal standing and visible backing.
Check the replication record of three psychology findings you repeat most often, and stop repeating any that did not survive.
books.not_for_you_if: You want the newest research rather than a classic textbook, or you find the situationist argument reads as excusing behaviour rather than explaining it.

verification.notes: First published 1972 by W. H. Freeman; revised through many later editions, with the more recent ones addressing replication problems directly. Not to be confused with David Brooks's 2011 book of the same title. Several studies described have been re-examined critically; the sparks say so. All prose original.

books.title: Think Again
books.subtitle: The Power of Knowing What You Don't Know
books.author: Adam Grant
books.why_it_matters: Most advice targets how to think. This targets how to abandon a thought you have already committed to, which is the harder skill and the one that decides whether anything you learn changes what you do.

crux.headline: Treat your opinions as hypotheses, not possessions
crux.body: When a belief becomes part of who you are, evidence against it feels like an attack on you, so you defend rather than update. The alternative is to hold opinions the way a scientist holds a hypothesis: interesting, provisional, and improved by being disproved. That requires separating your identity from your current conclusions and attaching it instead to the process — being someone who follows evidence rather than someone who was right.

sparks.hook: You have three default modes in an argument, and none of them is thinking.
sparks.insight: When a belief is challenged you tend to fall into one of three roles. You preach, defending a sacred position. You prosecute, attacking the flaws in theirs. Or you campaign, working out what your side wants to hear and saying it. All three feel like reasoning, and all three have already fixed the conclusion before the evidence is examined. The fourth option is rarer and duller: treat the question as open, decide what evidence would settle it, and be genuinely willing to lose.
sparks.why: Each of the three modes optimises for winning, defending or belonging rather than for accuracy. Naming which one you are in is what makes it possible to step out of it in the moment.
sparks.apply: In your next disagreement, name your mode silently before you speak. If it is one of the first three, ask a question instead of making your next point.

sparks.hook: Confidence in yourself and doubt about your view can coexist. That is the target.
sparks.insight: There are two dials, not one. Belief in your capacity to figure things out, and belief that your current answer is correct. Turn the first down and you get paralysis, where you have no faith in your ability to reach any conclusion. Turn the second up and you get arrogance. The productive combination is high on the first and moderate on the second: sure you can work it out, unsure you have yet. It sounds like a slogan until you try to hold both under pressure.
sparks.why: Certainty about a specific conclusion and confidence in one's ability to learn are separable, and only the second predicts revising a view when the evidence turns. Conflating them is what makes admitting error feel like admitting incompetence.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence about a live decision in this form: I am confident I can work this out, and I am roughly sixty percent sure of my current answer.

sparks.hook: Discovering you were wrong is information. Most people file it as humiliation.
sparks.insight: If your identity is attached to a conclusion, being corrected is a loss, and you will fight it. If your identity is attached to getting things right, being corrected is a gain — you just upgraded your model at somebody else's expense. The same event, opposite emotional sign, entirely because of what you decided to be attached to. This is not positive thinking. It is choosing an identity that is compatible with learning, since the one built on already knowing is not.
sparks.why: People who define themselves by their values and their standards rather than by their current opinions update more readily. The identity does the emotional work that willpower cannot do in the moment.
sparks.apply: Say out loud this week, once: I was wrong and I am glad I know now. Then note what you actually did differently as a result.

sparks.hook: Argue about the work all you like. Never argue about the person.
sparks.insight: There are two kinds of friction in a team. Disagreement about ideas, methods and priorities tends to improve decisions, because it surfaces information that consensus hides. Friction about respect, competence and character does the opposite: it makes people defensive, quiet and unwilling to share anything that could be used against them. High-performing teams are not the ones that argue least. They are the ones that argue hard about the first kind and have almost none of the second.
sparks.why: Task conflict is generally associated with better outcomes while relationship conflict is consistently harmful, though effects depend on the team having enough trust for a challenge to be read as a challenge rather than an attack.
sparks.apply: Before your next critique, rewrite it to be about the decision rather than the person. Say this approach has a problem, and name the problem precisely.

sparks.hook: Adding more arguments makes your case weaker, not stronger.
sparks.insight: The instinct in a debate is to pile on every reason you have. But an audience does not average your arguments, it notices the weakest one and uses it to dismiss the set. Presenting fewer and stronger points removes the easy target. The same logic applies to persuasion generally: the marginal argument you add is usually the one you believe least, and it hands the other side a cheap victory that costs you the ones you actually cared about.
sparks.why: Dilution effects are well documented in persuasion research: weak arguments reduce the impact of strong ones presented alongside them. Fewer points also leave the audience more room to generate their own reasons.
sparks.apply: Cut your next persuasive case to your two strongest points and delete the rest. Then ask a question that lets the other person supply the third themselves.

sparks.hook: People rarely change their minds because you pushed. They change because you asked.
sparks.insight: Direct contradiction produces defence, especially when the belief is tied to identity. The approach borrowed from motivational interviewing does something different: ask what would need to be true for the person to reconsider, listen for their own reasons to change, and reflect those back without adding pressure. It works because the argument is now theirs, and nobody has ever resisted their own reasoning. It is slower than confrontation and it is the only method that reliably moves anyone.
sparks.why: Motivational interviewing has good evidence in health behaviour change, and the mechanism is eliciting the person's own motivation rather than supplying yours. Confrontation typically strengthens the original position.
sparks.apply: In your next attempt to change someone's mind, ask what evidence would shift them and then stop talking. Do not answer your own question.

carousel.title: Drop the verdict
carousel.body: Go in without a conclusion you need them to reach today. People detect a script instantly, and detecting one converts a conversation into a defence.

carousel.title: Ask what would change it
carousel.body: Find out what evidence they would accept. Either you learn what to look for, or you both learn that the belief is not responsive to evidence at all.

carousel.title: Reflect their reasons back
carousel.body: Repeat the doubts they raise themselves, accurately and without adding pressure. Their own hesitations are the only arguments they cannot dismiss as yours.

carousel.title: Leave the exit open
carousel.body: Make it easy to move without losing face, and let it happen later and in private. Nobody concedes in the room when conceding looks like defeat.

sparks.hook: There are not two sides. There are usually about nine.
sparks.insight: Contested questions get compressed into two camps, and once that happens everyone defends a package they never assembled. Presenting an issue as genuinely complex, and showing disagreement among people on the same side, makes readers more open rather than less. Nuance does not read as weakness when it is specific: this part is well established, this part is contested, this part depends on a value judgement that evidence cannot settle. That structure gives someone a way to move without switching teams.
sparks.why: Binary framing increases polarisation, while presenting multiple perspectives and internal disagreement reduces defensiveness. Acknowledging complexity also raises perceived credibility rather than lowering it.
sparks.apply: Take a topic you argue about and write down three positions between the two obvious ones. Use one of them next time instead of your usual side.

sparks.hook: Best practice is a phrase that means stop improving this.
sparks.insight: Calling something a best practice implies the search is finished, and organisations then defend the method long after the conditions that justified it have gone. The alternative is to treat every established process as the current best guess with a review date attached. This is uncomfortable because stable procedures are genuinely valuable, and the point is not constant churn. It is that a process nobody is allowed to question will eventually be defended precisely when it needs replacing.
sparks.why: Escalation of commitment keeps organisations invested in approaches after the evidence turns, especially when the approach is tied to someone's reputation. Scheduled review makes reconsideration routine rather than an accusation.
sparks.apply: Pick one established process on your team and put a review date on it. On that date, ask what you would build if you were starting today.

sparks.hook: Your career plan was written by someone who no longer exists.
sparks.insight: People consistently underestimate how much they will change in the coming decade, while readily acknowledging how much they changed in the last one. So plans are made for a version of you that will be gone by the time they mature. The practical response is not to abandon planning but to schedule reconsideration: treat your direction like something with a check-up rather than a destination, and ask twice a year whether you would choose this path again from where you now stand.
sparks.why: The tendency to underestimate future personal change is a documented finding across age groups. Commitment to an identity chosen years earlier is a common source of persistence in work that no longer fits.
sparks.apply: Book two hours in your calendar twice a year to ask one question: knowing what I know now, would I choose this path again today?

sparks.hook: A team that cannot admit doubt will keep shipping its mistakes.
sparks.insight: In a group where uncertainty is read as incompetence, nobody reports the problem they half-noticed, and the organisation learns about it from a customer. Psychological safety is not comfort or niceness; groups with it argue more, not less. What it removes is the personal risk of speaking, so a junior person can say I think this is wrong without gambling their standing. The leader's part is small and specific: say what you were wrong about, in public, before asking anyone else to.
sparks.why: Psychological safety is associated with more error reporting and better learning, though it works only alongside accountability. Safety without standards produces comfort and no improvement at all.
sparks.apply: Open your next team meeting by describing something you got wrong recently and what you changed. Then ask what you might be wrong about now.

carousel.title: Go first, out loud
carousel.body: Name a real mistake of your own with a genuine cost attached. A trivial confession signals that only trivial admissions are actually welcome here.

carousel.title: Ask for the disagreement
carousel.body: Request the specific objection people are not saying, and wait through the silence. The first ten seconds of quiet is where most of these attempts fail.

carousel.title: Reward the messenger visibly
carousel.body: Thank whoever raises the problem in front of everyone, and act on it. Everyone in the room is watching what happens to the first person who speaks.

carousel.title: Keep the standards
carousel.body: Safety is not lowered expectations. Pair it with clear standards, or you get a pleasant team that reports everything and improves nothing.

actions: Write down two beliefs you hold strongly and, for each, the specific evidence that would change your mind. Then go and look for that evidence.
Run one conversation this month where your only goal is to understand the other side well enough to state their case to their satisfaction.
Put a review date on one established process at work and, on that date, ask what you would design from scratch today.
Open a team meeting by naming something you got wrong and what you changed, then ask the group what you might be wrong about now.
books.not_for_you_if: You want original research rather than a synthesis with stories, or you already practise structured disagreement and calibrated updating in your work.

verification.notes: First published February 2021 by Viking. Motivational interviewing and psychological safety are credited to their originating research traditions. All prose here is original.

books.title: Thinking in Bets
books.subtitle: Making Smarter Decisions When You Don't Have All the Facts
books.author: Annie Duke
books.why_it_matters: It gives you a working vocabulary for the thing that ruins most learning from experience: the gap between a decision and its outcome. A professional poker player is unusually well placed to explain how to keep score when luck is in every result.

crux.headline: Separate the quality of a decision from its result
crux.body: Every choice you make is a bet on an uncertain future, made with incomplete information. That means good decisions sometimes end badly and reckless ones sometimes pay. If you grade yourself on outcomes you will learn superstitions, because you will keep the habits that happened to work and drop the ones that were merely unlucky. Grade the process instead: what you knew, what you estimated, and how you handled the parts you could not know.

sparks.hook: A bad result does not prove a bad decision. Poker players have a word for the mistake.
sparks.insight: You sold the flat and prices rose, so you decide you were foolish. You drove home after two drinks and arrived safely, so nothing was wrong. In both cases you have graded the decision by the outcome, and in both cases you have learned something false. Outcomes are the product of your choice and a large amount of luck, and the two cannot be separated from a single case. The only honest question is whether the decision was reasonable given what could be known at the time.
sparks.why: Judging decisions by outcomes is unavoidable at first glance and corrosive over time. It teaches you to repeat lucky recklessness and abandon sound judgement that happened to fail once.
sparks.apply: Take one outcome you have been beating yourself up over and write down what you actually knew at the time. Grade the decision on that information only.

sparks.hook: You are betting on everything. You just do not say the odds out loud.
sparks.insight: Taking this job, trusting this supplier, marrying this person: each is a wager placed against a set of futures you cannot see. Calling it a bet sounds cynical until you notice what it fixes. It forces you to admit the alternatives you rejected, to attach a rough probability instead of a flat yes, and to accept that you can lose without having been stupid. Certainty is the thing you never actually had; the only choice is whether you price it or pretend.
sparks.why: Framing choices as bets makes hidden assumptions explicit and makes the decision auditable later. It also lowers the emotional cost of being wrong, since a lost bet does not imply a foolish one.
sparks.apply: Restate your next big decision as a bet: what you are wagering, against what alternative, and how confident you are as a number between zero and one hundred.

sparks.hook: You believe first and check afterwards, if you check at all.
sparks.insight: The intuitive model is that you hear a claim, evaluate it, then accept or reject it. Research on belief formation suggests the order is closer to the opposite: understanding a statement involves provisionally accepting it, and rejection is a separate effortful step that often never happens, especially when you are tired or busy. So the material you absorb while distracted does not sit in a holding pen awaiting review. It goes into the pile of things you know, and you will not remember where it came from.
sparks.why: Work by Gilbert and colleagues supports this two-stage account, with the vetting step being effortful and easily disrupted. It explains why repeated exposure to a false claim raises belief in it.
sparks.apply: Note the source and date of any claim you are about to rely on. If you cannot reconstruct where it came from, treat it as an assumption rather than a fact.

sparks.hook: Saying a number out loud is what makes you findable when you are wrong.
sparks.insight: There is a large difference between saying this will probably work and saying I am about seventy percent confident. The first cannot be wrong and so can never be improved. The second is a claim that can be tracked, argued with and scored across many predictions. It also changes the room: people correct a number far more readily than they contradict a confident assertion, because a number invites a counter-offer rather than a fight about who is right.
sparks.why: Calibration improves with explicit probability estimates and feedback, and it does not improve without them. Vague confidence produces no learnable record of how often you were actually correct.
sparks.apply: Attach a percentage to your next five predictions at work and write them down. In three months, check how often the seventy percent claims actually happened.

sparks.hook: Ask someone to bet on their claim and watch the certainty adjust.
sparks.insight: The question want to bet is not aggression. It is a request to move from expressing an attitude to making a claim with a price on it, and the shift is immediate. People reach for the caveats they left out, narrow the scope, and often discover they were repeating something they had never examined. You can run the same test on yourself. Deciding what odds you would actually accept is a far better probe of your belief than asking how sure you feel.
sparks.why: Attaching a cost to being wrong recruits scrutiny that free assertion never triggers. Prediction markets rely on the same mechanism, which is why they often outperform confident commentary.
sparks.apply: Next time you catch yourself asserting something strongly, ask what odds you would take on it. Adjust the assertion to match the odds, out loud.

sparks.hook: Find a group that rewards being accurate over being agreeable.
sparks.insight: Your normal circle is built for support: they take your side, agree the client was unreasonable, and confirm your account. That is valuable and it is useless for thinking. A truth-seeking group works on different rules, agreed in advance — everyone welcomes dissent, everyone shares information that hurts their own case, and nobody gets to know the outcome before assessing the decision. Membership costs something real, because the group will tell you that your good result came from luck.
sparks.why: Accountability to a group that values accuracy improves judgement, while accountability to a group that values loyalty degrades it. The rules have to be explicit or the group drifts back toward agreement.
sparks.apply: Recruit two or three people and agree three rules in writing: dissent is welcome, everyone reveals what weakens their own view, and outcomes come last.

carousel.title: Pick for disagreement
carousel.body: Choose people who will actually contradict you and who have something to lose from being wrong themselves. A group of admirers produces confidence and nothing else.

carousel.title: Agree the charter
carousel.body: Write the rules down before the first real disagreement arrives. Norms you never stated will not survive the moment someone's important decision is being questioned.

carousel.title: Present blind to outcome
carousel.body: Describe the decision and the information you had without saying how it turned out. The result contaminates every judgement of the reasoning that came before it.

carousel.title: Reward the unwelcome
carousel.body: Thank the person who found the flaw, visibly. A group only stays useful if the cost of raising an objection stays lower than the cost of staying quiet.

sparks.hook: Start from the failure and work backwards to find the cause you can prevent.
sparks.insight: Asking a team what could go wrong produces a polite list of nothing much. Telling them the project failed spectacularly and asking them to explain why produces something entirely different: specific, uncomfortable, actionable reasons that people were already carrying and had no permission to raise. The trick is that certainty removes the social cost. Nobody is now the pessimist predicting failure; they are historians explaining one, which is a far easier role to occupy in front of your boss.
sparks.why: The premortem technique, developed by Gary Klein, reliably surfaces more concrete risks than open-ended risk discussion, because hindsight framing makes specific causes easier to generate and safer to voice.
sparks.apply: Before your next launch, gather the team, state that it failed badly, and give everyone ten minutes alone to write the reasons before anyone speaks.

carousel.title: Declare it dead
carousel.body: Say the project has failed and the date it failed on. Speak in the past tense throughout, because the framing is what does the work here.

carousel.title: Write alone first
carousel.body: Give everyone silent time to list causes before discussion. The first person to speak otherwise sets the range of what everyone else considers sayable.

carousel.title: Collect without debate
carousel.body: Read every cause aloud with no defending or ranking yet. Arguing early teaches the room that raising an awkward risk means an argument they did not want.

carousel.title: Fix the cheap ones now
carousel.body: Pick the causes that are both plausible and cheap to prevent, and assign them today. A premortem that ends in a document changes nothing at all.

sparks.hook: Consult the version of you that has to live with this.
sparks.insight: In the moment, the present feels enormous and the future feels theoretical, so decisions get made by the loudest and most short-sighted part of you. A quick correction is to ask how you will feel about this in ten minutes, in ten months, and in ten years. Most of what feels urgent collapses under the second question. What survives all three is usually the thing that actually matters, and you have retrieved that answer without needing to be calmer than you currently are.
sparks.why: Temporal discounting makes immediate feelings dominate. Deliberately widening the time frame is a simple, testable correction, and the ten-ten-ten formulation comes from Suzy Welch.
sparks.apply: Before any decision made while angry or excited, write one line each on how this looks in ten minutes, ten months and ten years. Then decide.

sparks.hook: Decide the rules while you are calm, because you will not be later.
sparks.insight: There are states in which your judgement is reliably poor: on tilt after a loss, elated after a win, exhausted, humiliated. You cannot think your way out of those states while inside them, because the impairment applies to the thinking. What you can do is bind your future self in advance — a rule that you never renegotiate a contract after bad news, or that you stop trading after two losses, or that no email written after eleven at night gets sent before morning.
sparks.why: Precommitment works because it removes the decision from the moment of impairment. It fails when the rule is vague or when you leave yourself the authority to waive it in real time.
sparks.apply: Identify the state in which you make your worst calls and write one rule that takes the decision away from you in that state. Tell someone the rule.

sparks.hook: You attribute your wins to skill and your losses to the world. Everyone does.
sparks.insight: Sorting results into skill and luck is what makes experience educational, and your default sorting is corrupt: your good outcomes get filed under judgement, your bad ones under bad luck, and other people's get the reverse treatment. This is comfortable and it destroys the learning value of every result you ever get. The fix is not to become harsh with yourself. It is to make the sorting a deliberate, written, out-loud step rather than an automatic one that happens in the background.
sparks.why: Self-serving attribution is well replicated and largely unconscious. Making the attribution explicit, and having someone else check it, is what converts raw experience into calibrated judgement.
sparks.apply: After your next clear win and next clear loss, write two lists: what you controlled and what you did not. Have someone who was there mark them.

actions: Start a decision journal: the choice, the alternatives, your confidence as a percentage, and what you expect. Review it quarterly against what actually happened.
Set up a small truth-seeking group with three written rules, and bring one real decision to it before you know how it turned out.
Run a premortem on your current biggest project, with silent writing first and the cheap fixes assigned the same day.
Write one precommitment rule for the emotional state in which you make your worst decisions, and give it to someone who will hold you to it.
books.not_for_you_if: You want statistical decision theory rather than practical habits, or repeated poker examples do not hold your attention past the first few chapters.

verification.notes: First published 2018 by Portfolio. The premortem is credited to Gary Klein and the ten-ten-ten framing to Suzy Welch, both acknowledged as external sources. All prose here is original.

books.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
books.author: Daniel Kahneman
books.why_it_matters: It handed ordinary readers the vocabulary psychologists spent forty years building — anchoring, framing, loss aversion — and made the limits of your own judgement visible from the inside. Policy, medicine and finance now argue in its terms.

crux.headline: Your fast mind answers a question you never asked
crux.body: Most of your thinking is automatic, fluent and confident, and it finishes before the slow, effortful part of you has any say. That fast machinery is superb at pattern and hopeless at statistics, so when a hard question arrives it quietly swaps in an easier one and hands you the answer already labelled as certain. You cannot switch it off, and knowing about it barely helps in the moment. What helps is building the checks outside your own head.

sparks.hook: You have two minds, and only one of them is paying attention.
sparks.insight: One part of you answers instantly: it reads faces, finishes familiar phrases, judges a room in a second. The other part is slow, effortful and lazy — it does arithmetic, weighs evidence, and only shows up when called. The fast one runs almost all the time and hands its conclusions over already wrapped and labelled. So most of what feels like deciding is really a fast impression that the slow part agreed to endorse without ever checking the work.
sparks.why: The split is a working metaphor, not two brain regions. It earns its keep because it predicts when judgement fails: under time pressure, fatigue and fluency, the fast answer goes through unexamined.
sparks.apply: Before any decision that matters, name whether you are running on impression or on evidence. If it is impression, write down the one number you would need to check.

sparks.hook: Your mind builds a confident story out of whatever scraps it has.
sparks.insight: You do not feel the gaps in your information, and that is the problem. Given three facts, your mind assembles a coherent story from three facts and reports high confidence — the same confidence it would report with thirty. Coherence, not completeness, is what makes a story feel true. This is why a vivid anecdote beats a dull statistic, why first impressions harden so fast, and why the question that would change everything is so rarely asked: what would I need to know that I do not?
sparks.why: Confidence tracks how easily a story comes together, not how much evidence supports it. Since missing evidence is invisible by definition, nothing inside the feeling of certainty can warn you that it is thin.
sparks.apply: For your next important judgement, list three facts you do not have. Decide which one is cheap to get, then get it before you decide anything.

sparks.hook: Asked a hard question, you quietly answer an easier one instead.
sparks.insight: Hard questions have a way of getting replaced. Asked how satisfied you are with your life, you answer how your mood is right now. Asked whether an investment is wise, you answer whether you like the company. Asked whether a candidate can do the job, you answer whether they seem confident. The swap happens below awareness, so you never catch it happening — you just experience an answer arriving quickly to a question that should have been slow and hard.
sparks.why: Difficult questions have no ready answer but related easy ones do, and the fast system serves whatever is available. The tell is speed: an instant answer to a genuinely hard question is usually an answer to a different question.
sparks.apply: Write your hard question down word for word. Then write the answer you gave, and work out which question that answer actually belongs to.

sparks.hook: Losing a hundred hurts about twice as much as winning it feels good.
sparks.insight: Gains and losses are not weighed on the same scale. The pain of giving something up runs to roughly twice the pleasure of getting the same thing, which quietly bends most choices toward protecting whatever you already hold. It explains why people keep falling shares, stay in jobs they dislike, and demand far more to sell an object than they would ever pay to buy it. Where you happen to be standing does more work in your decisions than the outcomes themselves.
sparks.why: The two-to-one ratio is an average across lab and field studies, not a constant, and it shifts with stakes and culture. The asymmetry itself is one of the most reliably reproduced results in the field.
sparks.apply: Take a decision you keep postponing and rewrite both options as if you owned neither one. Ask which you would choose starting from zero today.

sparks.hook: A number you know is meaningless still drags your answer toward it.
sparks.insight: Show someone any figure before asking for an estimate and their estimate drifts toward it — even when the figure is obviously irrelevant, even when they have been warned, even when they are experts in the thing being estimated. Your mind treats the first number as a place to start and adjusts outward from there, and it always stops adjusting too early. Every asking price, opening offer and suggested donation amount is doing this work on you before the conversation begins.
sparks.why: Anchoring survives explicit warnings and professional expertise, which is what makes it more than a party trick. It is among the better-replicated effects in judgement research, though the size of the pull varies by task.
sparks.apply: Before you see a price or an offer, write your own number down and set it aside. Compare afterwards, and negotiate from your figure rather than theirs.

sparks.hook: You judge how common something is by how easily it comes to mind.
sparks.insight: Risk feels large when examples are easy to recall. Plane crashes, shark attacks and stranger abductions are vivid, heavily reported and rare; heart disease, bad driving and falls at home are dull, unreported and common. Because ease of recall is doing the estimating, anything covered intensively gets overweighted and anything quiet gets ignored entirely. Your private sense of what is dangerous is partly just a record of what you have recently been shown.
sparks.why: Recall ease is a fast proxy for frequency and works well enough in a small, stable world. It fails badly once media, memory and emotion decide which examples ever reach you.
sparks.apply: Name a risk you worry about. Look up its actual base rate once, then decide whether your precautions match the number rather than the feeling.

sparks.hook: A detailed story feels more likely than a vague one. It never is.
sparks.insight: Add details to a description and it becomes more believable and less probable at the same time. A specific portrait — the quiet reader who volunteers and cycles to work — matches a type you recognise, and matching is what your fast mind actually measures. But every extra condition narrows the set of people the description can possibly fit. Probability shrinks as the story grows richer while plausibility grows, and when those two pull apart, plausibility usually wins.
sparks.why: Judging by resemblance ignores how many such cases exist in the world at all. The conjunction effect is robust, though it shrinks noticeably when questions are posed in frequencies rather than percentages.
sparks.apply: For your next prediction, write the base rate first and the story second. Let the story move you off the base rate only a little, and say why.

carousel.title: Start with the base rate
carousel.body: Ask how often this outcome happens across all similar cases, before you look at anything specific about yours. That number is your honest starting point.

carousel.title: Score the resemblance
carousel.body: Now ask how well your case matches the picture in your head. Notice that this is a similarity judgement, not a probability, and that the two are different things.

carousel.title: Move a little, not a lot
carousel.body: Let the specifics shift your estimate away from the base rate, but only as far as your evidence is genuinely diagnostic. Most evidence is weaker than it feels.

carousel.title: Distrust extra detail
carousel.body: Every added condition makes the story better and the odds worse. If a forecast got more persuasive as it got more specific, lower your number rather than raising it.

sparks.hook: Praise looks like it backfires. Criticism looks like it works. Both are illusions.
sparks.insight: Extreme performances tend to be followed by ordinary ones, for no reason except chance. So the trainee who flew brilliantly and was praised does worse next time, and the one who flew badly and was shouted at does better — and the instructor learns a lesson about human nature that the data never taught. Any time you intervene right after an unusually bad result, some of the improvement that follows is just the world drifting back toward its average, and you will take the credit.
sparks.why: Wherever outcomes contain luck, extremes overstate ability and the next measurement moves toward the middle. This manufactures convincing but false evidence about what works, in coaching, medicine and management alike.
