carousel.body: Given where technology, demographics and buying behaviour are heading, what should you be doing in five years? Write it as a description, not as a target number.

carousel.title: Ask what it should not be
carousel.body: Name the activities that will no longer belong. This is the question everyone skips, and it is the only one that releases the resources the new answer requires.

carousel.title: Set the abandonment date
carousel.body: Attach a real date to stopping one thing. Without a date, abandonment becomes something the organisation intends to do after the current busy period, which never ends.

sparks.hook: People manage themselves better when they set the targets they are judged on.
sparks.insight: The proposal was that each manager should work out what their unit must contribute to the wider goals, agree it upward, and then be measured against their own stated commitment. The self-control part is the point. Someone who has defined their own target and can see their own results does not need supervision to correct course, because they get the feedback directly. It replaces control from above with control by the person doing the work, which is the only kind that operates fast enough to matter.
sparks.why: The idea was widely distorted into cascading numeric quotas imposed from the top, which is close to the opposite of what was proposed and which quality thinkers criticised heavily for driving people to hit numbers by any available means.
sparks.apply: Ask each direct report to write what their team should be judged on next quarter, negotiate rather than dictate it, and give them the data to see it.

sparks.hook: Every decision is about the future, which is why none of them are safe.
sparks.insight: A manager decides now and finds out later, always with incomplete information and always about circumstances that have not happened yet. Waiting for certainty is not a cautious strategy but a decision to let events choose for you. What makes the risk manageable is being explicit about the time dimension: how long until this commitment pays back, how long until it can be reversed, what the world would have to look like for it to be right. Those questions turn a gamble into a bet with known terms.
sparks.why: Naming the time horizon prevents the common error of judging a long commitment by short-term results, which is how sound investments get cancelled halfway through.
sparks.apply: For your next significant commitment, write the payback horizon and the point at which you could still reverse it, and share both with your team.

sparks.hook: Structure follows strategy, and most reorganisations get the order backwards.
sparks.insight: Organisational design is not a matter of taste or of copying whoever is admired this year. It follows from what the business has decided to do and what activities are genuinely critical to that. Reorganising first and hoping strategy emerges from the new boxes is common and produces years of disruption for nothing. Where possible, the aim is units small enough to see their own results, with real responsibility for a market, because that is what allows people to manage themselves rather than waiting for instruction.
sparks.why: The sequence matters because structure encodes priorities. A reorganisation done without a strategy simply redistributes power and then forces the strategy to fit the new arrangement.
sparks.apply: Before your next reorganisation, write the strategy it serves on one page. If you cannot, postpone the reorganisation rather than the strategy.

sparks.hook: Treat people as a cost and you will get exactly the output a cost provides.
sparks.insight: The insistence was that the people doing the work are a resource capable of judgement and improvement rather than a variable expense to be minimised. That has practical consequences: the person closest to a process usually knows most about it, so their knowledge should be sought rather than overridden, and responsibility should sit as close to the work as possible. It was a genuinely unpopular position when much of industry still treated labour as interchangeable, and it anticipated most of what later became standard practice.
sparks.why: Later evidence on autonomy and on frontline knowledge broadly supports the direction. The counterweight is that responsibility without matching authority or information produces stress rather than performance.
sparks.apply: Ask the people closest to your worst process what they would change, then implement one of their suggestions without modifying it.

sparks.hook: Do the job well and something else will still deteriorate. Plan for it.
sparks.insight: Managing means holding several obligations that pull in different directions: the results this year, the capacity to produce results in ten years, and the effect of the enterprise on the society it operates in. None can be sacrificed indefinitely without the others failing, and no formula resolves the tension. The practical response is to keep all three visible in the same conversation, because whichever one is absent from the discussion is the one being quietly funded by the others.
sparks.why: Making the trade-offs explicit does not resolve them, but it prevents the most common failure, which is optimising the measurable short-term obligation because it is the only one on the dashboard.
sparks.apply: Add one long-horizon measure and one external-impact measure to your regular review, next to the financial ones, and discuss all three together.

carousel.title: Name the immediate result
carousel.body: What the enterprise must deliver in the current period to remain viable. This is the obligation that will always be represented, because it is the easiest to count.

carousel.title: Name the future capacity
carousel.body: What must be built now to still be in business in a decade: people, capability, research, relationships. It has no deadline, which is why it is the first thing cut.

carousel.title: Name the external effect
carousel.body: The consequences of your operations for the people and communities around them. Ignoring it invites regulation that will be shaped by people who dislike you.

carousel.title: Review the three together
carousel.body: Put all three in the same meeting with the same seriousness. Whichever is absent from the discussion is being financed silently by the other two.

sparks.hook: It is enormous, occasionally repetitive, and still the reference nobody replaced.
sparks.insight: Two honest caveats. It is a very long book written for a world of large, mostly national, mostly manufacturing corporations, and the examples reflect that. And its most famous proposal was widely implemented as a top-down numbers regime that produced the opposite of what was intended, which is a fair criticism of how the idea travels even if not of the idea itself. What survives is the framing: that management is a genuine discipline with obligations, not a set of techniques for extracting more work from people.
sparks.why: The reasoning is observational and synthetic rather than empirical, so specific prescriptions should be tested rather than adopted. The framing has outlasted almost every management fashion published since.
sparks.apply: Read one section rather than the whole book, starting with the chapters on what your business is, and apply the questions before reading further.

actions: Write one paragraph on what your business is from the customer's side and one on what it should be in five years, then name what has to be abandoned.
Ask ten customers what they would lose if you disappeared, and compare their answers against how your company describes itself.
Ask each direct report to propose what their team should be judged on next quarter, negotiate it rather than dictating it, and give them the data.
Add a long-horizon measure and an external-impact measure to your regular review so they are discussed alongside the financial numbers.
books.not_for_you_if: You want something short and practical, or you need guidance for a small modern company rather than a treatise on the large corporation.

verification.notes: First published 1973 by Harper & Row; a revised edition with Joseph A. Maciariello appeared in 2008. Management by objectives was widely implemented as top-down quota setting and criticised on that basis. All prose here is original.

books.title: Measure What Matters
books.subtitle: How Google, Bono, and the Gates Foundation Rock the World with OKRs
books.author: John Doerr
books.why_it_matters: It took a goal-setting method Andy Grove built at Intel and Doerr carried into a very young Google, and wrote it down properly. Whatever your view of the acronym, the underlying discipline of separating what from how-we-know is genuinely useful.

crux.headline: Say what you want, then say how you will know
crux.body: An objective is the thing you are trying to achieve, stated in plain language a new joiner would understand. Key results are the small number of measurable outcomes that would prove you achieved it. Keep them few, make them public, review them often, and keep them away from anyone's bonus. The method's value is not the format. It is the argument the format forces about what actually counts as success.

sparks.hook: If you cannot measure it, it is not a key result. It is a hope.
sparks.insight: The whole discipline sits on one separation. The objective is qualitative and can be inspiring: it says where you are going and why anyone should care. The key results are numeric and unforgiving: they say what will be true at the end if you got there. Most goal-setting fails because the two are mashed together into a sentence that sounds ambitious and cannot be scored. If two reasonable people can disagree at the end about whether you hit it, you wrote an objective and forgot the results.
sparks.why: Ambiguity in goals gets resolved in whoever's favour is most senior. A number agreed in advance removes that negotiation and makes the quarterly review a fact-check rather than a debate.
sparks.apply: Take your team's current goals and rewrite each as one sentence of intent plus three numbers. Delete any goal where you cannot find the numbers.

carousel.title: Write the objective plainly
carousel.body: One sentence, no jargon, describing what will be different. If a new hire cannot repeat it back after one reading, it is a slogan rather than a direction.

carousel.title: Add outcomes, not activities
carousel.body: Shipping a feature is an activity. The share of customers who use it weekly is an outcome. Activities can be completed while nothing changes, which is how teams stay busy and flat.

carousel.title: Cap it at three or four
carousel.body: More than four key results means the objective has not been thought through. The cap forces the argument about which measures genuinely prove success and which are comfort.

carousel.title: Set the scoring rule now
carousel.body: Agree in advance what counts as done, partly done and missed. Deciding this at the end of the quarter reliably produces generous marking and no learning.

sparks.hook: The whole point of a goal is the things you refuse to do because of it.
sparks.insight: Teams write ten objectives because everything on the list matters to someone and cutting any of them means telling a colleague no. But a list of ten priorities allocates nothing, since the team will simply do whatever is loudest each week. Committing to three forces the organisation to make the trade-offs at the start, in a room, with everyone present, instead of leaving them to be settled by whoever escalates hardest in week six. The pain of choosing is the product, not a side effect.
sparks.why: Attention is the scarce resource in most organisations, not money or headcount. A goal list that does not deselect anything leaves the real allocation to interruption and seniority.
sparks.apply: Cut your team's objective list to three for the coming quarter and publish the list of things you have explicitly decided not to do.

sparks.hook: Goals kept private are goals nobody can help you with.
sparks.insight: Making everyone's goals visible across the company, including the chief executive's, changes behaviour more than the goals themselves do. Teams discover that two of them are building the same thing. A dependency that would have surfaced as a missed deadline in month three surfaces in week one instead. And the social effect is real: people write more careful goals when colleagues will read them, and they are more likely to finish something they said out loud. The cost is that vagueness becomes visible, which is why some leaders resist it.
sparks.why: Cross-team dependencies are the main cause of missed quarters in larger organisations, and they are invisible in a system where each group reports only upwards.
sparks.apply: Publish every team's objectives in one document this quarter, including yours, and give everyone read access with no approval step.

sparks.hook: Goals handed down from the top arrive without any owner attached.
sparks.insight: A purely cascading system, where each level decomposes its manager's goals, is efficient on paper and produces compliance rather than commitment. The teams closest to customers and code usually know about opportunities the executive layer cannot see, and those never enter the plan. A healthier pattern is that a meaningful share of goals originate from the bottom and are negotiated upwards. The leadership job then becomes checking coherence rather than authoring everything, which is also the only version that scales.
sparks.why: Ownership predicts follow-through far better than clarity does. People defend goals they helped write and merely report on goals they were assigned.
sparks.apply: Ask each team to propose half of their own objectives before you share yours, then reconcile the two lists together in one session.

sparks.hook: Attach a bonus to a goal and you have bought yourself sandbagging.
sparks.insight: The moment key results determine pay, everyone involved becomes an expert at setting targets they will certainly hit. Ambition disappears, honest mid-quarter reporting disappears with it, and the system quietly converts into a negotiation about next year's compensation. Keeping goals separate from pay is the most frequently skipped rule and the one whose absence does the most damage, because the failure looks like everyone succeeding. Performance and pay still need to be linked; they should just be linked through judgement rather than through the goal sheet.
sparks.why: Any measure used to allocate money becomes a target people manage rather than a signal you can read. The distortion is well documented across incentive schemes of every kind.
sparks.apply: Remove goal scores from your next compensation cycle and tell the team explicitly that missing an ambitious target will not cost them money.

sparks.hook: Two kinds of goal, and mixing them up breaks both.
sparks.insight: Some commitments have to land: the release date, the compliance deadline, the revenue the plan depends on. Those should be sized so a competent team hits them and treated as failures when missed. Others exist to change what people think is possible, and are supposed to be missed most of the time. Google's convention has been to treat roughly seventy percent attainment on those as a good result. Running both types under one scoring rule means either your commitments become soft or your ambitions become timid.
sparks.why: The two goal types need opposite responses to a miss. Without the label, teams average the two behaviours and end up with goals that are neither reliable nor ambitious.
sparks.apply: Label every objective as committed or aspirational before the quarter starts, and score the two groups by different rules at the end.

sparks.hook: You cannot get ten times better by working ten percent harder.
sparks.insight: A target far beyond the current trend does something a modest one cannot: it rules out the obvious approach. If the goal is a small improvement, the team optimises what already exists. If the goal is a different order of magnitude, incremental work is visibly pointless and someone has to propose a different method. That is the real mechanism, and it explains why stretch goals sometimes produce breakthroughs. It also explains why they fail when the team is given the number without the time, the budget or the permission to change approach.
sparks.why: Research on goal setting has warned that aggressive targets combined with pressure and consequences can drive shortcuts and unethical behaviour. Stretch goals need psychological safety and slack, or they produce fabrication instead of invention.
sparks.apply: Pick one goal, restate it at ten times the current scale, and spend an hour asking only what approach could possibly reach it.

sparks.hook: A goal you check once a quarter is a goal you check once.
sparks.insight: Goals set in January and reviewed in December are decoration, because the information that would have let you change course arrived in March. The cadence is what makes the system work: a short weekly look at the numbers, a proper mid-cycle conversation about whether the goal is still the right one, and a scored review at the end. Goals should be allowed to change when reality does, as long as the change is explicit and recorded rather than quietly forgotten when nobody hits them.
sparks.why: Regular check-ins convert goals from a commitment device into a feedback loop. The mid-cycle review matters most because it is the last point at which changing course is still cheap.
sparks.apply: Put a fifteen-minute goal check on your weekly team agenda and a full mid-quarter review in the calendar before the quarter begins.

carousel.title: Set with argument
carousel.body: Spend real time at the start disagreeing about which measures prove success. This is the only cheap moment to discover that two people meant different things by the same objective.

carousel.title: Check in weekly
carousel.body: A short look at the numbers and a confidence rating from each owner. Confidence dropping is the earliest signal you get, and it arrives weeks before the metric moves.

carousel.title: Re-decide at the midpoint
carousel.body: Ask whether each goal is still worth pursuing. Retiring a goal on purpose is a healthy outcome; discovering in week twelve that everyone abandoned it in week four is not.

carousel.title: Score, then ask why
carousel.body: Grade honestly and spend the longer half of the meeting on what the score taught you about your estimates, your capacity and your assumptions.

sparks.hook: Annual reviews are a summary of a year nobody can change any more.
sparks.insight: A once-a-year rating asks a manager to compress twelve months into a number, most of which they cannot remember accurately, and delivers it at the exact moment nothing can be done differently. The alternative is a rhythm rather than an event: frequent short conversations about direction, feedback given close to the work while it is still specific, and recognition that is public and tied to something concrete. It costs more manager time in total and far less anxiety, and the information reaches people while it is still actionable.
sparks.why: Feedback delivered months late loses its link to specific behaviour and gets heard as a verdict on the person. Proximity to the event is what makes it usable rather than threatening.
sparks.apply: Replace one annual review conversation with monthly thirty-minute check-ins, and give one specific piece of public recognition each week.

sparks.hook: The method is real. The evidence for it is a set of success stories.
sparks.insight: The case made here rests on organisations that already worked: a semiconductor company defending its business, a search engine on its way to dominance, a large foundation, a rock star's advocacy group. None of that shows the goal system caused the success, and plenty of companies have adopted the same acronym and produced nothing but a quarterly spreadsheet ritual. What survives scrutiny is narrower and still worth having: writing goals down, making them measurable, publishing them, and reviewing them on a rhythm.
sparks.why: The book is built from case studies of winners, so it carries obvious survivorship bias. Treat the mechanism as a sensible operating habit rather than as a proven cause of company performance.
sparks.apply: Run the system for two quarters, then ask your team whether it changed any decision. If the honest answer is no, simplify it rather than adding tooling.

actions: Write three objectives for the coming quarter, each with no more than four measurable key results, and publish them where the whole company can read them.
Label each objective as committed or aspirational and agree different scoring rules for the two groups before the quarter starts.
Remove goal scores from any pay or bonus decision this cycle, and say so explicitly to the team so they stop sandbagging targets.
Book a mid-quarter review now whose only purpose is deciding which goals to keep, change or kill while there is still time to act.
books.not_for_you_if: You already run a disciplined goal system, or you dislike books built from admiring case studies of famous organisations.

verification.notes: Published 2018 by Portfolio. Doerr learned the system from Andy Grove at Intel and introduced it to Google in 1999 as an early investor. All prose original.

books.title: No Rules Rules
books.subtitle: Netflix and the Culture of Reinvention
books.author: Reed Hastings and Erin Meyer
books.why_it_matters: It is the most detailed account of how one unusually successful company deliberately built its culture — high pay, few controls, blunt feedback. It made talent density and direct candour mainstream vocabulary in technology management.

crux.headline: Remove controls only after you raise talent density
crux.body: Rules exist to stop a small number of people doing damage, and they cost everyone else speed. The sequence matters more than the philosophy: concentrate excellent people first, then build a habit of blunt honest feedback so mistakes surface early, and only then remove the approvals, policies and controls. Do it in any other order and you get expensive chaos, which is what most companies copying the model actually produce.

sparks.hook: One weak performer costs more than the salary you saved on them.
sparks.insight: The argument is that a single weak person on a small team drags down everyone around them: colleagues spend time compensating, standards slip, and the best people quietly conclude that excellence is not really required here. That is why the recommended move is to pay at the top of the market for fewer, stronger people rather than filling more seats at the average rate. The cost of the policy is real and so is the discomfort, but the logic is about the team's ceiling.
sparks.why: This is an internal account by the company's own co-founder, so it carries obvious selection bias. Netflix's success has many causes — timing, capital, a licensing window — and the culture is not cleanly separable from any of them.
sparks.apply: Ask honestly which of your team you would fight to keep if they resigned tomorrow. The answer tells you where your standards actually sit.

sparks.hook: Being kind and being honest are not opposites. Being vague is the enemy.
sparks.insight: Most organisations run on polite silence: people notice problems, say nothing, and complain sideways. The alternative here is a formal expectation that feedback is given directly, promptly and with the intent to help rather than to score points. It is uncomfortable, and it only works when it runs upward as well as downward — the moment feedback flows only from senior to junior, the practice becomes a licence for rudeness with a corporate name attached to it.
sparks.why: Direct feedback improves performance when trust and psychological safety are already present, and damages it when they are not. Companies that import the candour without the safety reliably get the second outcome.
sparks.apply: Ask one person you manage for a specific criticism of your own behaviour, listen without defending yourself, and thank them for it in front of others.

sparks.hook: Say it to the person, not about them.
sparks.insight: A simple rule changes an office more than any values poster: if you would say it about someone in the corridor, you owe it to them directly. Making that the expected behaviour removes most of the energy that goes into politics, because there is nowhere for the sideways conversation to go. The hard part is not the rule, it is enforcing it upward, and leaders visibly taking criticism without punishing the person who offered it.
sparks.why: Norms of directness only survive if the first few instances go well. Senior people absorbing criticism publicly is the cheapest available demonstration that the rule is real rather than aspirational.
sparks.apply: Introduce one rule this month: any criticism must be given to the person within a week or dropped entirely. Model it yourself first.

carousel.title: Aim to assist
carousel.body: Give feedback only when you want the other person to do better, not when you want to be right. The distinction is visible to everyone, including the recipient.

carousel.title: Make it actionable
carousel.body: Name the specific behaviour and what to do differently. Feedback about someone's character cannot be acted on and simply lands as an attack.

carousel.title: Receive it visibly
carousel.body: Thank people who criticise you, in public, and act on something. The team is watching what happens to the first person brave enough to speak up.

carousel.title: Let them decide
carousel.body: The recipient chooses whether to act. Compulsory acceptance turns feedback into instruction, and people stop offering anything genuinely risky.

sparks.hook: Most expense policies cost more to enforce than they ever save.
sparks.insight: A detailed approval process consumes management time, slows decisions, and signals distrust to the many people who were never going to abuse it. Replacing it with a short principle — act in the company's interest — plus visible spending and consequences for abuse can be cheaper overall. It is not free: some money will be wasted, some people will take advantage, and you have to be willing to remove them rather than write a new rule for everybody else.
sparks.why: The trade-off is genuine but the accounting is rarely done honestly. This works best in high-margin businesses hiring senior people, and it translates poorly to thin-margin operations with large frontline workforces.
sparks.apply: Pick one approval step, calculate the management hours it consumes yearly, and compare that with the losses it actually prevented last year.

sparks.hook: Context beats control, but only if the context is genuinely shared.
sparks.insight: Telling people to use judgement without giving them the information that shaped yours produces bad decisions and then blame. The substitute for approval processes is unusual transparency: strategy, numbers, reasoning and mistakes shared far more widely than is comfortable. The manager's job shifts from approving decisions to making sure everyone has enough context to make them well, which is more work up front and considerably less work later on.
sparks.why: Decentralised decisions are only as good as the information available locally. Most delegation failures are information failures rather than judgement failures, though they get diagnosed as the latter.
sparks.apply: Before your next delegation, write down everything you would consider when deciding, and hand that over instead of handing over your decision.

sparks.hook: Netflix does not want to be a family, and it says so out loud.
sparks.insight: The claim is that a company is closer to a sports team than a family: everyone in a role is expected to be excellent at it, and someone who is no longer the strongest person available for that seat is let go with generous severance. It is brutally honest compared with employers who use family language and make people redundant anyway. It also produces genuine anxiety, and the account underplays how much of that anxiety falls on people with less bargaining power.
sparks.why: The honesty is a real advantage over the pretence most firms maintain. But security has independent value to people, and the model transfers badly to markets where employees cannot easily find another well-paid job.
sparks.apply: If you use family language about your team, either stop using it or make your actual severance and dismissal practice match what it implies.

sparks.hook: Unlimited holiday means nothing unless leaders visibly take it.
sparks.insight: Removing the vacation policy sounds generous and often functions as a cut, because people take less time off when there is no defined entitlement and no signal about what is acceptable. The thing that makes it work is behaviour at the top: senior people taking long, visible breaks and talking openly about them. Without that, employees read the ambiguity conservatively and the company quietly saves money on rest that its staff actually needed.
sparks.why: Evidence on unlimited leave is mixed, with several studies and company reports finding lower average usage than under fixed allowances. Ambiguity favours the more anxious party, which is usually the employee.
sparks.apply: If you offer open leave, publish how many days each leader took last year and set a stated minimum that people are expected to use.

sparks.hook: Pay the top of the market, then stop paying for performance.
sparks.insight: The approach here separates two things most firms fuse: how much someone is worth in the labour market, and how they did last quarter. People are paid at the top of their market rate and asked to check that rate regularly, with no bonuses attached to targets. The reasoning is that bonuses buy focus on the target rather than on the right thing, and that a person worrying about their number is not doing their best creative work.
sparks.why: There is real evidence that contingent bonuses narrow attention and can hurt performance on complex, non-routine tasks. It is much less applicable to sales or repetitive work, where targeted incentives generally do help.
sparks.apply: For one senior role, replace the variable bonus with a higher fixed salary at the top of market and compare output and retention over a year.

sparks.hook: Freedom without excellence is just an unsupervised mess.
sparks.insight: The order of operations is the part most imitators get wrong. Companies read about the freedom and remove controls while their talent density and feedback habits are unchanged, then discover that some people make expensive decisions with no oversight and nobody says anything about it. Each element only works because the others are already in place. Removing rules is the last step, not the first, and it should be reversed if the conditions stop holding.
sparks.why: The model is a system with dependencies rather than a menu of ideas. Partial adoption is common and predictably produces the costs of low control without the benefits of high talent density.
sparks.apply: Before removing any control, ask whether you would be comfortable with the weakest person in that team making the decision entirely alone.

carousel.title: Raise talent density
carousel.body: Concentrate strong people first, paying more for fewer of them. Every later step assumes the average person can be trusted with an unsupervised decision.

carousel.title: Build candour
carousel.body: Make direct feedback normal and safe, starting with leaders taking it. Without this, removing controls means mistakes stay hidden until they are expensive.

carousel.title: Remove controls slowly
carousel.body: Take away one approval at a time and watch what happens. Reinstate anything that fails rather than defending the philosophy that removed it.

carousel.title: Share the context
carousel.body: Give people the information and reasoning they need to decide well. Freedom without context produces confident decisions made on partial facts.

sparks.hook: A culture that suits California does not automatically travel.
sparks.insight: One genuinely useful contribution here is that it takes seriously what happened when the model met other countries: directness that reads as helpful in one place reads as humiliating in another, and comfort with dissent varies enormously by national norm. The response was not to abandon the culture but to adapt how it is delivered — more explicit framing, more prompting, more time. Any company exporting a culture built in one country faces the same translation problem.
sparks.why: Erin Meyer's research on cultural difference in feedback and hierarchy is the strongest independent element in the book, and it is the section least likely to be self-serving about Netflix itself.
sparks.apply: Ask your teams outside headquarters which of your cultural norms feel awkward locally, then change the delivery rather than the standard.

actions: Ask yourself which team members you would fight to keep if they resigned, then decide what you will do about everyone who is not on that list.
Ask one direct report for a specific criticism of your behaviour, act on part of it, and tell the team what you changed and who prompted it.
Pick one approval process, estimate the management hours it consumes each year, and compare that with the losses it demonstrably prevented.
Before removing any control, check that you would trust the weakest person in that team to decide alone, and fix that first if you would not.
books.not_for_you_if: You want an independent analysis rather than a company's account of itself, or you run a thin-margin business where paying top of market for everyone is impossible.

verification.notes: Published 2020 by Penguin. Co-authored by Netflix's own co-founder, so it is a company account with clear selection bias; Erin Meyer's cross-cultural research is the more independent element. All prose here is original.

books.title: Obviously Awesome
books.subtitle: How to Nail Product Positioning so Customers Get It, Buy It, Love It
books.author: April Dunford
books.why_it_matters: It is the first genuinely practical method for positioning rather than a philosophy of it — a repeatable sequence a team can run in a week. It became the default reference for product marketers working in business software.

crux.headline: Positioning is context, and context is chosen
crux.body: Customers decide what your product is by deciding what it is like. If you leave that comparison to them they will use the wrong one, and every strength you have will be judged against the wrong standard. So choose the context deliberately: the alternatives you want to be measured against, the capabilities only you have, the value those create, and the customers who care about that value most. Then set the market frame that makes all of it obvious.

sparks.hook: Customers judge you against whatever they already think you are.
sparks.insight: When someone meets a new product they immediately file it under something familiar, and everything after that is judged by that category's rules. If they file your workflow tool under project management, they will ask about Gantt charts and conclude you are weak. The features did not change; the comparison did. Positioning is the work of choosing that comparison deliberately, before the customer picks a worse one on your behalf.
sparks.why: People evaluate unfamiliar things by analogy to familiar ones, so the reference category quietly sets the criteria. Winning inside the wrong category is much harder than moving to a better one.
sparks.apply: Ask five recent prospects what they thought you were before the demo. If most named a category you lose in, your framing is the problem.

sparks.hook: Positioning is a sequence you can run, not a slogan you wait for.
sparks.insight: Most teams treat positioning as a creative act and stall waiting for the right phrase. It is closer to an audit. List what customers would genuinely use instead of you, find the things you can do that those alternatives cannot, translate each into value a buyer cares about, identify who cares most, and only then choose the market frame that makes the whole picture obvious. The tagline is the last five minutes of the work, not the first.
sparks.why: Working from real alternatives grounds the exercise in evidence rather than aspiration. Teams that start from the message tend to produce claims their own product cannot actually support.
sparks.apply: Book a two-hour session with sales and product to list what customers actually do instead of buying you, and start the sequence from that list.

carousel.title: List real alternatives
carousel.body: Write what a customer would do if you did not exist, including doing nothing and using a spreadsheet. The competitors named in your pitch deck are often not the real answer.

carousel.title: Find what only you do
carousel.body: Identify capabilities the alternatives genuinely lack. Features everyone has are table stakes and belong nowhere near your positioning.

carousel.title: Turn features into value
carousel.body: State what each unique capability lets a customer achieve. If you cannot name the outcome, the capability is not worth positioning around at all.

carousel.title: Find who cares most
carousel.body: Describe the customers for whom that value is urgent. The best segment is defined by the situation people are in, not by their company size.

carousel.title: Choose the frame
carousel.body: Pick the market context that makes your strengths obvious to that segment, then check that a salesperson can explain it inside one call.

sparks.hook: Your real competitor is often a spreadsheet and doing nothing.
sparks.insight: Sales decks list rival vendors, but the honest alternative for most buyers is inaction, a manual workaround, or a tool they already pay for. Positioning against a vendor you rarely lose to wastes your best arguments. Positioning against the status quo forces a different and much more useful conversation about why change is worth the disruption, which is the question the buyer is actually asking their colleagues behind closed doors.
sparks.why: Most losses in business software are to no decision rather than to a named competitor. A pitch built for a head-to-head comparison has nothing to say to a buyer choosing whether to bother at all.
sparks.apply: Review your last twenty lost deals and record what the customer actually did instead. Rewrite your pitch against the most common answer.

sparks.hook: A feature nobody else has is worth nothing until you name what it gives them.
sparks.insight: Teams love their differentiators and describe them as capabilities, which forces the buyer to do the translation. Most will not bother. The chain has to be completed for them: this thing we uniquely do, which means you can achieve this, which matters because of this pressure you are already under. Any unique capability that cannot survive that chain should come out of the pitch, however proud the engineering team happens to be of it.
sparks.why: Buyers are not paid to interpret vendor feature lists, and any translation you leave undone gets done badly or not at all. The chain also exposes differentiators that produce no value worth paying for.
sparks.apply: For every unique feature in your deck, write the sentence that ends in a business outcome a buyer would defend to their boss. Cut any that fail.

carousel.title: Name the capability
carousel.body: State plainly what your product does that the real alternatives cannot. Keep it factual and checkable; anything a competitor could also claim does not belong here.

carousel.title: Say what it enables
carousel.body: Translate the capability into something the customer can now do or stop doing. This is the step teams skip, assuming buyers will make the leap themselves.

carousel.title: Tie it to a pressure
carousel.body: Connect that ability to a problem the buyer is already accountable for. Value with no existing pressure behind it produces interest but never budget.

carousel.title: Cut what fails
carousel.body: Any differentiator that cannot complete all three steps comes out of the pitch. Keeping it dilutes the ones that can, and buyers remember only a couple anyway.

sparks.hook: The best segment is defined by a situation, not by a company size.
sparks.insight: Segments described as mid-market manufacturers tell you almost nothing about why someone buys. What predicts urgency is the situation: they just lost a major client, they are being audited, a key person left, they are opening a second site. Situations create deadlines and budget in a way that demographics never do. Finding the two or three trigger situations where your strengths matter most is usually a bigger revenue change than any messaging work.
sparks.why: Situational triggers correlate with buying intent far more strongly than firmographics, which is why intent-based targeting outperforms demographic targeting whenever both are available.
sparks.apply: Interview your last ten new customers about what happened in the month before they started looking, and target the two most common triggers.

sparks.hook: Change the market you are compared in and every objection changes with it.
sparks.insight: You can win a fight or you can change the venue. Framing a product as a cheaper version of an established category invites that category's whole comparison checklist, most of which you will fail. Framing it as the leading example of a narrower or newer category makes different questions relevant, ones your product answers well. This is legitimate only if the new frame means something to buyers, and pure fantasy if the category exists only in your own materials.
sparks.why: The reference class sets the evaluation criteria, so changing the class changes what counts as a weakness. The constraint is real buyer recognition, which is why inventing a category is expensive and often fails.
sparks.apply: Write down the market frame currently used in your pitch and one alternative, then test both on five prospects and compare the questions you get back.

sparks.hook: If sales cannot explain it on a call, it is not positioning.
sparks.insight: Positioning that lives in a document is worthless. The test is whether a salesperson can deliver it in a live conversation, under interruption, and whether the buyer's questions get easier afterwards. That is why the exercise should include the people who face customers rather than being handed to them as an output. If the new framing makes calls harder, the framing is wrong, no matter how elegant it looked in the workshop.
sparks.why: Front-line delivery is where positioning either works or does not, and the people delivering it hear the real objections. Excluding them produces internally consistent messaging that dies on contact.
sparks.apply: Have a salesperson deliver the new positioning cold on three real calls this week, then debrief on which questions got easier and which got worse.

sparks.hook: Positioning has a shelf life, and yours probably expired quietly.
sparks.insight: The market moves. New competitors change what the alternatives are, your product gains capabilities, and your best customers turn out to be a different group than you planned for. Positioning set at launch and never revisited slowly stops describing the company you now have — and the symptom is not dramatic. It looks like deals taking longer, more confused prospects, and sales quietly inventing their own version because the official one no longer helps them.
sparks.why: Positioning describes a relationship between a product and a moving market, so it decays even when the product improves. Sales inventing their own story is the reliable early warning sign.
sparks.apply: Ask three salespeople to describe the product without notes. If their answers differ from the official line, revisit positioning this quarter.

sparks.hook: Trying to be for everyone makes you unbelievable to anyone.
sparks.insight: Broad positioning is not neutral, it is weak. A product described as useful for teams of any size doing any kind of work gives a buyer no reason to believe it was built for their situation, and buyers assume — correctly — that something built for everyone is optimised for nobody. Narrow claims are more credible precisely because they exclude. The revenue you fear losing by narrowing was mostly never going to arrive in the first place.
sparks.why: Specificity signals that the vendor understands the buyer's problem, which is the main thing buyers screen for early. Broad claims fail that screen before any feature is discussed.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your homepage headline so it names a specific situation and would be wrong for at least half the visitors you currently attract.

sparks.hook: Nobody buys a product they cannot explain to a colleague.
sparks.insight: Most business purchases involve several people, and the one who found you has to sell it internally without you in the room. That means your positioning has to survive being repeated by an amateur to a sceptic. If the pitch requires a demo, a diagram and forty minutes, your champion will fail quietly and you will record it as a stalled deal. Building a version short enough to be relayed is not simplification for marketing, it is sales infrastructure.
sparks.why: In multi-stakeholder purchases the decisive conversation happens without the vendor present. Positioning that cannot be relayed accurately loses deals that appeared to be going perfectly well.
sparks.apply: Give your champion a single page they can forward internally, written for someone who has never spoken to you, then ask whether it got used.

actions: Run a two-hour session with sales and product listing what customers genuinely do instead of buying from you, including nothing, and rank those by frequency.
For each unique capability, write a sentence ending in a business outcome the buyer would defend to their boss, and cut every one that fails the test.
Interview your last ten customers about what happened in the month before they started looking, and target the two most common trigger situations.
Have a salesperson deliver revised positioning on three live calls this week and debrief on which buyer questions became easier.
books.not_for_you_if: You sell consumer products or work in brand advertising, since the method is built around considered business-to-business purchases with several decision makers.

verification.notes: Published 2019, based on the author's work positioning business software companies. It is a practitioner method with no empirical study behind it, and is strongly oriented to B2B. All prose here is original.

books.title: Only the Paranoid Survive
books.subtitle: How to Exploit the Crisis Points That Challenge Every Company
books.author: Andrew S. Grove
books.why_it_matters: Grove named the moment when the thing that made a company successful becomes the thing killing it, and described what it feels like from inside while the data is still ambiguous. Nearly every account of disruption since builds on that vocabulary.

crux.headline: The signal arrives long after the decision is due
crux.body: Occasionally one of the forces shaping your business changes by an order of magnitude, and the rules that made you successful quietly invert. You will not get clean evidence in time. What you get first is a growing gap between what leaders say the company is and what the people nearest customers are actually doing. Treat that gap as data, argue it out in the open, and be willing to abandon the business you are known for while it is still profitable.

sparks.hook: Some changes do not shift the game. They swap it for a different one.
sparks.insight: Ordinary competitive pressure changes by degrees, and the response is to work harder at what you already do. Occasionally one factor changes by roughly a factor of ten: a technology, a regulation, a channel, a customer habit, a supplier's power. When that happens, the strategy that produced twenty years of success becomes the specific reason you now lose, and doing more of it accelerates the damage. The difficulty is that both situations feel identical for the first year or two, and the standard managerial instinct fits only one of them.
sparks.why: The response to normal pressure and to a structural break are opposites: one calls for intensity, the other for abandoning a position. Misdiagnosing costs you the window in which action is still cheap.
sparks.apply: List the six forces shaping your business and mark any that could plausibly change tenfold within three years. Assign someone to watch each one.

sparks.hook: If the board fired you tomorrow, what would your replacement do?
sparks.insight: When a business you built is failing, your judgement is compromised by everything you had to believe to build it. The trick is to imagine you have been dismissed and a new leader walks in with no history, no promises to anyone, and no emotional stake in the old products. Ask what they would obviously do in their first week. Grove and Gordon Moore used exactly this device while Intel was losing money in memory chips, concluded the answer was to leave the business that had defined the company, and then decided to do it themselves.
sparks.why: Sunk costs and identity distort executive judgement more than missing information does. Removing yourself from the frame is a cheap way to see the decision the rest of the market already sees.
sparks.apply: Write what a newly hired successor would cancel in their first month, then pick one item from that list and cancel it yourself.

carousel.title: Fire yourself on paper
carousel.body: Write the situation as a briefing note for an incoming leader with no history here. Strip out every justification that depends on what you promised or built in the past.

carousel.title: Ask what they would obviously do
carousel.body: Not the clever move, the obvious one. If a stranger would immediately close a product line that you cannot bring yourself to close, that gap is the finding.

carousel.title: Then walk back in and do it
carousel.body: The advantage over an actual replacement is that you know the organisation and can move now. That advantage expires quickly, usually about the time the numbers become undeniable.

sparks.hook: The people who see it first are the ones you never invite to the meeting.
sparks.insight: Structural change reaches salespeople, support staff and mid-level engineers long before it reaches an executive dashboard, because they lose the deals and field the complaints. That information travels upward slowly, since each layer has an incentive to present a controlled version and nobody wants to be the person carrying bad news about the flagship product. By the time it arrives as a trend in a quarterly review, the window for a cheap response has usually closed. Seek out the people who keep saying something uncomfortable and listen properly.
sparks.why: Information decays as it moves up a hierarchy because every relay has a stake in the current strategy. Direct contact with the edge of the organisation is the only reliable correction.
sparks.apply: Book time this month with three people who talk to customers daily and ask what they have been saying that leadership keeps discounting.

sparks.hook: Watch the gap between what leaders say and what the company does.
sparks.insight: The most useful early warning is not a market statistic. It is a divergence: senior people describing the company one way while resources, hiring and the actual daily behaviour of teams point somewhere else. That mismatch usually means the organisation has already sensed the change and started adapting informally, while the official story has not caught up. Rather than correcting the behaviour back into line with the strategy, treat the behaviour as evidence and ask what the organisation already knows that the strategy has not admitted.
sparks.why: Resource allocation reveals real strategy more accurately than stated plans, because it reflects thousands of decisions made by people responding to what actually works.
sparks.apply: Compare where your engineering and sales time actually went last quarter against your stated priorities, and take the difference seriously.

sparks.hook: Let the arguing run, then stop it hard and commit.
sparks.insight: When you cannot tell which way the change is going, the correct behaviour is uncomfortable in both directions. First, allow genuine experimentation and open disagreement, including projects that contradict the official plan, because nobody knows enough yet and premature order is just guessing loudly. Then, once the picture clarifies, end the debate decisively and move resources with real force behind a single answer. Companies fail by getting stuck in either half: endless exploration, or a plan locked down before anyone understood the problem.
sparks.why: Exploration and commitment are both required and cannot run simultaneously. The judgement is entirely about timing, and it is easier to see in hindsight than to call in the moment.
sparks.apply: Name the date by which you will end the current internal argument, and say publicly what evidence you will use to decide.

carousel.title: Let the chaos run
carousel.body: Fund several incompatible bets and let people argue in public. Enforcing consensus early destroys the only information you have, which is disagreement among competent people.

carousel.title: Watch where the energy goes
carousel.body: Notice which experiments attract the best people and the most customer pull. That is a better signal than any forecast, because it aggregates judgement you cannot poll directly.

carousel.title: Rein it in
carousel.body: Pick one direction and say so plainly. Half-commitment is the most expensive option: it funds the transition without ever achieving the scale that makes the new business work.

carousel.title: Move the money, not just the message
carousel.body: Reassign budget, headcount and your own calendar. Organisations believe resource shifts and ignore announcements, and they are usually right to.

sparks.hook: The most expensive place to stand is halfway across.
sparks.insight: Crossing to a new business model means a stretch where you carry the costs of both the old and the new, revenues from the old are falling, and the new is not yet large enough to pay for anything. Leaders under pressure try to shorten that period by hedging: keeping the old business fully staffed while starting the new one small. That guarantees the longest possible crossing and the worst version of both. The transition is survivable only if you accept the damage, move quickly and tell everyone why.
sparks.why: Hedging spreads scarce resources over two subscale efforts. The arithmetic is unforgiving: the new business needs concentration precisely when the old one is loudest about needing support.
sparks.apply: If you are mid-transition, decide which business is now secondary and cut its investment this quarter rather than next year.

sparks.hook: Add a sixth force to Porter's five: the people whose products need yours.
sparks.insight: Competitors, suppliers, customers, new entrants and substitutes are the standard list. The one that gets missed is the set of companies whose products make yours more valuable, and whose fortunes are tied to yours without any contract between you. When a complementor's business changes shape, your position can collapse without a single competitor doing anything. Software platforms, hardware standards and retail ecosystems all live or die on this relationship, and it is the force least likely to appear in a strategy review.
sparks.why: Complementors change the value of your product without competing with you, so they sit outside most competitive analysis and outside most companies' monitoring.
sparks.apply: List the three products your customers must also have for yours to be worth buying, then assess what would happen to you if each one shifted.

sparks.hook: Debate the change before you have the data. Afterwards is a post-mortem.
sparks.insight: Waiting for conclusive evidence is intellectually respectable and strategically fatal, because conclusive evidence about a structural change arrives at roughly the same time as the consequences. What you can do earlier is argue seriously about ambiguous signals, in a forum where people with technical knowledge outrank people with titles, and where being wrong in an argument carries no career cost. Organisations that cannot hold that conversation do not get more time; they just get to be surprised later with better documentation.
sparks.why: Grove ran Intel on the principle that technical knowledge should beat hierarchy in a debate. It is uncomfortable to sustain and it is what makes early argument produce information rather than politics.
sparks.apply: Run one meeting where the most junior expert presents the case that your main product is on the wrong side of a change, with no consequences attached.

sparks.hook: Your career has inflection points too, and the same rules apply.
sparks.insight: Individuals face the same structure as companies. A skill that made you valuable for a decade can lose its premium in two years because a tool, a market or an industry changed shape, and the early evidence looks like ordinary bad luck: a few more rejections, slightly less demand, a colleague who seems oddly hard to compete with. Applying the same discipline works: name the force that changed, imagine what someone entering the field now would do, and reallocate your own time before the numbers make it obvious.
sparks.why: The mechanism is identical because it is about a system's fit with its environment, not about company size. The individual version is easier to act on and much easier to postpone.
sparks.apply: Name the one skill you are best paid for and ask what would make it half as valuable. Spend two hours a week hedging against that.

sparks.hook: The company that wrote this book later missed the next one.
sparks.insight: Intel executed the manoeuvre this describes brilliantly once, abandoning memory chips for microprocessors and dominating computing for two decades. It then failed the same test in mobile, declining the low-margin, low-power path that turned out to be the future, and later lost its long-held lead in manufacturing process. That is not a reason to dismiss the framework. It is the strongest possible evidence for its central claim: recognising an inflection point is a permanent discipline, and even the person who named it can miss the next one.
sparks.why: The failure is documented and undisputed, and it sharpens rather than undermines the argument. Frameworks do not protect organisations; sustained willingness to abandon a profitable position does.
sparks.apply: Write down the one business your company would never abandon, and ask honestly what evidence would change that. Revisit the note each year.

actions: Map the six forces around your business, including complementors, and assign one named person to monitor each for order-of-magnitude change.
Run the replacement-leader exercise in writing with your leadership team, then commit to acting on at least one thing a newcomer would obviously do.
Spend a day each quarter with people who talk to customers daily, asking specifically what they keep reporting that leadership discounts.
Compare last quarter's actual spend of money and engineering time against your stated strategy, and treat any large gap as a signal rather than a discipline problem.
books.not_for_you_if: You want current examples. The cases come from computing in the 1980s and 1990s and you will have to do the translation to your own industry.

verification.notes: Published 1996 by Currency Doubleday. Grove was chief executive of Intel from 1987 to 1998. The exit from memory chips took place in 1985. All prose original.

books.title: Playing to Win
books.subtitle: How Strategy Really Works
books.author: A.G. Lafley and Roger L. Martin
books.why_it_matters: It turns strategy from a document into a set of five linked choices a team can actually argue about and answer. For anyone who has sat through a planning cycle that produced ambitions instead of decisions, it is the most useful practical guide available.

crux.headline: Strategy is choosing what not to do
crux.body: A strategy is an integrated set of choices that places you somewhere specific and gives you a way to win there. It is not a vision, a plan, a budget or a list of aspirations, because none of those require giving anything up. If your strategy does not name markets you will not enter and customers you will not serve, you have written a statement of intent that every competitor could also have signed.

sparks.hook: If your rival could sign your strategy document, it is not a strategy.
sparks.insight: Most strategy statements survive because nobody could object to them: serve customers well, grow profitably, be a great place to work. The test is whether a competitor could adopt the same words without changing anything they do. A real strategy contains choices somebody in the room disagreed with, and it names what you are giving up. Discomfort at the moment of writing is the signal you have got one, since a choice that costs nothing to make is not a choice, it is a description of your current position with adjectives attached.
sparks.why: The test is fast and hard to argue with. It exposes the common failure where a planning process produces goals and budgets while carefully avoiding any commitment that forecloses an option.
sparks.apply: Take your current strategy statement and cross out every sentence a competitor could also sign. Judge what is left on its own.

sparks.hook: Five questions, answered together, or you do not have a strategy.
sparks.insight: The framework is a cascade rather than a checklist, because the answers have to reinforce each other. What does winning actually mean for you. Where will you compete, specifically. How will you win there, in a way rivals cannot easily copy. What capabilities must exist for that to be true. And what systems will build and sustain those capabilities. Answering any one in isolation produces an orphan: a bold aspiration with no market attached, or a capability programme serving no particular way of winning.
sparks.why: The cascade forces consistency, which is where most strategy work fails. Firms routinely choose a premium position and then build management systems that reward volume.
sparks.apply: Answer all five questions on one page with your leadership team, then check each answer against the one above and below it for contradictions.

carousel.title: Define winning
carousel.body: State what winning means in concrete terms for your specific business and customers. Playing to participate is a legitimate choice, but make it consciously rather than by default.

carousel.title: Choose where to play
carousel.body: Name the segments, geographies, channels and categories you will compete in, and by omission the ones you will not. Everywhere is not an answer to this question.

carousel.title: Decide how to win
carousel.body: Say what will make customers choose you there rather than a rival. Broadly this means being structurally cheaper or being genuinely different, and you must pick.

carousel.title: Name the capabilities
carousel.body: List the few things you must be excellent at for that way of winning to hold, and be honest about which of them you do not currently have.

carousel.title: Build the systems
carousel.body: Decide what measures, structures and processes will create and sustain those capabilities. Without this step the strategy stays on the page and nothing changes.

sparks.hook: Most companies are playing to play and pretending otherwise.
sparks.insight: There is a real difference between organising to win and organising to keep participating respectably. Playing to participate looks like reasonable targets, incremental improvement and an unwillingness to take any position that could be wrong. It is often the rational choice, particularly in a declining market where the sensible move is to harvest. What is corrosive is doing it while claiming otherwise, because the language of ambition combined with the behaviour of caution demoralises everyone who takes the language seriously.
sparks.why: Naming which one you are doing changes what you should measure and how you should invest. A harvesting business managed as if it were growing wastes capital in both directions.
sparks.apply: Ask your leadership team whether the current plan is designed to win or to participate. Write down which, and align the targets to that answer.

sparks.hook: Where you compete matters more than how well you compete there.
sparks.insight: Choosing the field is the higher-leverage decision, and it is the one most companies inherit rather than make. That means naming the customers, geographies, channels and product categories where you will play, which necessarily means naming where you will not. The exclusions are the substance. A strategy that keeps every option open cannot concentrate resources anywhere, and concentration is the only way a smaller player ever beats a larger one on any part of the board.
sparks.why: Position determines the difficulty of everything downstream. A modest capability in a well-chosen segment beats an excellent one in a segment where a stronger rival is already entrenched.
sparks.apply: Write the three segments you will not serve this year, and tell the sales team so they can stop spending time qualifying them.

sparks.hook: Being generally good at things is not a way to win.
sparks.insight: How you win has to be specific enough that it explains why a customer chooses you over the alternative in front of them. Broadly there are two coherent answers: you are structurally cheaper to run so you can undercut and survive, or you are different in a way people will pay a premium for. Wanting both, without changing the operating model that would make both possible, results in an offer that is neither. The test is whether you can name what you deliberately do worse than your rivals in order to be better at the thing that matters.
sparks.why: Advantage requires a trade-off. If you cannot name what you are deliberately worse at, you have described an ambition to be excellent rather than a mechanism for winning.
sparks.apply: Write the one thing you are deliberately worse at than your competitors and why that choice makes you better at what customers actually buy on.

sparks.hook: A capability that works alone is one a competitor can buy.
sparks.insight: Strength comes from a handful of capabilities that reinforce each other, not from any single excellent function. A rival can hire your best people or copy one process, but reproducing a set of activities that only work in combination requires them to change several things at once, which is expensive and usually contradicts something they already do well. So the question is not which capability is strongest but how the pieces support each other, and whether removing one would degrade the rest.
sparks.why: Systems of mutually reinforcing activities are far harder to imitate than individual strengths, because copying one piece without the others produces cost with no benefit.
sparks.apply: Draw your top five capabilities and the links between them. If none of them depend on each other, expect your position to be copied within two years.

sparks.hook: Whatever you measure quietly overrules whatever you decided.
sparks.insight: The last stage of the cascade is the one that gets skipped, and it is where strategies die. If you have chosen a premium position but the sales team is compensated on volume, the compensation wins. If you have chosen speed but every decision needs four approvals, the approvals win. Management systems, measures and incentives are the mechanism by which a strategy becomes behaviour, and until they change, the strategy exists only in a document that people have read and then returned to their normal work.
sparks.why: Incentives and processes describe the organisation's real priorities more accurately than any statement of intent, because they operate every day without anyone having to remember them.
sparks.apply: List your team's three main incentives and check each against your stated strategy. Change the one that most clearly rewards the opposite behaviour.

sparks.hook: Stop asking what is true. Ask what would have to be true.
sparks.insight: Strategy debates stall because each side defends a position and attacks the others, so the discussion becomes about who is right rather than about what is uncertain. The productive reversal is to take each option seriously and ask what conditions would have to hold for it to be the best choice. That converts an argument into a list of testable statements, and it usually reveals that the disagreement rests on one or two beliefs about the market. Then you go and find evidence on those rather than continuing to argue.
sparks.why: It lowers the social cost of changing your mind, because nobody has to be wrong. People will help test a condition they proposed, while they will defend a position they have staked.
sparks.apply: For your biggest open decision, list what would have to be true for each option, then rank the conditions by how uncertain and how important each one is.

carousel.title: Lay out real options
carousel.body: Generate several genuine possibilities, including one nobody in the room likes. A single proposal with a straw alternative is not a choice, it is a request for approval.

carousel.title: Ask what must be true
carousel.body: For each option, write the conditions that would have to hold for it to be the best one. Frame them as statements about the world, not about who is right.

carousel.title: Find the shakiest condition
carousel.body: Rank the conditions by how confident you are and how much rests on them. The one that is both uncertain and load-bearing is the only one worth researching.

carousel.title: Test it, then choose
carousel.body: Design the cheapest evidence that would settle that condition, gather it, and let the result decide. Agree the decision rule before you see the data.

sparks.hook: Certainty is not available, so stop designing processes that assume it.
sparks.insight: Strategy is a bet about the future made with incomplete information, and the aim is to improve the odds rather than to eliminate doubt. Planning processes that demand a confident forecast for every option systematically favour the safest choice, because only the familiar option can be forecast credibly. That is how organisations end up choosing the least ambitious path while believing they were being rigorous. The honest posture is to name the uncertainty, state what you are betting on, and set the checkpoints where you will find out.
sparks.why: Demanding certainty biases decisions towards incrementalism, since novel options can never produce the same quality of forecast as an extension of what you already do.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your next proposal to state the bet, the odds you assign, and the date you will know. Remove any forecast you cannot honestly defend.

sparks.hook: It is written by a chief executive about his own record, and that shows.
sparks.insight: The framework is genuinely useful and the evidence for it is not what it appears. The cases come mostly from one large consumer goods company during the period one of the authors ran it, described afterwards by the person responsible. That is testimony, not a test, and it cannot show that the method produced the results rather than describing them well. Some of the celebrated moves also aged poorly, including a very large shaving acquisition that was later written down by billions, and a portfolio that was subsequently cut back sharply.
sparks.why: Retrospective accounts by successful leaders overstate how deliberate the successes were and understate the role of conditions. Use the questions, which are sound, and discount the case evidence.
sparks.apply: Run the five questions on your own business rather than studying the examples, and record your answers so you can check them against reality in a year.

actions: Answer all five cascade questions on a single page with your leadership team, and check each answer for contradictions with the ones above and below it.
Cross out every sentence in your current strategy that a competitor could also sign, then judge whether anything meaningful is left.
Write down the three segments you will not serve this year and tell the sales team so they stop spending time on them.
Audit your team's three main incentives against the stated strategy and change the one that most clearly rewards the opposite behaviour.
books.not_for_you_if: You want independent evidence rather than a retrospective account, or you need theory rather than a practical process for a leadership team.

verification.notes: Published 2013 by Harvard Business Review Press. The case material is drawn largely from Lafley's own tenure at Procter & Gamble and is retrospective rather than tested. All prose here is original.

books.title: Positioning
books.subtitle: The Battle for Your Mind
books.author: Al Ries and Jack Trout
books.why_it_matters: It relocated marketing from the product to the customer's head, arguing that what matters is the slot you occupy in a crowded mind. The vocabulary it created — owning a position, category leadership, the mental ladder — is still how marketers talk.

crux.headline: You compete inside the customer's head, not in the market
crux.body: People cannot hold much. They keep a short mental list per category, roughly ranked, and mostly ignore everything below the top few. So the job is not to describe how good you are. It is to find a slot you can plausibly own and attach yourself to it with brutal repetition. If the good slots are taken, do not fight for them. Redefine the category until there is a slot where you are first.

sparks.hook: You are not fighting competitors. You are fighting how little anyone remembers.
sparks.insight: The average person is exposed to more brands in a day than they could name in a year, so the mind runs aggressive triage: a handful of names per category, roughly ranked, everything else discarded. Marketing that ignores this limit fails in a specific way — the message is received, understood and immediately dropped because there is nowhere to file it. Winning means offering a simple, distinctive slot the mind is willing to keep, not a complete account of your merits.
sparks.why: Memory for brands is limited and organised by category, a finding that has held up well across decades of consumer research. Complexity is the enemy because complex claims cost more to store.
sparks.apply: Write down the word or short phrase you want to own in your customer's mind. If it takes more than four words, you have not chosen yet.

sparks.hook: Being first in the mind beats being better in the product.
sparks.insight: The first credible entrant into a category tends to become the reference point everyone else is compared against, and later arrivals must dislodge a memory rather than merely win an argument. That is far harder than it sounds, because people do not enjoy revising things they already believe. This is why a technically superior product frequently loses to an earlier, worse one — the comparison is not happening on a level surface, it is happening on a surface the incumbent shaped.
sparks.why: The order-of-entry advantage is real but overstated here. Later research shows pioneers often lose to fast followers, and several famous first movers were themselves preceded by forgotten entrants.
sparks.apply: List the categories you could credibly claim to be first in by narrowing the definition, then test the narrowest one on real customers.

sparks.hook: If you cannot be first in a category, invent a category you can be first in.
sparks.insight: When every good slot is occupied, the productive move is not a better claim but a different frame. Split the category by use, by buyer, by moment, or by what you deliberately exclude, until you reach a definition where you are the obvious leader. This is not a trick if the new category is genuinely useful to buyers — narrowing usually makes your promise more specific and more believable. It becomes a trick only when the category exists solely inside your own marketing deck.
sparks.why: Reframing works because comparison sets are constructed rather than fixed. It fails when the new category has no meaning to buyers, which is how the technique degrades into an award nobody has heard of.
sparks.apply: Write five narrower definitions of your market, each excluding something real, and pick the one where you could honestly claim to be the best available choice.

carousel.title: Map the ladder
carousel.body: List who customers name first, second and third in your category today. If you are not on that list, competing on the same terms is spending money to stay invisible.

carousel.title: Find the split
carousel.body: Look for a dividing line buyers already feel: a type of user, a situation, a constraint, a value. The line has to exist in their heads before you name it.

carousel.title: Give up something
carousel.body: A category you can lead is one you narrowed by excluding real business. If the new definition costs you nothing, it is not a position, it is a slogan.

carousel.title: Repeat until dull
carousel.body: Say the same thing in the same words far past your own boredom. A position exists only when customers can repeat it back to each other without your help.

sparks.hook: The company that tries to be everything to everyone ends up owning nothing.
sparks.insight: Line extension is seductive because the numbers look free: the brand is already known, so put its name on the new thing and save on marketing. The cost is invisible and delayed. Every additional meaning attached to a name blurs the one meaning it had, and a name that stands for several things stands sharply for none. The short-term revenue arrives first and the erosion arrives years later, which is why the mistake is repeated so reliably.
sparks.why: Modern evidence complicates this. Extensions frequently succeed, especially into adjacent uses, and the blanket opposition here looks too absolute. The warning holds best where the parent brand's meaning is narrow and precise.
sparks.apply: List everything sold under your main brand name and write the single meaning each item adds. Retire or rename the one that contradicts the others.

sparks.hook: Naming yourself against the leader beats pretending they do not exist.
sparks.insight: If a category has a dominant name, ignoring it does not remove it from anyone's mind — it just leaves you undefined. Attaching yourself to the leader as the deliberate alternative borrows their recognition and hands the buyer a ready-made comparison. It works when the difference is real and you are honest about being second, and it fails when you claim the leader's position instead of a different one. You are asking for a slot next to them, not their slot.
sparks.why: Contrast makes an unfamiliar option easier to place, because the mind stores it against something it already holds. The risk is amplifying the leader's name while your own difference stays vague.
