Once you stop trying to correct them, you can start building for the world as they actually see it.
sparks.why: Projection is the default setting: people estimate others' preferences by consulting their own. It is a persistent, well-documented bias, and it is fatal in a job whose whole task is predicting what someone else wants.
sparks.apply: Find one thing your customers do that irritates you, and write out the version of the story in which their behaviour is completely sensible.

sparks.hook: You cannot make someone want something. You can find people who already do.
sparks.insight: Persuasion at scale barely works. What works is search: locating the people whose existing desires point at what you are building, then making it obvious to them. That reframes the whole job. You stop trying to change minds and start trying to be found by the right ones, which means clearer positioning, sharper language and a willingness to say plainly who this is not for. Saying who it is not for is what makes the yes credible.
sparks.why: Changing a settled preference is slow and expensive; matching an existing one is fast and cheap. Most marketing budgets are spent attempting the first while calling it awareness building.
sparks.apply: Add one line to your homepage stating clearly who this is not for, and watch what it does to the quality of the enquiries you receive.

sparks.hook: Tension moves people. Manufactured anxiety just makes them close the tab.
sparks.insight: Useful marketing creates a small gap between where someone is and where they could be, and holds it open until they act. That is tension, and it is honest — the person genuinely wants the thing on the other side. Manufactured fear is different: fake scarcity, countdown timers, invented threats. It converts in the short run and costs you the only asset that compounds, which is the belief that you tell the truth. The test is whether the gap would still exist if you had never mentioned it.
sparks.why: Pressure tactics work at the margin and damage repeat purchase and referral, which is where most durable value sits. The line between tension and manipulation is whether the problem is real without you.
sparks.apply: Audit your funnel for anything urgent that is not actually true — timers, false scarcity, invented deadlines — and delete one of them this week.

sparks.hook: Your best customers were sold to by other customers, not by you.
sparks.insight: Growth that lasts is almost always transmitted person to person, which means the marketing task is to make that transmission easy. That is partly product and partly language: giving people a clear, short way to describe what you do, an obvious moment when recommending you makes sense, and a result impressive enough to be worth attaching their own name to. Nobody recommends something that might embarrass them, so reliability is itself a marketing feature.
sparks.why: A recommendation carries the recommender's credibility, so its cost to them is reputational. Products that occasionally fail generate far less word of mouth than their average quality would suggest.
sparks.apply: Write the twelve-word description you want customers to use about you, then check whether your three most recent referrals said anything close to it.

sparks.hook: If nobody would miss you, you have not really made anything yet.
sparks.insight: The clean test of whether the work matters is subtraction. If your product disappeared tomorrow, who would notice within a week, and what specifically would be worse for them? A vague answer means you have built something substitutable, and substitutable things compete on price forever. A sharp answer tells you exactly who to serve, what to protect and where to invest, because you now know the precise reason you exist to somebody.
sparks.why: Missability is a proxy for switching cost and emotional attachment at the same time. It is harder to fool yourself about than satisfaction scores, which are famously generous and weakly linked to behaviour.
sparks.apply: Ask ten customers what they would use instead if you closed tomorrow. If most name a competitor without hesitating, you have a differentiation problem.

actions: Write a one-page description of the smallest group you could serve completely, covering what they already believe and what they do instead of buying from you.
Add a plain statement of who your product is not for to your website, and track whether enquiry quality improves over the following month.
Choose a publishing rhythm you could sustain through your worst month and hold it for twelve weeks before changing anything about the approach.
Ask ten customers what they would switch to if you closed tomorrow, and use the answers to find the one thing worth being irreplaceable at.
books.not_for_you_if: You want measurable tactics, channel mechanics or media buying rather than a philosophy of audience and trust, or you need evidence more than aphorism.

verification.notes: Published 2018 by Portfolio. Its niche-first advice sits in genuine tension with mass-reach research from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute; both views are noted in the sparks. All prose here is original.

books.title: Traction
books.subtitle: Get a Grip on Your Business
books.author: Gino Wickman
books.why_it_matters: It gave small companies a full operating routine — meetings, numbers, priorities, roles — instead of another book about vision. Thousands of firms now run some version of it. Treat it as a practitioner's system rather than researched truth: there is no independent evidence base behind the framework.

crux.headline: Rhythm beats brilliance in a small company
crux.body: A small business rarely dies of bad strategy. It dies of a hundred good intentions that never got a slot in the week. So install the plumbing: one page of direction everyone can repeat, a handful of priorities per quarter, a short sheet of weekly numbers, a meeting with a fixed shape, and one list where every problem waits its turn. Dull, repeatable machinery is what turns an owner's ideas into a company that runs without them.

sparks.hook: Your company is not short of ideas. It is short of a week that repeats.
sparks.insight: Small companies rarely fail because the founder ran out of good ideas. They fail because nothing in the calendar forces the good idea to become a shipped thing. An operating system fixes that by making a few rhythms non-negotiable: a yearly direction, a ninety-day set of priorities, a weekly meeting with a fixed shape, a short list of numbers checked every Monday. None of it is clever. Its power is that it runs whether or not anyone feels inspired, which is most weeks.
sparks.why: Founders over-index on strategy because strategy is fun and cheap. Execution is repetitive and dull, so it gets skipped first — which is exactly why a system that runs without motivation outperforms one that needs it.
sparks.apply: Block the same ninety minutes every week for a leadership meeting and do not move it for a customer, a fire or a flight. Protect the slot for a full quarter.

sparks.hook: If eight people describe the plan eight ways, you do not have a plan.
sparks.insight: A strategy that lives in the founder's head is a private hobby. The test is not whether you can explain it. It is whether every leader can state, without prompting, what the company is for, who it serves, what it refuses to do, and what has to be true in three years. Getting there means writing it on a single page and repeating it far past the point where you are bored of your own words. Boredom in the leader is roughly the point where the message starts landing with everyone else.
sparks.why: Repetition is not condescension. People hear a message intermittently, in fragments, while distracted by their own work, so the sender always hits saturation long before the audience reaches comprehension.
sparks.apply: Ask each leader separately to write the company's three-year picture in five lines, then compare the answers side by side without editing them.

sparks.hook: Two different questions: is this the right person, and is this the right seat?
sparks.insight: Hiring pain usually comes from collapsing two separate judgements into one. The first is about values: does this person behave the way the company needs, regardless of role. The second is about fit: do they understand the job, actually want it, and have the capacity to do it at the size you are becoming. A great person in the wrong seat looks like a performance problem and gets managed as one, which fixes nothing. Separate the questions and the right action becomes obvious — coach, move, or part ways.
sparks.why: Values misfits damage a team even when they perform, and seat misfits fail even when they are loved. Treating both as underperformance produces the wrong intervention about half the time.
sparks.apply: List your team on paper. Mark each person twice: values fit yes or no, and seat fit yes or no. Act only on the boxes that are honestly no.

carousel.title: Name the behaviours
carousel.body: Write the three or four behaviours the company actually rewards, drawn from your best people rather than from a poster. Vague values like integrity fail this test because nobody ever fails them.

carousel.title: Score people, not roles
carousel.body: Rate each person against those behaviours with evidence, not impressions. One recent example either way is enough. Ratings without examples turn into popularity contests.

carousel.title: Test the seat separately
carousel.body: Ask three things about the job: do they grasp it, do they want it, and can they carry it at next year's volume. A no on any one is a different problem with a different fix.

carousel.title: Choose within a quarter
carousel.body: Decide to coach, move or exit, and set a date. Leaving a known mismatch unresolved teaches everyone that the standards are decorative.

sparks.hook: A year is too long to plan and a week is too short. Ninety days is the unit.
sparks.insight: Annual goals rot quietly. By March the world has moved and nobody remembers what was agreed in January, so the year ends in a scramble. Quarterly priorities are short enough that you can still see the finish line and long enough to finish something real. The discipline is the number: three to seven for the company, and a handful each for a person. Anything longer is a wish list, because a list of fifteen priorities is a way of saying nothing is a priority while sounding organised.
sparks.why: Ninety days sits inside most people's planning horizon, so commitments stay vivid. Cutting the list creates the scarcity that forces the actual trade-off conversation, which is the part organisations avoid.
sparks.apply: Choose at most five things that must be finished this quarter, name one owner per item, and write the date each one is done by.

sparks.hook: A monthly profit report tells you about a month you can no longer influence.
sparks.insight: Financial statements are a lagging record of decisions already made. What a small company needs instead is a short weekly sheet of leading numbers — calls booked, quotes sent, jobs completed, cash collected, tickets open — each with a name and a target next to it. Five to fifteen lines, looked at every week by the same people. When a number goes off, you find out inside seven days instead of at the month-end review, and the fix is still cheap.
sparks.why: Leading measures move before the outcome does, so they buy reaction time. The weekly cadence matters as much as the metrics: monthly review means the average problem runs unchecked for a fortnight.
sparks.apply: Build a single sheet of no more than fifteen weekly numbers, each owned by one person with a target, and review it at the top of every leadership meeting.

sparks.hook: Your weekly meeting is a status update. That is why everyone hates it.
sparks.insight: Most leadership meetings spend their time on information that could have been an email, then run out of clock exactly when the hard thing surfaces. Flip the ratio. Keep reporting to a few tight minutes — numbers, priorities, headline news — and give the bulk of the hour to a ranked list of real problems, working them one at a time until they are actually resolved. Same day, same time, same shape, every week. Predictability is what lets people bring the awkward item instead of saving it.
sparks.why: A fixed agenda removes the negotiation about what the meeting is for, and the fixed slot removes the negotiation about whether it happens. Both negotiations are where good meeting habits usually die.
sparks.apply: Rewrite next week's agenda so at least half the time is reserved for solving a ranked list of problems, and cut every item that is pure reporting.

carousel.title: Start with the numbers
carousel.body: Run the weekly scorecard fast. Each owner says on track or off track, nothing more. Discussion of an off number goes to the problem list, not into the reporting section.

carousel.title: Check the quarter
carousel.body: Each priority owner says on track or off. Again, no explanation. The point is to surface drift early, not to hold a defence hearing in front of colleagues.

carousel.title: Build the list
carousel.body: Collect every problem worth the group's time, including new ones raised in the room, then rank the top three by the cost of leaving them alone for another week.

carousel.title: Solve one at a time
carousel.body: Take the first item, agree what the real problem is, argue it once, then decide. Move to the next only when someone owns an action with a date.

carousel.title: Close with actions
carousel.body: Read back every commitment made and who owns it. A meeting that ends without a written list of owners and dates has produced conversation, not progress.

sparks.hook: Half your arguments are about the symptom, not the thing underneath it.
sparks.insight: Teams burn hours debating a surface complaint — this client is difficult, the handover is messy — while the actual problem sits one layer down and never gets named. Before anyone proposes a solution, force the group to agree in one sentence on what the problem is. It usually takes several attempts and it feels like a delay. It is not. Once the real issue is stated plainly, the answer is often obvious and the discussion collapses from forty minutes to five.
sparks.why: Solution talk is more comfortable than problem talk because it feels productive. The cost is that a group can agree enthusiastically on a fix for something that was never the cause.
sparks.apply: Next time an argument passes ten minutes, stop and make someone state the problem in one sentence everyone accepts before any solution is allowed.

sparks.hook: Write down the annoying thing instead of discussing it right now.
sparks.insight: Most small companies have no place to put a problem, so problems get raised whenever they are felt — mid-corridor, mid-project, mid-someone-else's meeting. Keeping a single visible list changes the economics. Anything that is not on fire goes on the list and waits for the weekly slot where it can be properly argued and closed. Interruptions drop, the same complaint stops recirculating, and the list itself becomes an honest picture of what the company is avoiding.
sparks.why: A capture point separates noticing from solving. Without one, urgency sets the agenda, and urgency is a poor judge of importance in a business that is not actually on fire.
sparks.apply: Open one shared list today, name it plainly, and require that anything raised outside a genuine fire goes there first and gets worked in the weekly meeting.

sparks.hook: Design the seats your company needs, then see who fits them.
sparks.insight: The usual org chart is a map of who you happened to hire. Reverse it. Sketch the functions the business genuinely needs at the size you are heading toward, write the three to five outcomes each one owns, and only then put names in boxes. Founders find this uncomfortable because their own name lands in four boxes at once, which is precisely the diagnosis. Every function with no clear owner is a place where work quietly becomes nobody's job and shows up later as a fire.
sparks.why: Structure should follow the work, not the people, or you end up designing the company around the strengths and blind spots of whoever joined first. That constraint gets more expensive every year.
sparks.apply: Draw the structure your business needs eighteen months from now with outcomes written under each box, leave the names off, and fill them in last.

sparks.hook: You do not need a process manual. You need seven processes written thinly.
sparks.insight: Documentation projects die because people try to capture everything. The useful version is smaller: identify the handful of processes the business actually runs on — how you win work, deliver it, bill it, hire — and write only the steps that must not vary. A page each, not a binder. Then make everyone follow the same version. Consistency is what lets you hand work to a newer and less experienced person without quality collapsing, which is the only way an owner ever gets their week back.
sparks.why: Variation is where quality and margin leak. Capturing the critical few steps removes most of the variation at a fraction of the cost of full documentation, which almost nobody ever finishes anyway.
sparks.apply: Name your core processes on one page this week, then have each owner draft only the steps that must never change. Cap each at a single page.

actions: Write your company's direction on a single page, then ask every leader to reproduce it from memory a week later and fix whatever nobody could recall.
Cut next quarter's plan to five finished outcomes with one named owner and one due date each, and delete everything else from the list.
Build a fifteen-line weekly scorecard with a target and an owner per line, and start every leadership meeting by reading it in under five minutes.
Run the same meeting agenda for eight consecutive weeks before judging it, and keep a written list of every problem the company keeps postponing.
books.not_for_you_if: You run a large or highly technical organisation, or you find prescriptive branded frameworks with trademarked tool names harder to take seriously than plain advice.

verification.notes: Self-published in 2007 and widely reissued by BenBella in 2011; the framework is the Entrepreneurial Operating System. It is a practitioner framework with no independent research base. All prose here is original.

books.title: Zero to One
books.subtitle: Notes on Startups, or How to Build the Future
books.author: Peter Thiel and Blake Masters
books.why_it_matters: It is the sharpest available argument against the received wisdom that competition is healthy for the firms in it, and the clearest statement of how venture investing actually works. Whether or not you accept it, it forces you to defend your position.

crux.headline: Competition is not a badge. It is a tax
crux.body: A business in a genuinely competitive market makes no lasting profit, because rivals will keep bidding away whatever surplus appears. The businesses worth building are the ones that do something nobody else can do, and that keep doing it long enough for the returns to accumulate. So the aim is not to be a better version of an existing company but to make something new, then own the small market it creates before expanding outward.

sparks.hook: Every happy company is different. Every miserable one has competitors.
sparks.insight: Businesses that make sustained profits are doing something nobody else can do, which means each of them is unusual in its own way. Businesses stuck in fierce competition all look alike, because competition forces them to converge on the same practices and the same prices. The argument runs against how competition is normally described in business culture, where rivalry is treated as evidence of a healthy market and of your own toughness. For consumers it often is healthy. For the firms inside it, it is mostly a transfer of value to the buyer.
sparks.why: Read it as a claim about where profit accumulates, not as a policy position. Economists agree competitive markets compress producer margins; the disagreement is whether that is a problem to be solved or the point of the system.
sparks.apply: Write down what your company does that no rival could do within two years. If nothing survives that test, you are competing rather than building.

sparks.hook: What important truth do very few people agree with you about?
sparks.insight: The most useful question to ask a founder, or yourself, is where your beliefs diverge from consensus in a way you could defend. It is hard because most contrarian answers are either wrong or merely unpopular rather than genuinely unrecognised. But valuable companies are built on something true that most people have not yet accepted, since anything obvious has already been done by somebody better resourced than you. If your idea is widely agreed to be good, the returns have been competed away before you start.
sparks.why: The test filters for asymmetry of information or judgement, which is what an edge actually is. Its failure mode is rewarding contrarianism for its own sake, which produces confident nonsense rather than insight.
sparks.apply: Write one belief you hold that most people in your field reject, plus the evidence you would show them. Then ask a smart sceptic to attack it.

sparks.hook: Being first is worth little. Being last is worth everything.
sparks.insight: Moving early is often mistaken for the source of advantage, but the early mover carries the cost of educating a market and is frequently overtaken. What actually matters is generating the majority of the cash flows in your market for years after the excitement has passed. That reframes the question from how quickly you can launch to whether the business will still be dominant in a decade. Most valuations are made of distant cash flows, so a business that fades in five years is worth far less than its early growth suggests.
sparks.why: The point is that value sits in duration rather than in timing. Testing durability is hard and speculative, but asking it early prevents you from mistaking a fast start for a lasting position.
sparks.apply: Ask what your business will look like in ten years and what would have to be true for you to still lead. Write the three biggest threats to that.

sparks.hook: Four things separate a durable business from a lucky one.
sparks.insight: A position that lasts usually rests on some combination of four things: technology so much better that copying is impractical rather than merely expensive, a product that improves as more people use it, a cost structure that gets better with scale rather than worse, and a brand that buyers trust enough to pay for. One of these alone is fragile. Several together are why some businesses hold their position for decades while apparently similar rivals with more funding never establish one at all.
sparks.why: These are recognisable in most durably profitable businesses, though the framing is an argument rather than a study. Brand in particular can be a consequence of dominance rather than a cause of it.
sparks.apply: Score your business honestly on all four. If you cannot claim two of them, decide which one you will build before you spend on growth.

carousel.title: Proprietary technology
carousel.body: Not slightly better, but so much better on a dimension buyers care about that matching it would take a rival years. Marginal improvements get copied within a release cycle.

carousel.title: Network effects
carousel.body: The product gets more valuable as more people use it. These are powerful once established and brutally hard to start, since the early product is worth little to the first users.

carousel.title: Economies of scale
carousel.body: Costs per unit fall as you grow, so size itself becomes a defence. Service businesses often lack this, which is why they rarely produce durable dominance.

carousel.title: Branding
carousel.body: A name buyers trust enough to choose without comparison shopping. Real only when it rests on a genuine product difference, otherwise it is marketing spend with a short half-life.

sparks.hook: Start with a market so small that people laugh at the ambition.
sparks.insight: The instinct is to describe a huge addressable market, because a big number makes a plan look exciting. In practice a large market means a fragmented one with entrenched competitors, and a small share of it is worth very little. It is far better to dominate a tiny, specific group of users completely, because that gives you real revenue, real feedback and a defensible base. Expansion then happens outward into adjacent groups from a position of strength rather than as a scramble for scraps.
sparks.why: Dominating a niche gives you pricing power and word of mouth inside a group that talks to itself. The risk is picking a niche with no adjacent markets to expand into, which produces a comfortable business that cannot grow.
sparks.apply: Define a group of users small enough that you could serve most of them personally, and write down what winning all of them would take.

sparks.hook: One investment returns more than the entire rest of the fund.
sparks.insight: Venture returns are not spread evenly. A very small number of investments produce almost all the gains, and the rest collectively return roughly nothing. That has consequences beyond investing. It means a fund should only make bets that could plausibly be the outlier, since a moderately successful company does not move the total. It also means a founder should think hard about which company to join and which project to pursue, because effort spread across many options mostly lands in the part of the distribution that returns nothing.
sparks.why: Extreme skew in venture outcomes is well documented across funds. Applying the same logic to careers is an extension rather than a finding, and it understates how much people learn from the bets that fail.
sparks.apply: List where your time went last quarter. If it was spread across five things, pick the one that could matter most and give it half your hours.

sparks.hook: If you cannot name your distribution channel, you do not have one.
sparks.insight: Technical people systematically undervalue selling, because good selling is invisible when done well and embarrassing when done badly. But a product does not spread on merit alone, and the cost of acquiring a customer has to be lower than what that customer is worth over their lifetime, or the business does not work at whatever scale you reach. The right method depends almost entirely on deal size: an enterprise contract needs a person, a mid-sized purchase needs a repeatable sales process, and a cheap product needs distribution that costs almost nothing per user.
sparks.why: The distinction is practical and easy to check. Most failures here come from applying a sales model suited to one price point to a product priced at a completely different one.
sparks.apply: Calculate what a customer is worth over their lifetime and what you spend to get one. If the ratio is under three, fix distribution before building more product.

carousel.title: Work out the deal size
carousel.body: Average revenue per customer decides everything else about how you sell. Write it down before choosing a channel, because the channel has to be cheaper than the deal.

carousel.title: Match the method
carousel.body: Large contracts justify a person and a long cycle. Mid-sized ones need a repeatable process. Small ones need marketing or word of mouth, since no human can be involved profitably.

carousel.title: Check the arithmetic
carousel.body: Compare lifetime value against acquisition cost. A gap that only works at hypothetical future scale is not a business model, it is an argument for more funding.

carousel.title: Own one channel first
carousel.body: One channel working reliably beats five that half work. Spreading effort across channels usually means none of them reaches the volume where the economics improve.

sparks.hook: The belief that everything worth finding has been found is the mistake.
sparks.insight: There is a widespread assumption that the easy discoveries are done and the remaining questions belong to large institutions with large budgets. That assumption is convenient because it excuses not looking. Yet plenty of valuable things are unpopular to investigate, socially awkward to raise, or simply outside the areas where credentialled attention is currently pointed. The practical version is not mysticism: pick a domain, examine what everyone assumes without checking, and look specifically at the places where the assumption has never been tested.
sparks.why: Areas that are unfashionable are systematically under-searched because attention follows funding and status. That is a real structural gap, though it is also where a great deal of genuinely worthless work sits.
sparks.apply: Pick one thing everyone in your field takes for granted and spend a week trying to verify it from primary sources rather than from repetition.

sparks.hook: A plan you believe in beats optimism with no plan behind it.
sparks.insight: You can be optimistic or pessimistic about the future, and separately you can have a specific plan or none. The combination that builds things is optimism with a definite plan: the belief that the future can be better and a concrete idea of how to make it so. The dominant modern posture is optimism without a plan, which shows up as diversification, endless optionality and keeping doors open. That posture is rational for an individual managing risk and terrible for anyone trying to build something specific.
sparks.why: The distinction is a useful lens rather than a tested claim. It does explain why institutions that hedge everything struggle to produce anything, and why concentrated conviction is required for large projects.
sparks.apply: Write the specific future you are working towards and the sequence of steps to it. If you cannot, you are keeping options open rather than building.

sparks.hook: This is an argument from an investor with a stake in the conclusion.
sparks.insight: Two caveats belong with the book. It is written by a venture investor whose returns depend on the small number of firms that escape competition, so the advice to seek dominance describes what is good for that portfolio as much as what is good for the world. And the evidence is illustrative rather than systematic: memorable examples selected after the fact, without any account of the many founders who followed the same advice and failed. The reasoning is worth engaging with. The confidence exceeds what it can support.
sparks.why: The strongest objection is that concentrated market power benefits owners and often harms buyers, which the book treats as a secondary concern. Read it as a sharp partial argument rather than a balanced account.
sparks.apply: For each claim you find persuasive, ask who benefits if you believe it, then look for one counter-example before acting on it.

actions: Write down what your company does that no competitor could replicate within two years, and be honest if the list comes out empty.
Define a group of users small enough that you could serve nearly all of them, then plan what taking that whole group would require.
Calculate customer lifetime value against acquisition cost, and fix distribution before adding features if the ratio is weak.
Take the argument you found most convincing and spend an hour looking for the strongest published objection to it.
books.not_for_you_if: You want systematic evidence rather than argument, or you are uncomfortable taking strategic advice framed around building market power.

verification.notes: Published 2014 by Crown Business, developed from Blake Masters's notes on a Stanford course taught by Thiel in 2012. The argument is polemical and its examples are chosen retrospectively. All prose here is original.

books.title: $100M Offers
books.subtitle: How to Make Offers So Good People Feel Stupid Saying No
books.author: Alex Hormozi
books.why_it_matters: A blunt, unusually specific treatment of the thing most founders leave vague: what exactly you are selling and why anyone should pay a premium for it. It reset how a generation of small service businesses package and price their work.

crux.headline: Build an offer nobody can price-compare
crux.body: If a customer can line you up beside three alternatives, the cheapest one wins and your margin disappears. The escape is to construct an offer specific enough that no direct comparison exists: a defined outcome for a defined person, with the obstacles between them and that outcome removed, the risk shifted onto you, and a price set by the value of the result rather than by what competitors charge.

sparks.hook: If customers can compare you like for like, you have already lost.
sparks.insight: Selling something that looks like everyone else's version forces the conversation onto price, and there is always somebody willing to go lower. The way out is not better salesmanship but a different offer: aimed at a narrower customer, promising a specific result rather than a service category, and bundled so that no competitor's package maps onto yours. When there is nothing directly comparable, the customer has to evaluate the outcome instead of the rate, and that is a conversation you can win.
sparks.why: Price competition is a consequence of substitutability. Reduce how substitutable you look and you change what the buyer is actually weighing up, without changing what you deliver.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your main offer to name one specific customer and one specific result, and remove every phrase a competitor could also honestly use.

sparks.hook: Choose the hungry market first. A great offer cannot rescue a bad one.
sparks.insight: The most carefully built offer will fail if it is pointed at people who do not urgently want the outcome or cannot pay for it. Market choice comes first and it dominates everything after. Look for people in real pain about this problem, with money to spend, who can be reached as a group, in a category that is growing rather than shrinking. Get those four right and a mediocre offer still sells. Get them wrong and no amount of packaging will rescue the business.
sparks.why: Demand is a property of the market, not of your marketing. Persuasion can shift which supplier a motivated buyer chooses; it cannot manufacture urgency in people who do not have the problem.
sparks.apply: Score your current market on pain, purchasing power, reachability and growth. If any score is low, fix the market before touching the offer.

carousel.title: Find real pain
carousel.body: Look for a problem people already lose sleep, money or status over. Mild inconvenience does not produce buyers, however elegantly you describe the solution.

carousel.title: Check they can pay
carousel.body: Confirm the buyer has budget and the authority to spend it. Serving people who genuinely need you and cannot afford you is charity with a pricing page.

carousel.title: Check you can reach them
carousel.body: Ask how you would put a message in front of a thousand of these people next month. A group with no gathering place is expensive to sell to for ever.

carousel.title: Check the direction
carousel.body: Prefer a market growing for structural reasons. Rising demand forgives ordinary execution; a shrinking market punishes even very good work.

sparks.hook: Four levers set perceived value, and only one of them is the result.
sparks.insight: What a buyer feels an offer is worth rises with the outcome they want and how likely they think you are to deliver it. It falls with how long they will wait and how much effort or sacrifice it demands from them. Most sellers push only on the first lever by promising bigger results. The other three are usually easier to move and far more credible: prove the likelihood with evidence, shorten the time to a first visible win, and take work off the customer's plate.
sparks.why: The framework is a practitioner heuristic rather than a measured model, but it directs attention usefully, because effort and delay are the objections buyers raise most and sellers address least.
sparks.apply: Take your offer and improve one lever other than the promise: cut the time to first result, or remove one thing the customer has to do.

carousel.title: Sharpen the outcome
carousel.body: State the result in the customer's own terms and make it concrete. A vague benefit cannot be valued, so buyers default to comparing your price instead.

carousel.title: Raise believability
carousel.body: Show evidence that it works: case detail, references, a trial, a guarantee. Most buyers doubt the likelihood far more than they doubt the value.

carousel.title: Shorten the wait
carousel.body: Engineer a visible win in the first days rather than the first quarter. Delayed payoff reduces perceived value and increases the chance of cancellation.

carousel.title: Remove the effort
carousel.body: Every task you hand back to the customer lowers what your offer is worth. Do it for them wherever the cost to you is less than the value they place on it.

sparks.hook: Charging more can improve the results your customers get.
sparks.insight: A higher price changes who buys and how they behave after buying. People who pay seriously turn up, do the work and take the advice, and consequently get better outcomes, which produces better testimonials and more referrals. A low price attracts buyers who are least committed and most demanding, which is a miserable combination. Raising prices also funds a better product. The obvious caveat is that this only holds if you can genuinely deliver at the higher price.
sparks.why: Higher commitment correlates with follow-through, which is the mechanism behind the effect. It is not magic, and a premium price attached to a weak service produces refunds and reputational damage quickly.
sparks.apply: Raise the price of your main offer for the next five prospects only, and record the conversion rate and the quality of clients you get.

sparks.hook: Never discount. Add something instead.
sparks.insight: Cutting price to close a deal teaches the buyer that your first number was not real and sets the anchor for every renewal. Adding something of value keeps the price intact and gives the customer more reason to say yes. The addition should cost you far less than it is worth to them, which is why templates, extra access, a faster start or an extended guarantee work well. You are moving the perceived value up rather than the price down, and only one of those is reversible.
sparks.why: Discounts anchor future expectations and signal that the price was arbitrary. Additions preserve the anchor and are far easier to withdraw later without a confrontation.
sparks.apply: Prepare three additions you can offer instead of a discount, each costing you little and clearly worth something to the buyer.

sparks.hook: List everything standing between the customer and the result, then remove it.
sparks.insight: A structured way to build an offer is to write down every obstacle a customer would hit on the way to the outcome they want, including the ones that are their own fault: no time, no confidence, a previous bad experience, a spouse to convince. Each obstacle becomes something you can solve, and the solutions become the components of your package. This is why strong offers feel comprehensive. They were assembled from a real list of reasons people fail rather than from a list of features you happen to have.
sparks.why: Buyers weigh the whole path to the outcome, not the product in isolation. An offer that only addresses the central task leaves every peripheral obstacle as an unanswered objection.
sparks.apply: Write twenty reasons a customer would fail to get the result, and design one small component of your offer for the five most common.

sparks.hook: A guarantee moves the risk from the buyer onto you, where it belongs.
sparks.insight: Most hesitation is about risk rather than price. The buyer is not sure it will work for them specifically, and they have been disappointed before. A guarantee answers that directly, and the stronger and more specific it is, the more it says about your own confidence. It will be exploited occasionally, and that cost is usually far smaller than the sales it wins. The condition is that you can genuinely deliver, because a guarantee attached to a weak service simply accelerates the refunds.
sparks.why: Shifting risk works because buyers weigh potential losses more heavily than equivalent gains. A guarantee also functions as a costly signal, which is why a specific one persuades more than a vague reassurance.
sparks.apply: Write a guarantee specific enough to be uncomfortable, run it for a quarter, and track refund rate alongside conversion rate.

sparks.hook: Scarcity works, which is exactly why faking it is a bad idea.
sparks.insight: Limits on quantity or time move people to decide, and both are legitimate when true: you really can only take six clients this month, the price really does rise in January. Manufactured urgency is a different thing. Customers eventually notice the countdown that resets, the last few places that never run out, and once they do, everything else you say gets discounted too. In several countries these tactics are also regulated. Use real constraints, state them plainly, and then honour them.
sparks.why: Urgency raises the cost of deferring a decision, which is often the actual competitor. The effect depends entirely on being believed, so a discovered fake destroys the mechanism permanently.
sparks.apply: Identify a genuine constraint in your business, such as delivery capacity, and build your next offer honestly around that real limit.

sparks.hook: The name of the offer does a surprising amount of the selling.
sparks.insight: The same service sells very differently depending on what it is called. A name that states who it is for, what result it delivers and over what period does work that the sales conversation would otherwise have to do, and it makes the offer feel like a specific thing rather than a block of hours. This is packaging rather than substance, which is precisely why it is worth attention: the substance is often fine and the packaging is what stopped anyone finding out.
sparks.why: A name sets expectations before any explanation happens, and buyers judge relevance in seconds. Naming works only when the thing behind it delivers, otherwise it just raises the disappointment.
sparks.apply: Rename your main offer so the title alone contains the customer, the outcome and the timeframe, then test it on ten prospects.

sparks.hook: Written by someone selling to people who want to sell things.
sparks.insight: The tactics here work best in high-margin service and information businesses, which is where the author made his money and where his audience sits. They transfer poorly to thin-margin products, long enterprise sales with procurement departments, and regulated markets where claims and guarantees are constrained by law. The core reasoning about differentiation, risk and perceived value is sound and general. The aggressive packaging and pricing advice is specific to a business type, and the book does not always mark the boundary.
sparks.why: The examples are drawn from the author's own successes and from his coaching clients, which is a selected sample with a commercial interest attached. Take the mechanisms and check each one against your own margins and regulator.
sparks.apply: Before applying any tactic here, ask whether your gross margin and your regulator permit it. Adapt the reasoning rather than copying the script.

actions: Score your market on pain, purchasing power, reachability and growth, and change market before changing offer if any of the four is weak.
Rebuild your main offer from a written list of every obstacle between a customer and their desired result, adding one component per common obstacle.
Write a guarantee specific enough to make you slightly uncomfortable, then run it for a quarter and measure refunds against conversion.
Raise your price for the next five prospects and record both the conversion rate and the quality of the clients who accept.
books.not_for_you_if: You sell thin-margin products, or into enterprises with procurement processes. The pricing and packaging tactics assume a market that most businesses do not operate in.

verification.notes: Self-published 2021 by Acquisition.com. Advice is drawn from the author's own gym and services businesses; applicability outside high-margin services is limited. Prose original.

books.title: Anything You Want
books.subtitle: 40 Lessons for a New Kind of Entrepreneur
books.author: Derek Sivers
books.why_it_matters: A short, stubborn correction to the idea that a company has to get big to count. Sivers built CD Baby into a business worth tens of millions without taking a cent of outside money, then wrote the anti-playbook: revenue over funding, one delighted customer over a market study.

crux.headline: Design the small world you actually want to live in
crux.body: Most startup advice assumes you want scale, investors and an exit. Start somewhere else. Decide what kind of days you want, then build a business shaped to produce them. Fund it with customers instead of investors, so nobody else's timeline overrides yours. Stay small enough to still talk to the people who pay you. A company is an invented thing, and you are allowed to invent a different one.

sparks.hook: A company is an invented thing. You are allowed to invent a different one.
sparks.insight: Nothing about a business is handed down. Opening hours, who you serve, how big you get, whether you take investment, what happens when someone calls — every one of those is a choice somebody made, and you can make it differently. Most founders inherit a default shape from the people around them and then spend a decade unhappy inside it. Decide first what an ordinary Tuesday should feel like. Then work backwards to the business that produces that Tuesday, even if it looks nothing like the ones being written about.
sparks.why: Business form follows no natural law. The dominant model is dominant because it suits investors who need outsized returns, not because it is the only structure that survives contact with customers.
sparks.apply: Write a page describing your ideal working week in detail, then list every part of your current plan that quietly contradicts it.

sparks.hook: If nobody has paid you, you do not have a business yet.
sparks.insight: Enthusiasm is free, so people give it away. Friends say they love the idea, surveys say people would definitely buy, and none of that survives contact with a card reader. The only real signal is money leaving somebody else's account for the thing you made. That makes the fastest test of an idea also the cheapest: put a price on it and try to collect. If you cannot collect, you have learned something enormous in a week instead of after two funded years.
sparks.why: Stated intent and paid behaviour diverge badly, because saying yes to a survey costs nothing. Charging converts a vague opinion into a decision with a cost attached, and only that kind predicts anything.
sparks.apply: Take your current idea and try to sell one unit this week, before it is finished. Charge real money, even a small amount, and see who actually pays.

sparks.hook: If your answer is not an obvious yes, treat it as a no.
sparks.insight: Founders drown in decent opportunities. A partnership that might work, a client who is almost right, a feature one person asked for. Each is defensible on its own and together they eat the year. The filter is brutally simple: if a chance does not make you genuinely eager, refuse it. Saying no to the merely good is what leaves room for the rare thing worth everything you have. The cost of a mild yes is invisible, which is exactly why it keeps getting paid.
sparks.why: Your time is the fixed input. Mediocre commitments do not fail loudly, they just occupy the slot the exceptional thing needed, and you never get to see the trade you made.
sparks.apply: List every commitment currently on your plate. Mark each as genuinely exciting or merely fine, and start exiting one merely-fine item this month.

sparks.hook: You need no funding, no plan and no permission to begin this week.
sparks.insight: The gap between wanting to start and starting is usually filled with preparation nobody asked for: a plan, a brand, an entity, a round. Sivers began by selling one album from a page he coded himself, then added the next thing only when a musician asked for it. Starting tiny is not humility, it is speed of learning. You find out what people actually want while your costs are still near zero and there is nobody who can stop you changing direction.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: he could already code, and in the late nineties there was no other way for an independent musician to sell online. Scrappy starts still work, but a market opening that wide is rare and should not be assumed.
sparks.apply: Strip your idea to the smallest version you could deliver by hand to one person, and deliver it to that person before you register a company.

carousel.title: Sell before you build
carousel.body: Offer the thing to one real person and take their money first. What they ask for next is a better specification than anything you would have written alone in a room.

carousel.title: Keep costs near zero
carousel.body: Low overheads buy you the right to be wrong. No office, no hires and no debt means a bad month is a lesson rather than a crisis you must fundraise your way out of.

carousel.title: Add only what is asked for
carousel.body: Build the next feature when a paying customer requests it, not when you imagine somebody might. Requests arrive with evidence attached; imagination does not.

carousel.title: Delay the machinery
carousel.body: Entities, brand systems and funding rounds feel like progress and produce none. Set them up when revenue makes them necessary, not before.

sparks.hook: Your paying customers will write the roadmap if you let them.
sparks.insight: CD Baby's features arrived as a queue of small requests from musicians who were already paying. Someone needed a barcode, someone needed a sales report, so those got built next. This is unglamorous and it beats planning, because a request from a paying customer carries proof that at least one person wants it, and usually means dozens more do. The discipline is to ship the small thing quickly rather than bundling requests into a grand release that lands a year late.
sparks.why: A feature request from a paying user is a demand signal with money behind it. A feature from a roadmap workshop is a guess with a deadline behind it, and the deadline is the only part that is real.
sparks.apply: Start a running list of every unprompted customer request. Ship the smallest one this week and tell the person who asked that it is live.

sparks.hook: The dullest message you send is the cheapest place to be memorable.
sparks.insight: Every business has moments everybody treats as plumbing: the order confirmation, the invoice, the hold music, the packaging. Because they are ignored by default, a small amount of personality in one of them stands out enormously. Sivers rewrote his shipping confirmation as a piece of comic theatre and customers forwarded it to friends for years, which cost nothing and did more than advertising would have. Delight is cheapest exactly where nobody else bothers to look.
sparks.why: Attention is relative. A modest effort placed where the standard is zero reads as remarkable, while the same effort inside an already-crowded channel disappears without trace.
sparks.apply: Pick one routine message your business sends automatically and rewrite it as though a human wrote it for a person they liked.

sparks.hook: Being small can be the destination, not a stage you pass through.
sparks.insight: Growth is treated as automatic: get bigger until something stops you. But bigger buys you management, meetings, financing and a great many people whose problems are now yours. If the business already pays for the life you want, the question of what further growth is actually for deserves a real answer. Some of the best businesses ever run deliberately capped their size so the founder could keep doing the work instead of supervising it. Choosing not to expand is a strategy, not a failure of nerve.
sparks.why: Scale changes what your job is. Past a certain headcount you stop making the thing and start operating a system for making it, which many founders discover only once it is expensive to reverse.
sparks.apply: Calculate the annual revenue that would fund the life you want. Write it down, and treat everything above that line as optional rather than obligatory.

sparks.hook: Handing over the work is fine. Handing over your attention is not.
sparks.insight: Founders who hate managing often solve it by disappearing: appoint people, stop attending, hope. Sivers did a version of this and later found decisions being made in his own company that he would never have made himself. The alternative is not micromanagement. It is being transparent about how you decide. Write your reasoning down so other people can apply it without you in the room, then stay close enough to the work to notice when reality has drifted from the rules you wrote.
sparks.why: Delegation transfers a task; it does not transfer judgement. Judgement only transfers when the criteria behind your decisions are written somewhere other people can actually read them.
sparks.apply: Next time you settle a recurring decision, write the rule you used in one short paragraph and put it where your team can find it.

carousel.title: Decide out loud
carousel.body: When you make a judgement call, say why in front of people. The reasoning is the reusable part; the decision itself only solves today's version of the problem.

carousel.title: Write the rule down
carousel.body: Turn repeated reasoning into a short written policy anyone can apply. A team holding your criteria makes your decisions without having to wait for you.

carousel.title: Let them use it
carousel.body: Ask people to decide using the rule and tell you afterwards. Correcting a rule is cheap; approving every case one at a time is a full-time job you will resent.

carousel.title: Stay in the room
carousel.body: Keep standing contact with the work itself, not just the reports about it. Distance is how founders end up surprised by their own company.

sparks.hook: An idea is a multiplier on execution, and most multipliers are small.
sparks.insight: People guard ideas as though the idea were the asset. Treat it instead as a number that gets multiplied by what you actually build. A brilliant idea with nothing built is still worth nothing, because anything times zero is zero. A modest idea executed well beats a spectacular one described well, every time. This is why secrecy is usually wasted energy: telling somebody your idea costs you close to nothing, while getting an honest reaction to it can change what you build.
sparks.why: The scarce input is finished work, not conception. Ideas are abundant and cheap to generate; the willingness to spend years making one of them real is not.
sparks.apply: Tell three people your idea in full this week and ask each what would stop them buying it, then build the smallest testable piece.

sparks.hook: Say clearly who you are not for, and the right people will find you.
sparks.insight: Trying to be acceptable to everyone produces a business nobody chooses on purpose. Naming your exclusions does the opposite: it tells a smaller group that this thing was made specifically for them. CD Baby existed for independent musicians shut out by the major labels, which was a narrow claim and exactly why those musicians felt it belonged to them. A sharp no to most of the market is what makes the yes worth having.
sparks.why: Positioning works by contrast. A business that fits everybody has no contrast to trade on, so nothing about it is distinct enough for a customer to describe to a friend.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence naming the customer your business is deliberately not for, and put it somewhere public on your website.

actions: Write a one-page description of the life you want this business to fund, then audit your current plan against it and cut the parts that only serve someone else's idea of success.
Charge money for the smallest usable version of your idea this month, even if you deliver it by hand, and treat the first payment as your only real validation.
Start a decisions file. Each time you settle a recurring question, write down the rule and the reasoning so somebody else can apply it without asking you.
Rewrite one routine customer message so it sounds like a person wrote it, then watch whether anyone mentions it unprompted.
books.not_for_you_if: You are raising venture money and need tactics for scale. This is a short personal account of doing the opposite, and it does not pretend to be a general system.

verification.notes: Published 2011 by The Domino Project. All prose original; no wording reproduced from the book.

books.title: Blitzscaling
books.subtitle: The Lightning-Fast Path to Building Massively Valuable Companies
books.author: Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh
books.why_it_matters: It names and defends a strategy Silicon Valley had been running for a decade without a manual: choose speed over efficiency while a winner-take-most market is still open. Useful as much for showing you when not to do it.

crux.headline: Trade efficiency for speed when the prize is winner-take-most
crux.body: Blitzscaling is prioritising growth over sane management while a market is still up for grabs. You accept known waste, unfinished products and half-run departments to reach scale before a rival does. It is a bet, not a virtue, and it only pays where network effects, huge market size and strong margins let a leader lock in the position. Everywhere else it is a costly way to buy customers who leave.

sparks.hook: Growing faster than you can manage is sometimes the correct decision.
sparks.insight: Blitzscaling means choosing to grow faster than you can comfortably run the company, deliberately, while the market is still open. You will hire people you would not hire in calmer times, ship things that are unfinished, and let whole functions operate badly. That is the trade: known waste in exchange for reaching scale before anybody else can. Efficiency is what you buy later with the position you won. The mistake is not the chaos, it is running the play without admitting you are placing a bet.
sparks.why: Where one winner takes most of the value, being second with a cleaner operation is worth far less than being first with a messy one. Outside those markets the same behaviour is just an expensive way to fail.
sparks.apply: Before spending on speed, write down the specific mechanism that would let a leader lock in this market. If you cannot name one, optimise for margin instead.

sparks.hook: Most companies should never blitzscale, and yours is probably one.
sparks.insight: The strategy only pays when the market has winner-take-most dynamics: real network effects, a very large addressable market, or distribution that compounds. Without those, growing faster than your economics simply converts investor money into customers who churn. The advice also has an era attached. It was written when capital was abundant and cheap, and the same playbook wrecked companies once funding tightened. Read it as a conditional strategy with a short list of preconditions, not as a description of how ambitious companies behave.
sparks.why: The famous examples are survivors selected after the fact. For every company that outran its own chaos, many did the identical things and ran out of money before scale ever arrived.
sparks.apply: Score your market honestly on network effects, size, gross margin and distribution. Two weak scores out of the four means the answer is no.

sparks.hook: Four properties decide whether fast growth can actually stick.
sparks.insight: Some businesses can absorb explosive growth and some cannot, and the difference is structural rather than a matter of effort. Market size caps how far you can run. Distribution decides how cheaply you reach the next customer. Gross margin decides how much of each sale is left over to fund the next one. Network effects decide whether early scale makes you harder to beat or merely bigger. Check all four before you spend, because a weakness in any one turns aggressive growth into an expensive treadmill.
sparks.why: These are the properties that make growth self-reinforcing rather than self-funded. A business missing them can still be excellent; it just has to be built patiently instead of quickly.
sparks.apply: Rate your business from one to five on each of the four factors, then show the ratings to somebody who has no reason to flatter you.

carousel.title: Size the real market
carousel.body: Count the customers who could plausibly buy, not the industry the analysts describe. A market that is too small caps your outcome however well you execute.

carousel.title: Find compounding distribution
carousel.body: Look for a channel whose cost per customer falls as you grow: referrals, a platform, an existing user base. Paid channels that stay expensive cannot carry this strategy.

carousel.title: Protect gross margin
carousel.body: High margin means each sale funds the next one. Thin margins mean growth burns cash faster the better it goes, which is the worst kind of success.

carousel.title: Test for network effects
carousel.body: Ask whether each new user makes the product measurably better for the existing ones. If not, scale gives you size with no defence attached.

sparks.hook: Two things stop growth: nobody wants it, or you cannot serve them.
sparks.insight: Growth stalls for boring reasons. Either people do not want the thing enough to stay, or the company physically cannot serve more of them without falling over. The first is fatal and cannot be spent past, since pouring money on weak product fit buys you a bigger leak. The second is solvable, but only with time, hiring and systems, which is why founders in a hypergrowth phase spend their nights on operations rather than strategy. Diagnose which one is biting before you pick a remedy.
sparks.why: Marketing amplifies whatever the product already does. If retention is weak, amplification raises your costs and your churn at the same time and hides the problem behind a rising top line.
sparks.apply: Look at retention by signup cohort before you increase spend. If cohorts decay to zero, fix the product; if they flatten and hold, fix the operations.

sparks.hook: Your job changes completely each time headcount multiplies by ten.
sparks.insight: A company at five people, fifty, five hundred and five thousand is four different organisms wearing the same name. What works at each size actively breaks the next one. At the smallest scale everyone does everything and information travels because you can hear each other. Later you need specialists, written process, managers of managers, and a way to communicate that does not depend on your voice reaching the room. Founders usually fail not by doing the wrong thing but by continuing to do the thing that worked one stage ago.
sparks.why: Coordination cost grows faster than headcount does. The structures that feel like bureaucracy at ten people are the same ones that stop five hundred people working at cross purposes.
sparks.apply: Write down the three habits that make your team effective today, then ask which of them becomes impossible at four times your current size.

carousel.title: Everyone does everything
carousel.body: At a handful of people, generalists win and process is pure overhead. Communication happens because you can overhear it. Optimise for range and speed, not job titles.

carousel.title: Hire the first specialists
carousel.body: In the tens, gaps open that a generalist cannot fill. Bring in people genuinely better than you at one thing, and let them own it rather than reviewing their every move.

carousel.title: Manage the managers
carousel.body: In the hundreds you stop directing work and start choosing the people who direct work. Your leverage becomes hiring, standards, and deciding what the company will not do.

carousel.title: Broadcast, do not chat
carousel.body: Past a certain size you cannot repeat context in conversation. Write things down, say them repeatedly in public, and accept that under-communicating is now the default failure.

sparks.hook: You cannot put out every fire. Choose the one that kills you.
sparks.insight: A fast-growing company is on fire in several places at once: support is drowning, the infrastructure is fragile, finance is improvised, half the team is unmanaged. Trying to fix everything guarantees everything gets fixed badly. Rank the fires by what actually ends the company this quarter, put your attention there, and consciously let the others burn. Letting something burn is a decision you make and announce, not neglect you apologise for eighteen months later.
sparks.why: Attention is the binding constraint in a scaling company, not money. Spreading it evenly across problems of wildly different severity is how founders end up with a dozen half-solved crises.
sparks.apply: List every problem you know about and mark only the ones that could end the company within ninety days. Work those, and tell your team the rest are deferred.

sparks.hook: Hire the person who fits the next year, not the next decade.
sparks.insight: Founders stall for months hunting an executive who could run the function at a size the company may never reach. In a fast-moving business the role will be unrecognisable in eighteen months anyway, so the candidate who is excellent for the stage you are actually in beats the impressive one waiting for you to catch up. This does mean people will outgrow their jobs, and the honest version involves saying so at offer stage rather than pretending every hire is permanent.
sparks.why: Stage fit predicts performance better than pedigree, because the required skills genuinely differ by stage. The real cost is turnover among your leaders, which is uncomfortable and often handled badly.
sparks.apply: Write the job description for the next twelve months only, hire against that, and say plainly in the offer conversation that the role will change.

sparks.hook: Do the unscalable thing now and plan to throw it away.
sparks.insight: Manual work that could never survive at scale is often the fastest route to scale. Onboard the first customers yourself, deliver the service by hand, personally recruit the first hundred users. It teaches you precisely what the product must eventually automate, and it produces customers who stay because a person paid attention to them. The discipline is treating it as temporary scaffolding with a planned demolition date, instead of accidentally building your company around permanent heroics.
sparks.why: Manual delivery gives you high-resolution information about what customers actually need, which is exactly what you lack early on. It only fails when nobody ever decides to replace it.
sparks.apply: Pick one part of your product you plan to automate and do it by hand for ten customers first, writing down every exception you hit.

sparks.hook: The crew that wins the raid cannot be trusted to run the fleet.
sparks.insight: Early teams win by being fast, informal and slightly lawless. Later the same company needs predictability, coordination and people who will follow a plan they did not invent. Both cultures are correct for their moment, which is what makes the transition so painful: the people who got you here are being asked to behave in the exact way that would once have killed the company. Handle it explicitly. Name the change, explain why, and find new roles for those who cannot make the switch.
sparks.why: Neither mode is superior. What changes is the cost of error: at five people an unreviewed decision is cheap, at five hundred it silently commits hundreds of hours of other people's work.
sparks.apply: Name one process you have resisted adding because it feels corporate, then add the lightest possible version of it this quarter.

sparks.hook: Speed transfers risk onto people who never agreed to the bet.
sparks.insight: Growing faster than you can govern means shipping decisions before you understand them. Safety work gets postponed, moderation gets outsourced, and the people carrying the cost are usually users, contractors and the cities the company moves through, rather than the founders or the investors. Hoffman is unusually direct about this and still concludes the strategy is worth running, which is the part worth arguing with. If you choose speed, know whose downside you are spending.
sparks.why: The last decade supplied the evidence. Platforms scaled well past their ability to police what they had built, and the correction arrived as regulation, litigation and permanently lost trust.
sparks.apply: List three harms your product could cause at a hundred times its current size, and decide now which one you will resource before it happens.

actions: Score your market on network effects, addressable size, gross margin and distribution cost, and only consider a growth-at-all-costs plan if all four are strong.
Build a cohort retention chart before you raise your marketing budget, and treat decaying cohorts as a signal to stop spending rather than to spend harder.
Write down the three biggest fires in your company, pick the single one that could kill you this quarter, and tell your team the others are deliberately deferred.
Draft the twelve-month version of your next senior job description, and rehearse the honest conversation about how the role will change as you grow.
books.not_for_you_if: You run a services, retail or hardware business with normal margins. Almost none of this applies, and following it would mean spending money you can never earn back.

verification.notes: Published 2018 by Currency. Written during an era of unusually cheap capital; several of its case companies later contracted sharply. Prose here is original.

books.title: Build
books.subtitle: An Unorthodox Guide to Making Things Worth Making
books.author: Tony Fadell
books.why_it_matters: Detailed, unsentimental advice from someone who shipped the iPod and the iPhone and then founded Nest. Rare in covering the whole arc from your first job to running a company, with the hardware specifics most product books skip.

crux.headline: Make the intangible tangible before you build it
crux.body: Most products fail because nobody could explain, in ordinary language, why anyone would want them. Before writing code or cutting metal, write the story: the problem a real person has, why existing solutions fail, and what changes for them. If that story is not compelling on a page, no amount of engineering will rescue it. The story is not marketing that comes later; it is the specification everything else is built against.

sparks.hook: Choose your next job for what you will learn, not what you will be called.
sparks.insight: Early in a career the compounding asset is skill and the people you meet, not salary or title. That argues for going where the interesting problems are and where you will be the least capable person in the room, even when the money is worse and the company might fail. A failed company you learned enormously at leaves you more valuable than three comfortable years somewhere stable. The rule weakens as obligations accumulate, so the time to take this seriously is now.
sparks.why: Skills and relationships compound over decades while a salary increment does not. The honest caveat is that taking risky jobs requires a financial cushion that not everybody has.
sparks.apply: Write down the three capabilities you most want in five years, then judge your next role only on how much of each it would give you.

sparks.hook: If you cannot tell the story on one page, do not build the thing.
sparks.insight: Before anything is designed, write out in plain language who has the problem, why what exists today annoys them, and what is different afterwards. Reading that page back tells you quickly whether there is a product here at all. If the reason to care needs a diagram, a market projection or a technical explanation, real customers will not follow it either. The story is not something the marketing team writes at the end. It is the specification everyone builds against.
sparks.why: Writing forces the vagueness out. A product idea can survive indefinitely inside a slide deck of features and will not survive one honest paragraph explaining why a stranger would change their behaviour.
sparks.apply: Write one page describing your product as a story about a person with a problem, then read it aloud to somebody outside your company.

sparks.hook: Answer why enough times that a customer stops asking it.
sparks.insight: A convincing product story chains reasons together: this happens, which causes that, which is why the thing you have now does not work, which is why we built this. Each link has to be one a customer would nod at from their own experience rather than one you had to teach them. When the chain is solid, people finish it themselves and feel they arrived at the conclusion. When a link is weak, the pitch collapses at exactly that point, every time, with every audience.
sparks.why: Buyers accept conclusions they reach themselves and resist ones they are handed. The chain also exposes assumptions you were relying on quietly, because each link has to be independently believable.
sparks.apply: Write your pitch as a chain of because statements and test it on five strangers, noting the exact link where each of them hesitates.

carousel.title: Start where they already are
carousel.body: Open with a situation the customer recognises from their own life. Beginning with your technology means the audience is doing translation work instead of listening.

carousel.title: Name the real cost
carousel.body: Say what the current situation costs in money, time or frustration. Without a cost there is no reason to change, however clever the alternative is.

carousel.title: Explain why nothing fixes it
carousel.body: Show why the obvious solutions fail. If the audience can think of an easy answer you have not addressed, they stop believing the rest of the chain.

carousel.title: Land the change
carousel.body: Describe what is different afterwards in concrete, everyday terms. Specifics are persuasive; adjectives about how revolutionary it is are not.

sparks.hook: Disrupt one thing, maybe two. Three at once and you will not ship.
sparks.insight: Every genuinely new thing in your product multiplies the risk, because each one can fail independently and all of them have to work together. A new technology plus a new business model plus a new category is three simultaneous bets, and the odds compound against you. Choose the one or two things that are truly novel and be conventional about everything else. Being ordinary in the areas that do not differentiate you is not a compromise, it is how the novel part gets a chance to reach anybody.
sparks.why: Risks multiply rather than add. Two independent novel elements each with a decent chance of working still give you a project more likely to fail than to succeed.
sparks.apply: List everything genuinely new in your product. Keep the two that matter most to the customer and make deliberately conventional choices elsewhere.

sparks.hook: Plan three generations before you ship the first one.
sparks.insight: The first version of anything will be worse than you imagined, constrained by cost, time and what is physically possible. That is normal, and it becomes a problem only if the first version was designed as though it were the last. Knowing roughly what the second and third versions do lets you make architecture decisions now that will not have to be undone later, and lets you cut features from version one without panic, because you know when they are coming back.
sparks.why: Early architecture choices constrain everything after them. Planning ahead separates a deliberate omission from a permanent limitation, which is the difference between a lean first release and a dead end.
sparks.apply: Sketch what versions two and three of your product do, then check that nothing in your current architecture makes those versions impossible.

sparks.hook: Some decisions have no data, and hiding behind numbers is a decision too.
sparks.insight: Plenty of choices can be settled by measurement, and those should be. But the important early ones usually cannot, because the thing does not exist yet and nobody can tell you whether they would want it. Those calls are made on judgement, taste and conviction, and pretending otherwise leads to endless research that answers a smaller question than the one you have. Know which kind of decision you are facing. Demanding data for an opinion-driven call is a way of delaying it while looking rigorous.
sparks.why: Data describes what exists. For a genuinely new product the relevant evidence has not been generated yet, so waiting for it means either never deciding or deciding on evidence about something else.
sparks.apply: Label your next three big decisions as data-driven or opinion-driven, and for the opinion ones set a date and decide without further research.

sparks.hook: Becoming a manager is starting a new career from zero.
sparks.insight: Being excellent at the work is the usual reason people get promoted to managing it, and the two jobs share almost nothing. The new one is about hiring, standards, communication, uncomfortable conversations and getting results through people who do the task differently from you. Expect to be bad at it for a while, in the same way you were bad at your craft when you started. The common failure is refusing to accept the reset and continuing to do the old job while your team waits.
sparks.why: Management is a distinct skill set with a distinct learning curve. Treating it as a promotion rather than a change of profession is why so many strong specialists become poor managers and lose their craft too.
sparks.apply: Name the part of your old job you are still doing because it is comfortable, and hand it to somebody on your team this month.

sparks.hook: The product includes the advert, the box and the support call.
sparks.insight: Customers do not experience your product in isolation. They meet the advertisement, the website, the price, the packaging, the setup, the first week, the moment something breaks, and the person who answers the phone. Every one of those shapes what they think of you, and most companies leave the majority of them to whoever happens to own that department. Fadell's approach at Nest treated the unboxing and the support script as design problems with the same seriousness as the hardware.
sparks.why: Judgement of a product is formed across the whole journey, and the worst moment tends to dominate the memory. Excellence confined to the object itself gets undone by a bad delivery or a hopeless help page.
sparks.apply: Map every touchpoint from first advert to first support contact, then pick the worst one and assign it an owner this week.

sparks.hook: A company needs a heartbeat: a rhythm it ships to.
sparks.insight: Organisations without a predictable cadence drift, because everything can always be improved slightly more.
