books.why_it_matters: It reframed the goal of working for yourself from accumulating money to buying back time, and popularised remote work, outsourcing and small automated product businesses years before any of that was normal. Much of the advice has aged badly; the reframing has not.

crux.headline: Wealth is measured in time and mobility, not income
crux.body: A high income that consumes every waking hour is a worse deal than a modest one that leaves you free, and most people never run that comparison because they only track the money. Once the target changes to hours and control, the tactics follow: cut the work that produces nothing, set short deadlines that force decisions, hand off what remains, and build something small that earns without your continuous attention. The reframe is the durable part.

sparks.hook: An income that eats every hour you have is not a good income.
sparks.insight: Two people earning the same amount can live completely different lives, because one works sixty hours in a fixed location and the other twenty from anywhere. Judging a job or a business only by the total ignores the terms it comes attached to. The comparison that actually matters is money per hour worked, combined with how much control you have over where and when. Once you start measuring that way, opportunities that looked obviously good frequently turn out to be expensive.
sparks.why: Absolute income says nothing about the hours and constraints attached to it. Comparing on a per-hour basis with autonomy included changes which options look attractive, and that is the useful part of the reframe.
sparks.apply: Divide your annual income by the hours it genuinely consumes, including commuting and recovery, then compare that figure against an alternative you dismissed.

sparks.hook: Write the worst case down in detail and most of it stops being scary.
sparks.insight: Vague dread is worse than a specific risk, because an unnamed fear cannot be evaluated or planned around. Writing out exactly what could go wrong, how likely it is, what you would do to repair it, and how you would recover breaks the paralysis. The final step matters most and is usually skipped: cost out staying exactly where you are for one, three and five more years. Inaction feels safe because its costs arrive slowly and nobody sends you an invoice for them.
sparks.why: Naming a fear precisely makes it assessable, and most feared outcomes turn out to be reversible. Comparing action against the cost of inaction corrects a well-documented bias towards defaulting to the status quo.
sparks.apply: Take the decision you have been avoiding and fill four columns: what could go wrong, how you would prevent it, how you would repair it, and the cost of doing nothing.

carousel.title: Name the nightmare
carousel.body: Write the worst realistic outcome in concrete detail. Specific fears can be assessed and planned for; vague ones simply circulate and drain you.

carousel.title: Rate and prevent
carousel.body: For each item, estimate how likely it is and what would reduce the chance. Most bad outcomes have obvious cheap precautions nobody has taken yet.

carousel.title: Plan the repair
carousel.body: Describe how you would get back to where you are now if it happened. Almost everything is reversible, and knowing how makes the risk bearable.

carousel.title: Price the delay
carousel.body: Write what staying put costs you over one, three and five years. Inaction has a bill; it just arrives quietly and without an invoice attached.

sparks.hook: A short deadline forces the decision a long one lets you avoid.
sparks.insight: Work expands to fill whatever time you give it, mostly through deliberation, polishing and postponement rather than through useful effort. Cutting the time available forces the trade-offs that would otherwise be dodged: what to leave out, what is good enough, what nobody will notice. The effect is real and it has limits. Compressed deadlines improve output on tasks with a clear finish line and degrade it badly on work that genuinely requires depth or care.
sparks.why: The observation is an aphorism rather than a tested law, but it describes a familiar pattern. It works because a constraint forces prioritisation, and it fails wherever quality depends on unhurried thinking.
sparks.apply: Take a task currently scheduled for a week, give it a single day, and note precisely which parts you cut. Keep the cuts that nobody noticed afterwards.

sparks.hook: Eliminate first. Automating a task you should have deleted is worse.
sparks.insight: The order matters and most people get it backwards. Start by removing the work that produces nothing, which is usually more of your week than you expect. Then simplify what remains until it is dull and repeatable. Only then automate it or hand it over, because paying somebody to run a badly designed process makes that process permanent. Delegation applied too early buys you a monthly cost, a person to manage, and a task you still cannot explain properly.
sparks.why: Each step reduces the surface area of the next one. Automating or delegating first locks in whatever inefficiency already exists, and adds a coordination cost on top of it.
sparks.apply: List everything you did last week, delete the items nobody would miss, simplify the next tier down, and only then decide what to hand over or automate.

sparks.hook: A small fraction of your customers cause most of your problems.
sparks.insight: Look at any client list for long enough and it splits. A small group produce most of the revenue and almost none of the trouble. Another small group produce endless work, argue about price, and take up the hours you would rather spend on the first group. Ending the second set of relationships feels reckless and usually raises profit immediately, because the time released goes to customers who already pay well and are inclined to buy more.
sparks.why: Uneven distributions of this kind are common in commercial data, though the exact split varies a great deal and the tidy ratio often quoted is a rule of thumb rather than a finding.
sparks.apply: Rank your customers by profit and by hours consumed, then stop working with the bottom group for one quarter and see what happens to your income.

sparks.hook: Check messages twice a day and tell people that is what you do.
sparks.insight: Constant availability is expensive, because every interruption costs more than the message it delivered. Batching communication into set windows recovers long stretches of usable time, and the reason it usually fails is social rather than technical: people react badly to a slower response they were not warned about. Announcing the schedule in advance and giving an escape route for genuine emergencies converts it from rudeness into a policy that others can plan around.
sparks.why: Task switching carries a recovery cost that repeats with every interruption. Batching works because it reduces the number of switches, not because the messages themselves take long to answer.
sparks.apply: Set two fixed times to handle messages, add a line to your signature saying when you check, and give one clear route for anything genuinely urgent.

sparks.hook: Test whether anyone will pay before you build the thing.
sparks.insight: The cheapest test of a product idea is an attempt to sell it before it exists: a simple page describing the offer, a price, and a way to express interest or pay. What people click is more honest than what they say in a survey, and you learn in a week what building would have taken months to reveal. Take payment only if you can deliver or refund promptly, because collecting money for something that does not exist is a promise, not an experiment.
sparks.why: Behavioural signals from real purchase attempts predict demand better than stated intent does. The ethical line is that anyone who pays must receive the product or a prompt refund, without argument.
sparks.apply: Build a one-page description of your product idea with a real price, drive a small amount of traffic to it, and count how many people try to buy.

carousel.title: Write the offer
carousel.body: Describe the product as a buyer would experience it, with a price and a delivery promise. Vague descriptions produce clicks that mean nothing at all.

carousel.title: Send a little traffic
carousel.body: Spend a small capped amount reaching the specific people who should want it. You need enough visitors to see a pattern, not a full campaign.

carousel.title: Count the attempts
carousel.body: Measure how many people try to buy, not how many liked the page. Intent to pay is the only signal that predicts a real business.

carousel.title: Deliver or refund
carousel.body: Anyone who paid must get the product quickly or their money back without argument. A test that harms the people who trusted you is not a test.

sparks.hook: The book is not actually a description of a four-hour week.
sparks.insight: Setting up an automated product business takes long weeks of unglamorous work, and the maintenance never quite reaches zero. The title describes a destination a small number of people reach, usually after a stretch of working far more than forty hours. Read it as a set of tactics for reducing the work that does not matter, and ignore the arithmetic in the title. People who tried to follow it literally mostly ended up with an unfinished business and a lot of subscriptions.
sparks.why: The promise is a marketing frame rather than a typical outcome. The underlying tactics of elimination, batching and testing demand hold up much better than the headline result they are attached to.
sparks.apply: Set a realistic target instead: remove five hours of pointless work from your week this month, and measure it before you try to automate anything.

sparks.hook: The businesses it describes were built in a much emptier market.
sparks.insight: In the years after publication, the tactics it recommends became widely known and the channels it relied on became crowded and more expensive. Advertising costs rose, platforms tightened their rules, and the easy product niches filled up with people who had read the same instructions. The underlying method still works, but the specific opportunities described are largely gone, and the accounts you read come from people who got there early. Expect the approach to survive and the shortcuts not to.
sparks.why: Early movers in a newly cheap channel earn returns that later entrants cannot replicate. This is standard for arbitrage opportunities, and it means the case studies describe conditions rather than a repeatable method.
sparks.apply: Before copying any tactic from a book of this age, check what the channel costs today and whether the platform still permits what is being described.

sparks.hook: Nobody warns you how uncomfortable unstructured time can be.
sparks.insight: People who succeed at freeing up their week frequently discover that work had been holding a lot in place: their sense of usefulness, most of their social contact, and the shape of the day. Without a plan for what replaces it, the free time gets filled with anxiety, or with new work invented to relieve the anxiety. Deciding in advance what the time is actually for, learning something, building something, being with particular people, is the part almost everybody skips.
sparks.why: Occupational identity and routine provide structure and social contact that do not transfer automatically when the work stops. This pattern is well documented in research on retirement transitions.
sparks.apply: Write down what you would do with an extra fifteen hours a week, specifically enough to start on Monday, before you spend any effort creating them.

actions: Divide your income by the hours it actually consumes, including recovery time, and compare that figure with one alternative you have dismissed.
Fill in four columns for the decision you have been avoiding: what could go wrong, prevention, repair, and the cost of doing nothing at all.
List last week's tasks, delete what nobody would miss, simplify the rest, and only then decide what to automate or hand over.
Test one product idea with a priced page and a small traffic budget before building anything, and refund anyone who pays promptly.
books.not_for_you_if: You want realistic expectations or a durable plan. The title oversells, several tactics have aged out, and the advice on outsourcing personal work raises questions it never addresses.

verification.notes: First published 2007 by Crown, with an expanded edition in 2009. Prose is original. Several tactics rely on channels and costs that have changed substantially since.

books.title: The Art of the Start 2.0
books.subtitle: The Time-Tested, Battle-Hardened Guide for Anyone Starting Anything
books.author: Guy Kawasaki
books.why_it_matters: A blunt practical checklist for the first year of anything new, from someone who spent decades on both sides of the pitch. Its rules for presenting and positioning have become defaults across the startup world, quoted far beyond the book itself.

crux.headline: Start by deciding what you actually want to change
crux.body: Companies built to make money struggle to attract the people, customers and attention they need in the early years, because nothing about the goal is contagious. Companies built to change something specific find that recruiting, selling and pitching all get easier, because there is something worth repeating. Then get concrete fast: a short phrase anyone can remember, a product with something genuinely deep in it, and a first version shipped before you feel ready.

sparks.hook: Companies built only to make money find everything harder.
sparks.insight: A goal of getting rich does not travel. It cannot be repeated by a customer, it will not persuade a talented person to take a pay cut, and it gives you nothing to say when somebody asks why you exist. A specific change in the world does all three. This is not sentimentality: meaning is a practical recruiting and marketing asset, and the useful test is whether somebody outside the company could explain in one sentence what would be worse if you disappeared tomorrow.
sparks.why: Purpose functions as compression. It makes the company explicable in a single sentence, which is what allows other people to carry your message when you are not in the room.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence naming what would be worse in the world if your company stopped existing. If you cannot write it, keep working until you can.

sparks.hook: Replace your mission statement with three words anybody can repeat.
sparks.insight: Mission statements are written by committees and read by nobody, which is why staff cannot recite them. A short phrase of two or three words does the actual job: it tells everyone inside the company what the work is for, and it survives being repeated. The point is not marketing language. It is a decision rule people can apply on their own when you are absent, which is the only kind of guidance that reaches the thousand small choices you never hear about.
sparks.why: Short phrases get remembered and applied; long ones get filed. Guidance only affects behaviour when it can be recalled at the exact moment a decision is being made.
sparks.apply: Write your company's purpose in three words or fewer, test it by asking two colleagues to repeat it a day later, and rewrite it if they cannot.

sparks.hook: Good products solve the problem. Great ones keep revealing more.
sparks.insight: Products that people love share a set of traits worth checking against. They have depth, so they keep being useful as you get better at using them. They show evidence that somebody understood the real problem rather than the stated one. They are complete, including the unglamorous parts like documentation and support. They leave the user more capable rather than more dependent. And they are elegant enough that using them is not a chore. Most products fail on more than one of these.
sparks.why: These traits describe why particular products retain users rather than merely attracting them. It is a design checklist rather than a theory, which is precisely what makes it usable.
sparks.apply: Score your product against those five traits honestly, ask three users to do the same, and fix whichever one has the widest gap between your score and theirs.

carousel.title: Add depth
carousel.body: Make sure the product still has something to offer after a month of use. Shallow products get adopted quickly and then abandoned just as quickly.

carousel.title: Show intelligence
carousel.body: Solve the problem the user actually has, including the part they did not mention. Evidence of understanding is what makes a product feel considered.

carousel.title: Finish the edges
carousel.body: Documentation, support, packaging and error messages are part of the product. Users judge the whole experience, not the part you enjoyed building.

carousel.title: Empower the user
carousel.body: Leave people more capable than you found them. Products that create dependence get resented long before they finally get replaced.

carousel.title: Make it elegant
carousel.body: Remove whatever is not needed until using it feels effortless. Elegance is not decoration, it is the absence of things you failed to justify.

sparks.hook: Ten slides, twenty minutes, and text nobody has to squint at.
sparks.insight: Most pitches fail through sheer volume. Forty slides of dense text in a small font means the audience is reading instead of listening, and you will run out of time before the part that mattered. The constraint that fixes it is arbitrary and effective: about ten slides, delivered in twenty minutes so there is room for questions, in a font large enough that filler will not fit. The discipline is not aesthetic. Being unable to hide behind text forces you to know your argument.
sparks.why: Attention for a new proposition is short, and audiences cannot read and listen at the same time. Hard constraints on slide count and text size force the prioritisation that willpower alone does not.
sparks.apply: Cut your next pitch to ten slides in a large font and rehearse it to twenty minutes, then move everything else into questions or an appendix.

sparks.hook: Ship the thing, then improve it. Waiting will not make it right.
sparks.insight: Products released late and perfect are still wrong, because the errors you cannot see from inside the building are the ones that matter. Getting something real into use replaces speculation with information, and the resulting second version is usually better than any amount of additional planning would have produced. The obvious caveat is that this applies where a bad first impression is recoverable. In medicine, finance or safety-critical work the calculation is different, and it is not close.
sparks.why: Feedback from actual use is more informative than internal review, so an earlier release usually produces a better second version. The exception is any domain where a defective release causes real harm.
sparks.apply: Set a shipping date for the smallest useful version of your product, tell somebody outside the company about it, and hold that date even if features get cut.

sparks.hook: Recruit believers, not credentials. Enthusiasm cannot be taught later.
sparks.insight: Early hiring is not the same as filling a role at an established company. What you need is people who want the thing to exist, because the compensation is uncertain, the job description will change twice, and nobody is going to supervise them properly. Experience matters, but not more than conviction. A person who does not care about the problem will do exactly the work assigned and then stop, and in a young company most of the important work is never assigned by anyone.
sparks.why: Early roles are undefined, so motivation substitutes for management. This is genuinely different from hiring into a structured organisation, where process can carry an indifferent but competent person.
sparks.apply: In your next interview, ask what the candidate would build if nobody gave them instructions for a month. Hire on the specificity of the answer.

sparks.hook: Let the market tell you who your customer is, then go there.
sparks.insight: The customers you designed for often are not the ones who show up. Sell to anybody willing to buy at first and watch carefully who keeps coming back, because the pattern will surprise you and it is far more reliable than your original theory. Then concentrate everything on that group. The mistake is stubbornness: continuing to market to the segment in the plan while ignoring the smaller group who are actually paying, using it strangely and telling their colleagues about it.
sparks.why: Real usage data beats a positioning hypothesis, because buyers reveal fit through behaviour. The discipline is following the evidence, which usually means abandoning a segment you had grown attached to.
sparks.apply: List your last thirty customers by how much they paid and how often they return, then find the pattern you did not expect and target it deliberately.

sparks.hook: Give people something to join, not just something to buy.
sparks.insight: The strongest early growth comes from people who talk about you without being paid to. That happens when there is a cause to identify with, when enthusiasts are given something useful to do, and when the company treats them as participants rather than as an audience. It is slower than advertising and considerably cheaper, and it produces customers who defend you during a bad week. The failure mode is manufacturing a community around a product nobody actually cares about.
sparks.why: Advocacy requires identification, which advertising cannot buy. It only works where the product is genuinely good enough that recommending it costs the recommender nothing socially.
sparks.apply: Find the ten users who already talk about you, ask each what would make it easier to bring somebody else in, and build the first thing two of them say.

carousel.title: Name the cause
carousel.body: State what you are for in terms a supporter would use about themselves. People join identities far more readily than they join products.

carousel.title: Find the enthusiasts
carousel.body: Identify the small number of users who already recommend you unprompted. They are your distribution, and most companies never learn their names.

carousel.title: Give them a job
carousel.body: Provide something concrete to do: early access, a place to help others, a say in what gets built. Enthusiasm without an outlet decays quickly.

carousel.title: Remove the friction
carousel.body: Make recommending you easy and make it safe. People will not vouch for something that might embarrass them in front of a colleague.

sparks.hook: Advice from Silicon Valley quietly assumes Silicon Valley.
sparks.insight: Much of this comes from a career inside one industry, in one region, during a run of unusually cheap capital and rapid adoption. The pitching conventions describe what a particular set of investors expected. The launch tactics assume a market where being early is rewarded and a rough first version is forgiven. Outside those conditions, in regulated sectors, in other countries, or when selling to cautious buyers, several of these rules invert. Take the reasoning and test the tactics locally.
sparks.why: Playbooks encode the conditions of their origin. Rules about speed, risk and self-promotion transfer poorly to markets where trust is slow to build and reputational damage is permanent.
sparks.apply: For each tactic you adopt, name one condition in your own market that might break it, and run a small version of the tactic before committing to it.

sparks.hook: Milestones, assumptions and tasks fit on one page. Use it weekly.
sparks.insight: A young company needs less planning than it thinks and more tracking than it does. Three lists cover it: the handful of events that would prove real progress, the beliefs everything depends on with a number attached to each, and the specific work happening this week. Reviewing all three together stops the common failure where a team is busy every day while the assumptions quietly go untested and the milestones never move any closer at all.
sparks.why: Separating milestones from assumptions makes it visible when activity is not producing evidence. Most stalled early companies are executing tasks that test nothing whatsoever.
sparks.apply: Build a single page with your five milestones, your ten key assumptions with numbers attached, and this week's tasks. Review it every Monday for a month.

actions: Write one sentence naming what would be worse in the world if your company disappeared, and put it at the top of every plan you write.
Cut your pitch to ten slides in a large font, rehearse it to twenty minutes, and move everything else into an appendix.
List your last thirty customers by spend and repeat rate, find the pattern you did not expect, and aim next quarter at that group.
Build one page holding your milestones, your numbered assumptions and this week's tasks, and review it every Monday morning.
books.not_for_you_if: You want depth or evidence. It is a fast checklist shaped by one industry and one region, and several of its tactics assume a forgiving, fast-moving market.

verification.notes: This edition published 2015 by Portfolio; the first edition appeared in 2004. All prose here is original and the rules are described in our own words.

books.title: The Cold Start Problem
books.subtitle: How to Start and Scale Network Effects
books.author: Andrew Chen
books.why_it_matters: Network effects were treated as a mystical property that either appeared or did not. This breaks them into a lifecycle with named stages and specific tactics, drawing on how marketplaces and social products were actually launched.

crux.headline: Do not launch a network. Launch one tiny network that works
crux.body: A product whose value comes from other users is worthless on day one, and no amount of marketing fixes an empty room. The escape is to ignore the market entirely and build the smallest group that is genuinely useful to itself: one campus, one office, one neighbourhood on one night. Get that group self-sustaining, then repeat it. Networks grow by copying a working cell, not by broadcasting to everyone at once.

sparks.hook: A network product is worthless on the day you launch it.
sparks.insight: Anything whose value comes from other people using it starts at zero and stays there until enough of them arrive. The first user of a messaging app has nobody to message. The first driver has no riders. This is not a marketing problem and cannot be spent past, because paid users arrive into an empty room and leave. Every successful network product got past this somehow, usually with tactics that look ridiculous at scale, and copying the mature version of a network tells you nothing about how it began.
sparks.why: Value depends on participation, so the product genuinely is bad early. Ordinary growth tactics assume the product already delivers value on arrival, which is precisely what is missing here.
sparks.apply: Write down what a single new user experiences if nobody else joins that week. If the answer is nothing, your first job is density rather than reach.

sparks.hook: Find the smallest group that would be useful to itself.
sparks.insight: The unit that matters is not the market, it is the smallest collection of people that keeps working without any help from you. For a workplace tool that might be one team of five in one office. For a ride service it might be a handful of drivers covering a few square miles on a Friday night. Get one of those to stability and you have proof plus a template. Aiming at a city or an industry from the start spreads your users so thinly that no group anywhere ever reaches the density that makes the product good.
sparks.why: Network value is local rather than global. A million scattered users can each have an empty experience, while a few hundred concentrated in one place have a working product.
sparks.apply: Define your smallest self-sustaining unit in one sentence with a place and a number in it, then pour everything into filling exactly one of them.

sparks.hook: Every network has a hard side, and it is not the one you count.
sparks.insight: Networks are lopsided. A small minority does most of the work that makes the thing valuable: the drivers, the hosts, the sellers, the people who actually post. That group is harder to recruit, harder to keep and usually has better alternatives. Yet product effort tends to flow to the easy side, because those users are numerous and their metrics move. Ask who does the work in your network, then build for them first, pay them properly and make their job easier before you optimise anything else.
sparks.why: Supply-side participants have higher switching flexibility and higher effort costs, so they defect faster. Losing them collapses the value proposition for everybody else almost immediately.
sparks.apply: Name the hard side of your network in one word, then find the single most tedious part of their experience and fix it this month.

sparks.hook: Give people a reason to show up before the network exists.
sparks.insight: A common escape from the empty room is to ship something useful to a single person alone, then let the network form on top of it. Photo filters were worth having before anybody followed you. A calendar or a document editor is useful before your colleagues join. The tool creates a reason to arrive and a reason to return, and the network quietly assembles in the background. The tool has to be genuinely good on its own, though, or you are simply describing an empty product with a slogan attached.
sparks.why: Single-player value removes the dependency on other users during the period when there are none, which is exactly when a network product is at its weakest.
sparks.apply: Design one feature that is worth using when the user is completely alone, and make it the first thing they encounter on signup.

sparks.hook: Fake the supply by hand until real supply turns up.
sparks.insight: Many networks were bootstrapped with work that looks nothing like software. Founders posted the first listings themselves, drove the first cars, staffed the first requests, copied content from elsewhere, or simply stood in the street recruiting. It is unglamorous, unscalable and entirely legitimate, because the alternative is a product that never demonstrates its value to anyone. The trap is being unwilling to do it. Founders who insist the system must work on its own from day one usually get a system that works for nobody.
sparks.why: Manual supply substitutes founder labour for network density during the period when density cannot exist. It becomes a problem only when nobody plans the handover to real participants.
sparks.apply: Choose one side of your network and supply it yourself for the next two weeks, with a written date for when real participants must take over.

carousel.title: Pick one side to fake
carousel.body: Decide which side of the network you will personally supply. Usually it is the hard side, because that is the one nobody joins voluntarily into an empty room.

carousel.title: Do it embarrassingly manually
carousel.body: Post the listings, make the calls, deliver the service yourself. Every awkward part you hit is a specification for what the product eventually has to automate.

carousel.title: Concentrate it in one place
carousel.body: Put all of your manual effort into a single network unit rather than spreading it. Density in one location beats a thin presence across ten of them.

carousel.title: Set a handover date
carousel.body: Write down when real participants must replace you and what threshold proves it. Without that date the manual work quietly becomes the business model.

sparks.hook: Grow by copying a working network, not by adding users.
sparks.insight: Once one small network works, growth becomes a repeatable operation rather than a marketing budget. You go to the next campus, the next city, the next company, and reproduce the same conditions that made the first one succeed. This is why network businesses launch geographically and why their playbooks read like field manuals. It also gives you a real test: if a second unit fails using the same method, you have not yet understood why the first one worked.
sparks.why: Replication converts a lucky success into a process. It also isolates variables, since a unit that fails in a new place reveals which local conditions the original success quietly depended on.
sparks.apply: Write down the exact conditions present when your first network unit succeeded, then attempt to reproduce all of them in a second unit.

sparks.hook: Sustained growth needs three loops running, not one growth hack.
sparks.insight: Fast growth in a network product comes from loops that feed themselves. The acquisition loop means existing users bring new ones, through invitations, shared content or visible use. The engagement loop means the product gives people reasons to return without a prompt from you. The economic loop means the money earned from users funds acquiring more of them. Any one loop alone stalls. Together they compound, and the job of a growth team is to find which of the three is currently broken.
sparks.why: Loops compound where campaigns do not. A channel spends money once for each customer, while a loop uses the output of the last cycle as the input to the next.
sparks.apply: Draw your three loops on one page and mark where each breaks. Fix the broken link rather than adding a fourth acquisition channel.

carousel.title: Acquisition loop
carousel.body: Users bring users, through invitations, shared content or visible public use. If new arrivals come only from paid channels, you have a funnel and not a loop.

carousel.title: Engagement loop
carousel.body: Something the network produces gives people a reason to come back on their own. Notifications count only when the thing they announce is genuinely worth returning for.

carousel.title: Economic loop
carousel.body: Revenue from existing users pays to bring in more. If each new customer costs more than they will ever return, growth is a countdown rather than a strategy.

sparks.hook: Every acquisition channel decays. Assume yours is already decaying.
sparks.insight: A channel that works well attracts everybody else, audiences get saturated, and response rates fall. This happens to banner ads, email, referral schemes, social feeds and whatever is currently working for you. It means growth teams are never finished, and it means a company that built its whole model on one cheap channel has a hidden expiry date. Plan for channel decay in the same way you plan for equipment wearing out, rather than treating each decline as a failure of execution.
sparks.why: Channels degrade because attention is finite and competitors copy anything that works. The decline is structural, so it continues regardless of how well your team executes.
sparks.apply: Chart the cost per acquisition of your main channel over the past year. If the line is rising, start testing a second channel now.

sparks.hook: Networks stop growing for reasons your team cannot work harder at.
sparks.insight: Growth eventually slows and the internal instinct is to blame effort. Usually the causes are structural. The easiest users have already joined, so each new one is harder to reach. Scale attracts spam and low-quality participants, which degrades the experience for everyone. Crowding makes the network less useful, as anybody who has watched a feed fill with noise knows. Recognising a ceiling for what it is changes the response from pushing harder to changing the product.
sparks.why: Saturation, quality degradation and overcrowding are properties of large networks rather than symptoms of poor management. They arrive on schedule for products that are working exactly as designed.
sparks.apply: Split your growth curve by cohort and by segment to find which specific group has stalled, then treat that as a product problem rather than a marketing one.

sparks.hook: The big launch is the wrong weapon against a network incumbent.
sparks.insight: Attacking an established network with an enormous simultaneous launch tends to fail, even with a great deal of money behind it. Everyone arrives at once into a product with no local density, finds nobody they know, and leaves. The approach that works is to find an edge of the incumbent's network where the experience is bad or a group they serve poorly, take that segment properly, and grow inward. Networks are beaten at their weakest corner, not at their strongest point.
sparks.why: Mass launches spread users too thinly for any single group to reach density, so the product feels empty precisely when curiosity is highest and first impressions are being formed.
sparks.apply: Identify one group your dominant competitor serves badly and build a product that is unmistakably the best option for that group alone.

actions: Define your atomic network in one sentence that includes a place and a number, then concentrate all acquisition effort on filling exactly one of them.
Name the hard side of your network and spend a week doing their job yourself, listing every friction point you encounter along the way.
Draw your acquisition, engagement and economic loops on a single page, mark where each one breaks, and fix the weakest link before adding a channel.
Chart cost per acquisition for your main channel across the last twelve months and begin testing an alternative if the trend is upward.
books.not_for_you_if: Your product delivers full value to a single user with no one else involved. Most of this concerns problems your business will never have.

verification.notes: Published 2021 by Harper Business. Chen is a venture investor and formerly led growth at Uber. Prose here is original.

books.title: The Four Steps to the Epiphany
books.subtitle: Successful Strategies for Products that Win
books.author: Steve Blank
books.why_it_matters: It named the central error of startup practice: running a product schedule as though the customer were already known. The customer development process it laid out became the backbone of lean startup method and of how early-stage companies are taught today.

crux.headline: A startup searches. A company executes
crux.body: Established firms have known customers, known channels and known problems, so they can plan and execute. A startup has none of those and is instead searching for them, which is a different activity requiring a different process. Treating the search as though it were execution produces the classic failure: a launch date, a sales team and a marketing budget all committed before anyone has established that the customer exists. Learn first, in a structured way, then scale.

sparks.hook: A startup is not a small company. It is a search for a business model.
sparks.insight: Large companies execute a model that is already known: who buys, why, through which channel, at what price. A startup knows none of that and is looking for it. The mistake is importing the tools of execution, detailed plans and launch dates and functional departments, into an organisation whose real job is learning. Every one of those tools assumes facts that do not yet exist. The right early structure is small, cheap and able to change its mind quickly, because being wrong is the expected condition.
sparks.why: Planning tools assume a stable, known environment. Applied to genuine uncertainty they convert guesses into commitments and make the organisation slower to notice that it is wrong.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your current plan as a numbered list of assumptions rather than a schedule, and rank them by how badly you would be hurt if any one turned out false.

sparks.hook: There are no facts inside your own office. Go and find some.
sparks.insight: Everything in the plan is a guess: who the customer is, what problem they have, what they would pay, how they buy. Those guesses cannot be resolved by more discussion, better slides or a hired research firm. They get resolved by founders talking to real potential customers repeatedly, in person, and updating the plan afterwards. Delegating this is the common failure, because the founders are the only people who can actually change the company in response to what they hear.
sparks.why: The value of customer conversations lies in the update they cause, so the people with authority to change direction have to be the ones hearing the answers directly and unfiltered.
sparks.apply: Book ten conversations with potential customers in the next fortnight and go to them yourself. Update at least one written assumption after each one.

sparks.hook: Find the customer, prove they buy, then build the machine to sell.
sparks.insight: The sequence matters more than any individual technique. First, establish whether the problem and the customer you imagined actually exist. Second, prove that somebody will hand over money in a repeatable way, which means selling it yourself before hiring anyone to sell it. Third, create demand beyond the early enthusiasts. Fourth, and only then, build the departments, processes and headcount of an operating company. Skipping ahead is the standard cause of expensive failure, because it scales an unverified guess.
sparks.why: Each stage produces the evidence the next one depends on. Scaling sales or marketing before a repeatable sale exists multiplies the cost of being wrong without improving your odds at all.
sparks.apply: Identify which of the four stages you are honestly in, then stop any spending that belongs to a later stage until the current one is genuinely finished.

carousel.title: Discover the customer
carousel.body: Turn your plan into testable assumptions about who has the problem and how badly. Then talk to those people until the assumptions are confirmed or replaced.

carousel.title: Validate the sale
carousel.body: Sell to a handful of real buyers yourself and write down what worked. If you cannot repeat the sale, there is nothing yet to hand over to a sales team.

carousel.title: Create the demand
carousel.body: Now spend on marketing to reach buyers beyond the early enthusiasts, using the message that already proved itself in real sales conversations.

carousel.title: Build the company
carousel.body: Replace the informal search structure with departments and process, but only once the model is known. Do it earlier and you institutionalise a guess.

sparks.hook: Your first customers are not typical, and that is why they buy.
sparks.insight: The people who buy an unfinished product from an unknown company are unusual. They already know they have the problem, have been actively looking for a fix, have improvised something inadequate themselves, and can find budget without a long approval process. That profile is the search target for early sales. Selling to anyone else this early wastes months, because a customer who does not yet believe they have the problem needs the whole market educated first, and you cannot afford that.
sparks.why: Early adopters buy on the strength of the problem rather than the polish of the solution. Screening for that profile is what makes early sales possible at all with an incomplete product.
sparks.apply: Write the five characteristics of someone desperate enough to buy your unfinished product, then disqualify any prospect who is missing more than one of them.

sparks.hook: Ask what kind of market you are in before you plan anything.
sparks.insight: Entering an existing market means competing on features against known rivals, with customers who already understand the category. Creating a new one means nobody is searching for you, adoption takes years, and your main cost is education. Resegmenting means finding a niche or a cheaper position inside a market that already exists. These three demand completely different spending, timelines and messages, and the most common expensive error is running a new-market company on an existing-market budget.
sparks.why: Market type determines how long adoption takes and how customers find you. Applying the wrong playbook produces a launch that spends heavily into a market which has not formed yet.
sparks.apply: State in one sentence which market type you are in and what that implies for your first year of spending. Then check that sentence against how you are actually budgeting.

sparks.hook: Hiring a sales leader before you can sell is an expensive lesson.
sparks.insight: A senior sales hire is built to scale a process that already works. When there is no proven process, they arrive to find there is nothing to run, burn through your best early leads while working it out, and usually leave. Founders have to make the first sales themselves, badly and slowly, because that is how the repeatable pattern gets found. Only once you can explain who buys, why, at what price and through which conversation is there a job worth hiring for.
sparks.why: Sales leaders are hired for execution capability, which is the wrong skill during a search. The cost is not only salary but the early prospects consumed during a failed experiment.
sparks.apply: Do not hire a sales lead until you can write down a repeatable sales sequence that has closed several similar customers. Make those first sales yourself.

sparks.hook: The plan is not wrong at the end. It is wrong the whole way through.
sparks.insight: Startups do not follow a straight line from plan to product, and the process should expect that. After each round of customer contact you either confirm the assumption and continue, or change it and go back. Returning to an earlier stage is not a setback, it is the process working, and that matters because organisations which treat backtracking as failure hide the evidence instead. Build the loop in deliberately, so changing your mind is a normal event rather than a crisis.
sparks.why: Iteration only helps if the organisation permits it socially. Where reversing a decision is treated as incompetence, teams keep executing a plan they privately already know is wrong.
sparks.apply: Add a written checkpoint after each round of customer conversations, with two options on the page: continue as planned, or change a stated assumption and repeat.

sparks.hook: Premature scaling kills more startups than competitors do.
sparks.insight: Money raised on optimism gets spent on headcount, offices and campaigns that all assume the model is settled. When it is not, the company has simply increased its burn rate while learning nothing extra, and now needs a larger success in order to survive. Staying small during the search phase is not caution, it is what preserves enough runway to be wrong several times. The right moment to spend heavily is when spending more predictably produces more revenue, and not a month earlier.
sparks.why: During a search, additional spending rarely accelerates learning, but it always shortens runway. That asymmetry is why over-hiring straight after a funding round is such a common cause of failure.
sparks.apply: Write down what evidence would justify doubling your spending, then check whether you actually have it. If not, cut back and preserve six more months of search.

sparks.hook: The framework is dense, dated in places, and still largely right.
sparks.insight: It is written like a manual, in the technology-sales context of its era, with long checklists and enterprise assumptions that fit business software better than consumer products. Later work simplified and popularised the same ideas. What has held up is the core claim: that early-stage companies fail mainly because they execute a plan instead of testing one, and that the fix is a structured search run by the founders themselves. The packaging has aged. The diagnosis has not.
sparks.why: Its examples come mostly from enterprise technology, so the specific tactics transfer unevenly. The underlying process has been widely adopted since, which is weak evidence but a broad one.
sparks.apply: Take the sequence rather than the checklists. Adapt each stage to how buying actually happens in your market before adopting any specific template from it.

sparks.hook: Write down what would prove you wrong, before you build anything.
sparks.insight: Assumptions that stay in your head cannot be tested, because you will quietly adjust them to fit whatever you hear. Writing them as specific claims, with a number or a condition attached, makes them falsifiable: buyers of this type will pay this much, this channel will produce enquiries at this rate. Then each customer conversation becomes evidence for or against something specific, and the team can argue about facts rather than about competing intuitions.
sparks.why: Explicit, written predictions resist retrospective adjustment. This is the practical mechanism behind most of the process, and it is also the step teams most often skip entirely.
sparks.apply: Write your ten riskiest assumptions as testable claims with numbers in them, then design the cheapest test for the one you would most hate to be wrong about.

carousel.title: List the risky ones
carousel.body: Write every belief your business depends on, then keep the ones that would end the company if false. Those are the only ones worth testing early.

carousel.title: Add a number
carousel.body: Rewrite each as a claim with a figure or a condition attached. Vague beliefs cannot fail, which is exactly why they survive so long unexamined.

carousel.title: Design a cheap test
carousel.body: Find the least expensive way to get evidence: ten conversations, a landing page, a pre-order. A test does not have to be conclusive, only informative.

carousel.title: Update in writing
carousel.body: Record what the evidence showed and what you changed. Without that record the team will remember having believed whatever turned out to be true.

actions: Rewrite your business plan as a numbered list of assumptions, ranked by how much damage each would do if it turned out to be false.
Book ten customer conversations in the next fortnight, go to them yourself, and update a written assumption after every one.
Decide which of the four stages you are actually in, and stop any spending that belongs to a later stage than that.
Name your market type in one sentence and check that your first-year budget matches what that type of market actually requires.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a short readable introduction. It is a dense manual written for technology companies of its era, and later books cover the same ideas more accessibly.

verification.notes: First published 2005, self-published by the author. All prose here is original; the process is described in our own words.

books.title: The Mom Test
books.subtitle: How to Talk to Customers and Learn if Your Business is a Good Idea When Everyone is Lying to You
books.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
books.why_it_matters: It fixed the most common failure in early-stage building: founders running conversations that generate encouragement instead of evidence. Short, blunt, and still the standard reference for asking questions that can actually prove you wrong.

crux.headline: Ask about their life, never about your idea
crux.body: People lie to you in customer conversations, mostly out of kindness. They praise the idea, agree it is a problem, and promise to buy, because that is what politeness sounds like. The fix is not better wording but a different subject: stop discussing the thing you want to build and ask what they actually did the last time the problem occurred, what it cost them, and what they have already paid to fix it. Facts about the past are the only answers that carry information.

sparks.hook: A good meeting where nobody commits to anything is a bad meeting.
sparks.insight: The most dangerous outcome of a customer conversation is warmth. You leave energised, they said it sounded interesting, everybody smiled, and nothing about your situation has changed. Enthusiasm is free to give, so it tells you nothing. The only signals with weight are the ones that cost the other person something: time booked in a diary, money, or their reputation staked on an introduction to a colleague. Judge every conversation by what was given up, not by how it felt on the way out.
sparks.why: Verbal support has no cost, so it does not discriminate between people who will buy and people who are being kind. Costly signals do, which is why commitment is the only reliable early measurement available to you.
sparks.apply: End your next customer conversation by asking for something concrete: a follow-up with their manager, a paid trial, or a date in the diary. Record what they actually gave.

sparks.hook: Compliments are the sound of a conversation failing politely.
sparks.insight: When somebody says your idea is great, the interview has already gone wrong. They are being nice, which is the socially correct thing to do, and you have just spent the meeting talking rather than learning. The repair is to stop presenting entirely. Ask what they currently do about the problem, when it last happened, and what they did about it then. If the compliment arrives anyway, deflect it and return to their life, because praise is the least informative thing a potential customer can offer you.
sparks.why: Politeness norms make encouragement the default response to any pitch, which is why enthusiastic feedback correlates poorly with later purchasing. The information is in behaviour, not in approval.
sparks.apply: In your next three conversations, do not describe what you are building until the final two minutes. Spend the rest of the time asking how they handle the problem now.

sparks.hook: Stop asking what people want. Ask what they already did about it.
sparks.insight: Predictions about future behaviour are unreliable even when the person is trying hard to be honest, because nobody has good access to what they will do under conditions that have not happened yet. Their past is different. It is a record, not a guess. So the useful questions all point backwards: when did this last bite you, what did you do, how long did it take, what did you spend, who else was involved. Everything you learn that way is a fact, and facts survive contact with your business plan.
sparks.why: Stated preferences and revealed preferences diverge widely, especially for hypothetical purchases. Past behaviour is the closest thing to evidence you can obtain before you have a product to sell.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your interview script so that every question refers to something that has already happened, and delete anything containing the word would.

carousel.title: Narrow the segment
carousel.body: Keep splitting your target group until you can name where these people are and what they have in common. A segment you cannot find is a segment you cannot test.

carousel.title: Open with their day
carousel.body: Start with how the work actually happens now, step by step. You are mapping a routine, and the pain will show up inside it without you having to name it.

carousel.title: Find the last time
carousel.body: Ask when the problem last occurred and walk through it in detail. Specific incidents produce specific answers; general questions produce general noise.

carousel.title: Price the pain
carousel.body: Ask what it cost them: hours, money, a lost client, an argument with a colleague. A problem with no measurable cost is one nobody will pay to remove.

carousel.title: Ask for a step
carousel.body: Close by requesting something real: an introduction, a deposit, a scheduled trial. Their answer will tell you more than the previous half hour did.

sparks.hook: Asking someone whether they would buy this is close to useless.
sparks.insight: Asked directly, most people say yes. Refusing a hopeful founder feels unkind, and imagining a purchase is nothing like making one. The question also invites the other person to speculate about a version of themselves who does not exist yet. Replace it with questions about now: what are you using, what did it cost, how did you choose it, what would have to be true for you to switch. If you want a real answer about whether they will buy, offer to take their money today.
sparks.why: Hypothetical purchase intent overstates real demand, because the imagined transaction carries no budget, no approval process and no competing uses for the money attached to it.
sparks.apply: Replace every would-you question in your script with a what-do-you-currently question, then test the real one by asking for a pre-order or a deposit.

sparks.hook: The more formal the meeting, the worse the information you get.
sparks.insight: A scheduled interview with a slide deck puts the other person into a role: reviewer, adviser, polite audience. They start giving feedback on your presentation instead of describing their life. Casual conversations produce better data because nobody is performing. Ask your questions over coffee, in a corridor, in a message thread. You are not running a study. You are finding out how somebody actually works, and people describe that most accurately when they do not feel they are being surveyed.
sparks.why: Framing a conversation as an evaluation shifts the other person into critique mode, which produces opinions about your idea rather than descriptions of their behaviour. Informality lowers that pressure.
sparks.apply: Have your next three learning conversations without a deck, a demo or a scheduled slot. Keep the questions in your head and write the answers down straight afterwards.

sparks.hook: Find out who signs, or you are selling to someone who cannot buy.
sparks.insight: Enthusiasm from the person who feels the problem is not the same as a purchase, because in most organisations they are not the one who releases money. Part of every early conversation should map the machinery: who owns this budget, what does a purchase of this size require, who has stopped a similar decision before, and how long did the last comparable purchase take. Founders who skip this spend months delighting a champion who was never able to say yes on their own.
sparks.why: Buying processes contain several distinct roles: the user, the budget holder, and whoever can veto. Selling to only one of them is the most common way a promising pipeline stalls without any clear explanation.
sparks.apply: In your next sales conversation, ask how the last purchase of this kind was approved, who was involved, and how long it took from first meeting to payment.

sparks.hook: If you cannot describe how you might be wrong, you are not testing.
sparks.insight: Most founders enter customer conversations wanting to hear that the idea is good, and they get what they came for, because questions can be shaped to produce almost any answer. The discipline is to write down beforehand the specific belief you are checking and what evidence would count against it. Three questions per conversation is enough. If none of them could produce an answer you would find disappointing, you are collecting encouragement rather than information, and encouragement does not survive launch day.
sparks.why: Confirmation bias operates through question selection more than through interpretation. Pre-committing to a disconfirming test is the standard defence, and it works in commercial settings as well as scientific ones.
sparks.apply: Before your next conversation, write the three questions you most fear the answer to. Ask those first, while you still have the other person's full attention.

sparks.hook: Three kinds of answer sound useful and contain nothing at all.
sparks.insight: Bad data is dangerous because it feels like progress. Compliments are praise for you rather than facts about them. Fluff is anything hypothetical, general or about the future: what they usually do, what they would do, what they intend to do next year. Feature requests are the customer doing your job badly, guessing at a solution instead of describing the problem underneath it. Each has a repair, and running the repair turns a wasted meeting into a useful one without starting again.
sparks.why: These three categories cover most of what founders bring back from customer conversations. Naming them makes the failure visible in the moment, which is the only time it can actually be corrected.
sparks.apply: Read your last set of interview notes and mark each line as fact or non-fact. If most of the page is non-fact, rerun those conversations with better questions.

carousel.title: Deflect the praise
carousel.body: When someone compliments the idea, thank them briefly and immediately ask what they currently do instead. Praise is the moment to change subject, not to relax.

carousel.title: Anchor the fluff
carousel.body: When an answer is general or hypothetical, pull it into a specific event: when did that last happen, what did you do, and what did it cost you that day.

carousel.title: Dig under the request
carousel.body: When they ask for a feature, ask why they want it and what they are doing about it now. The reason is real data; the requested feature usually is not.

sparks.hook: Everyone is not a segment. Neither is small businesses.
sparks.insight: A group defined too broadly gives you contradictory answers, because you are averaging across people with different problems. Keep slicing until the segment shares a job, a workflow and a reason to care: not runners, but people training for a first marathon on a coached plan. The test of a good segment is practical. You should be able to say where to find twenty of them this week. If you cannot, the segment is a description rather than a market, and your interviews will keep producing noise.
sparks.why: Aggregating dissimilar users hides the signal, since strong demand in a narrow group looks like weak demand across a broad one. Narrow segments also make early distribution tractable rather than theoretical.
sparks.apply: Take your current target market and split it three times, until you can name a specific place where twenty of these people could be reached this week.

sparks.hook: The notes you did not write down are the ones you will invent later.
sparks.insight: Memory reconstructs conversations in a way that favours whatever you already believed. Within a day an ambiguous answer becomes supportive and a hesitation becomes enthusiasm, and there is no way to notice this from the inside. Write down what people said in their own words, as close to verbatim as you can manage, and mark clearly which parts are quotation and which are your interpretation. That record is what lets you and your co-founder argue about evidence instead of about recollections.
sparks.why: Reconstructive memory reliably drifts towards prior belief, and the drift is invisible to the person doing it. Contemporaneous notes are the cheapest correction available to a small team.
sparks.apply: Write up each customer conversation within an hour, separating what they said from what you concluded, and share both with whoever else makes product decisions.

actions: Book five conversations with people in one narrow segment and run all of them without describing what you are building until the final minutes.
Rewrite your interview script so every question is about something that has already happened, and delete anything hypothetical.
Ask for a real commitment at the end of every conversation, then track who gave time, money or an introduction and who gave only praise.
Map the buying process for your product: who uses it, who pays, who can veto, and how long the last comparable purchase took.
books.not_for_you_if: You already have paying customers and a working sales process, or you want a broad startup manual rather than one narrow discipline done properly.

verification.notes: First published 2013, self-published by the author. Prose here is original; the framework is described in our own words with no wording reproduced.

books.title: The Personal MBA
books.subtitle: Master the Art of Business
books.author: Josh Kaufman
books.why_it_matters: It argues that the useful content of a business degree is a set of mental models you can learn in a year of reading, then supplies them in one volume. As a map of how any company actually functions it has no obvious rival at this length.

crux.headline: Every business does the same five things
crux.body: Strip away the industry and every company runs the same loop: it creates something people want, gets those people to notice it, persuades enough of them to pay, delivers what was promised, and takes in more money than it spends doing so. If any one of the five is missing you have a project rather than a business. Most confusion about strategy dissolves once you can say which of the five is currently broken.

sparks.hook: A business is five processes. Yours is failing at one of them.
sparks.insight: Value creation, attention, persuasion, delivery, and money left over. Every company that survives does all five, and every company in trouble can usually name the one that has stopped working. This is more useful than it sounds, because founders tend to fix whichever part they enjoy. Engineers rebuild the product when the real problem is that nobody knows it exists. Marketers buy more traffic when delivery is so poor that customers leave anyway. Diagnose first and the correct work is usually obvious.
sparks.why: The five-part model is descriptive rather than predictive, but it works well as a checklist. Most persistent business problems turn out to be a single broken stage that was quietly being compensated for elsewhere.
sparks.apply: Score each of the five stages of your business from one to ten this week, then spend the following month working only on the lowest one.

carousel.title: Create something wanted
carousel.body: Make a thing that solves a problem people already have. If nobody has the problem, no amount of skill further down the chain can rescue it.

carousel.title: Earn attention
carousel.body: Get in front of people likely to want it. Attention is a separate discipline from building, and it does not arrive automatically because the product is good.

carousel.title: Convert to payment
carousel.body: Turn interest into a transaction by removing the specific reasons this buyer would hesitate. Interest that never becomes payment is a cost, not an asset.

carousel.title: Deliver reliably
carousel.body: Provide what was promised at a standard that produces repeat business. Delivery failures are the most expensive kind, since you already paid to acquire that customer.

carousel.title: Keep a margin
carousel.body: Take in more than you spend, with enough left to survive a bad quarter. Revenue without margin only accelerates the arrival of the problem.

sparks.hook: No market, no business. Everything else is a detail.
sparks.insight: The most common startup failure is not bad execution. It is building something skilfully for a group of people who do not want it badly enough to pay. Nothing downstream repairs this: better design, lower pricing, harder selling, all of it fails against an absent market. So the first question is never how to build the thing. It is whether a group of people already have this problem urgently, can be reached, and have money. Answering badly wastes years; answering early costs a few weeks.
sparks.why: Demand is the binding constraint most of the time. Execution quality matters enormously, but only within a market that exists, which is why market selection outranks nearly every other early decision.
sparks.apply: Before building further, write down where your buyers gather, how urgent the problem is, and what they currently spend on it. Any blank is a research task for this week.

sparks.hook: There are only about a dozen ways to charge for anything.
sparks.insight: Under the surface, business models repeat: sell a product, sell your time, rent shared access, charge a recurring fee, buy and resell, lease an asset, take a cut as an agent, gather an audience and sell its attention, lend money, sell an option, insure against a risk, or invest capital for a share. Knowing the list is practical, because many stuck businesses are simply running the wrong one. The same underlying value can often be delivered under a model that fits your costs far better.
sparks.why: The number of distinct ways value gets exchanged is small and stable across industries. Treating the model as a variable rather than a given opens options that product changes cannot reach.
sparks.apply: Write down your current model, then describe how you would deliver the same value as a subscription, as a shared resource, and as an agency. Cost each one roughly.

sparks.hook: Value is not in the thing. It is in what the buyer already wants.
sparks.insight: Nothing has value on its own. A product is worth what it does for a particular person given what they are already trying to achieve: to acquire something, to belong, to understand, to protect what they have, or to feel differently. Two customers can pay wildly different amounts for an identical item because the underlying drive differs. This is why arguing that your product is objectively good rarely moves anyone. You are not raising the quality. You are failing to connect it to a motive that already exists.
sparks.why: Value is subjective and contextual, which is standard economics rather than a novel claim. The practical consequence is that positioning against an existing motive beats improving the specification.
sparks.apply: For your main product, write down which human motive it serves most directly, then rewrite your headline so that motive appears in the first six words.

sparks.hook: You can grow revenue in only four ways. Pick one deliberately.
sparks.insight: Serve more customers, make each purchase larger, get people to buy more often, or charge more per unit. That is the whole list, and each option carries a different cost. Acquiring new customers is usually the most expensive and the most popular, because it feels like growth. Raising prices is the cheapest and the most feared. Increasing purchase frequency often requires the least new work of all, since the relationship and the delivery system already exist and the customers already trust you.
sparks.why: The four levers are arithmetically exhaustive for revenue. They differ enormously in marginal cost, so choosing the wrong one is the difference between profitable growth and expensive growth.
sparks.apply: Estimate what a ten percent gain would cost you through each of the four levers, then pursue only the cheapest one for the next quarter.

sparks.hook: The price is a decision you make, not a fact you discover.
sparks.insight: Most small businesses price by looking at competitors, which imports somebody else's cost structure and somebody else's mistakes. Other anchors are available. What would it cost this buyer to solve the problem another way, or to do nothing? What is the measurable financial gain from your work? Prices are also information: too low and buyers assume poor quality, too high and you attract customers expecting more support than they pay for. Choose the anchor consciously, then test it rather than defending it.
sparks.why: Price is one of the few variables that moves straight to profit, since raising it costs almost nothing to implement. It is also the variable founders adjust least often, usually out of fear.
sparks.apply: Raise the price of one offer by twenty percent for the next ten enquiries, and record what actually happens to your conversion rate before deciding anything.

carousel.title: Cost of replacement
carousel.body: Work out what it would cost the buyer to build or arrange this themselves, including their own time. That figure sets a rough ceiling on any discount.

carousel.title: Compare the market
carousel.body: Look at what similar things sell for, but treat it as a reference point rather than an instruction. Your competitors are guessing about price too.

carousel.title: Estimate the gain
carousel.body: Where the outcome is financial, estimate what your work is worth to the buyer over a year, then price as a defensible fraction of that number.

carousel.title: Test, do not agonise
carousel.body: Change the price and watch behaviour for a fixed period. Ten real enquiries tell you more than a month of internal debate ever will.

sparks.hook: Profit is an opinion. Cash in the account is a fact.
sparks.insight: A business can report profit while running out of money, because profit counts sales you have made and cash counts money you have actually received. The gap between them fills with unpaid invoices, stock sitting in a warehouse, and expenses paid in advance. Owners who watch only the profit line get ambushed by a payroll they cannot meet during their best quarter. Watching cash weekly is unglamorous, and it is the single financial habit most likely to keep a small business alive.
sparks.why: Accrual accounting recognises revenue when it is earned rather than when it is received. That is useful for measuring performance and actively dangerous as a guide to solvency.
sparks.apply: Set up a simple weekly view of money in, money out and the closing balance, and look at it every Monday before you look at any other number.

sparks.hook: Improving anything except the bottleneck improves nothing at all.
sparks.insight: Every system has one constraint that sets its total output, and work spent anywhere else just piles up inventory in front of it. A studio that can sell ten projects a month but deliver six is not helped by better marketing. A production line moves at the speed of its slowest station. The discipline is to find the constraint honestly, improve it until it moves somewhere else, then repeat. Most efficiency effort in small companies goes instead to whichever part was easiest to optimise.
sparks.why: This is the theory of constraints, and it holds for any system with sequential dependencies. The counter-intuitive part is that local improvements away from the bottleneck can make overall performance worse.
sparks.apply: Draw your delivery process as a sequence of stages with a capacity number on each. Find the smallest number and spend the next month on that stage alone.

sparks.hook: Automating a broken process gives you the same mess, faster.
sparks.insight: Software applied to a process nobody understands produces errors at a higher rate and hides them behind an interface. The order to work in is: do it manually until it is boring, write down the actual steps including the exceptions, simplify until several steps disappear, and only then automate what is left. Automation is also brittle in a way manual work is not. When it fails, the people who could have handled the exception have forgotten how, because the system was doing it for them.
sparks.why: Automation multiplies whatever the process already does, errors included. It also removes the practice that keeps human fallback capability alive, which is why the failures tend to arrive as surprises.
sparks.apply: Take the process you were about to automate and simplify it manually first. Remove two steps, then automate what remains and keep a written fallback procedure.

sparks.hook: Decide what enough looks like before the business decides for you.
sparks.insight: Companies expand to fill whatever ambition is available, and without a stated target the default is more of everything, indefinitely. Working out the number that would cover your costs, pay you properly and leave a buffer turns an open-ended race into a finite problem you can solve. It also changes decisions: once the target exists, an opportunity that doubles revenue and triples your working hours can be declined without it feeling like failure. Growth becomes a choice rather than an obligation.
sparks.why: Explicit targets convert vague ambition into a decision rule. Without one, every opportunity looks like a reason to expand, because there is no defined standard against which to decline it.
sparks.apply: Calculate the annual revenue and profit that would genuinely be enough for you, write it down, and use it to decline the next opportunity that misses it.

actions: Score each of the five stages of your business from one to ten, then spend the next month improving only the lowest-scoring stage.
Build a weekly cash view showing money in, money out and closing balance, and check it before any other number each Monday morning.
Map your delivery process stage by stage with a capacity figure on each, find the bottleneck, and work on nothing else until it moves.
Test a twenty percent price rise on one offer across your next ten enquiries and record the effect on conversion before deciding.
books.not_for_you_if: You want depth in one discipline, or you already run a business and know the fundamentals. It is deliberately broad, and each model gets only a few pages.

verification.notes: First published 2010 by Portfolio, with a revised edition later. All prose here is original and the models are described in our own words.

books.title: The Startup Owner's Manual
books.subtitle: The Step-by-Step Guide for Building a Great Company
books.author: Steve Blank and Bob Dorf
books.why_it_matters: The full checklist version of customer development, the method that gave the lean startup movement its engine. Nearly every accelerator curriculum in the world is a compressed version of what is set out here.

crux.headline: A startup is a search party, not a small company
crux.body: An established company executes a business model it already understands. A startup has only a stack of guesses about who the customer is, what hurts, and what they will pay. Confusing the two makes you build the wrong thing efficiently. Organise to search instead: numbered assumptions, cheap tests run by the founders themselves, and a rule that failing a test sends you backwards rather than forwards.

sparks.hook: A startup is not a small company. It is a search party.
sparks.insight: A company executes a business model it already knows. A startup does not have one yet — it has a set of guesses about who the customer is, what problem they have, and what they will pay. Confusing the two is the most expensive mistake in early business. If you organise like a company, with a sales target, a launch date and a functional org chart, you will spend the money building the wrong thing very efficiently. Organise to search instead: cheap experiments, fast rewrites, no permanent structures.
sparks.why: The failure mode is structural rather than personal. Execution machinery makes commitments hard to reverse, and a search phase needs everything to stay reversible until the model is proven.
sparks.apply: Write your business model as a list of numbered guesses. Mark the one that kills everything if it is wrong, and go and test that one first.

sparks.hook: There are no facts inside your building. Go outside and get some.
sparks.insight: Everything inside the office is opinion dressed as analysis: your roadmap, your persona document, your pricing, your competitive matrix. The facts live with the people who might pay you, and the only way to get them is to sit in front of those people repeatedly and ask. Founders have to do this themselves rather than hiring a research agency, because the point is not the report. The point is that the person deciding what to build has heard a customer be unimpressed, in their own voice.
sparks.why: Second-hand research strips out the tone, the hesitation and the ugly workaround the customer has already built, which is usually where the actual product is hiding.
