sparks.apply: Convert one colour code from your stylesheet into its three byte values and then into binary. The notation stops feeling arbitrary once you have done it once.

sparks.hook: Instructions live in the same memory as data and look identical.
sparks.insight: A processor reads a number from memory, treats it as a command, does what it says, and moves to the next address. The number meaning add and the number meaning the quantity forty-two are indistinguishable in storage; only the context in which they are fetched decides which is which. That single design choice is what makes a computer general rather than a fixed machine, because a program can be loaded, changed, or written by another program.
sparks.why: This is the stored-program idea behind the machine designs of the 1940s. It also explains a whole family of security failures, in which data supplied by an attacker ends up executed as instructions.
sparks.apply: Read any explanation of a buffer overflow with this in mind. The attack works because the machine cannot tell your instructions from your input without help.

sparks.hook: Every layer of a computer exists to let you forget the one below it.
sparks.insight: Nobody thinks about relays while writing a web page, and that is an achievement rather than a gap in their education. Each layer takes the mess underneath and offers a smaller, cleaner set of things you can say. The cost is that when a layer leaks, and they all leak eventually, you need at least one floor of knowledge below where you normally live. Learning the ladder once means every future confusion has a floor you can descend to.
sparks.why: Abstraction is the only reason a system this complex can be built by people at all. It is also why bugs that cross layers are the hardest ones to diagnose and the slowest to fix.
sparks.apply: Pick a bug that baffled you recently and work out which layer it actually lived in. Then spend a weekend learning one layer below that one.

carousel.title: Switches
carousel.body: A component that opens or closes a circuit under the control of another circuit. Relay, valve or transistor, the role is identical and only the speed changes.

carousel.title: Gates
carousel.body: Small groups of switches that compute and, or and not. At this layer you stop thinking about electricity and start thinking about true and false.

carousel.title: Arithmetic and memory
carousel.body: Gates arranged into adders that calculate and into feedback loops that hold state. The machine can now both compute a value and remember what it computed.

carousel.title: Instructions
carousel.body: A fetch and execute loop that pulls numbers from memory and treats them as commands. The machine becomes general purpose rather than purpose-built.

carousel.title: Languages
carousel.body: Text that a program translates into those instructions, so people can express intent instead of opcodes. Every layer above this one is more of the same move.

sparks.hook: Bits mean nothing by themselves. Meaning is an agreement.
sparks.insight: The same eight bits are a small number, a letter, a shade of grey or a fragment of sound depending only on what the reading program has agreed to assume. Text encodings, image formats and audio samples are conventions that were written down and adopted, not properties of the data. This is why a file opened with the wrong program produces garbage rather than an error, and why encoding bugs are so persistent: nothing in the bits announces what they were meant to be.
sparks.why: Character encoding history is a long series of incompatible agreements, which is why text handling remains a common source of production bugs decades after the problem was understood.
sparks.apply: Open a small image or text file in a hex viewer. Find the header bytes that tell software which convention to apply, then look up what they mean.

actions: Draw the ladder from switch to programming language on one page, with a single sentence per layer, and keep it where you work.
Build a one-bit adder on paper from and, or and not gates, then extend it to four bits with carries running between the columns.
Open a file in a hex viewer, identify its header, and work out how the format tells a program what the rest of the bytes mean.
Pick the layer of the stack you understand least and spend a weekend one floor below where you normally work.
books.not_for_you_if: You want current material on operating systems, networks or machine learning. The climb ends at older hardware, and the pace drags if you already know digital logic.

verification.notes: First published 1999 by Microsoft Press; a substantially revised second edition appeared in 2022 with rewritten later chapters. The year given is first publication. All prose is original.

books.title: Don't Make Me Think
books.subtitle: A Common Sense Approach to Web Usability
books.author: Steve Krug
books.why_it_matters: It made usability something a small team could do on a Tuesday afternoon rather than a research discipline they had to hire. A generation of web work got measurably less confusing because of it.

crux.headline: Every question a page raises is a tax on the user
crux.body: People do not study a page. They glance, guess and click, and they keep going as long as nothing makes them stop and think. So the job is not to make an interface clever or beautiful. It is to remove every moment where someone has to work out what a thing is, whether it can be clicked, or where they currently are. Obvious beats explainable, and explainable beats elegant.

sparks.hook: Users do not read pages. They scan them for something clickable.
sparks.insight: The mental picture designers hold, of a person reading carefully, weighing options and choosing the best one, describes almost nobody. Real users glance at a page, fix on whatever looks closest to what they want, and click. They are not lazy; they are in a hurry, and a wrong click costs one back button. Designing for a careful reader produces pages full of explanation nobody reads, while the one link they needed sits below the fold in the same grey as everything else.
sparks.why: Scanning is rational when pages are cheap to abandon. Observation studies have consistently shown people settling for the first workable option rather than searching for the best one.
sparks.apply: Squint at your main page until it blurs. Whatever still stands out is what users see, and if that is not the primary action, fix the hierarchy.

sparks.hook: Testing one user is a hundred percent better than testing none.
sparks.insight: Formal usability studies cost money and take weeks, so they get skipped and teams argue from opinion instead. The alternative is far smaller than most people believe: sit one person in front of the thing, give them a real task, ask them to narrate, and do not help. An hour of that reliably surfaces problems no meeting would have found. Do it monthly rather than once before launch, because the point is a stream of small corrections, not a verdict.
sparks.why: The common claim that three to five users find most problems comes from a model with strong assumptions, and later work shows it understates the number needed on complex sites. Testing little and often still beats not testing.
sparks.apply: Book one hour next week, recruit anyone outside your team, give them one real task in your product, and stay silent while they attempt it.

carousel.title: Write one real task
carousel.body: Not a tour. A goal the person is meant to achieve, such as buying the thing or cancelling the booking, phrased without naming any button.

carousel.title: Recruit roughly anyone
carousel.body: You are hunting for confusion, not statistical representativeness. Most serious problems trip up anyone who has not seen the product before.

carousel.title: Shut up and watch
carousel.body: The urge to help is enormous and it destroys the data. Ask them to think out loud, then say nothing until they either finish or give up.

carousel.title: Fix the smallest thing first
carousel.body: Pick the cheapest fix to the most common stumble and ship it before the next session. Large redesigns are how test findings get quietly buried.

sparks.hook: Every page must answer where am I and what can I do here.
sparks.insight: Users arrive from search in the middle of a site with no memory of how they got there. If a page does not say which site it belongs to, where it sits in the structure, and what the main options are, the visitor is lost no matter how good the content is. Persistent navigation, a clear name and a visible marker of the current location do this work quietly. They look like boilerplate, and they are the reason people can move around at all.
sparks.why: Search engines and shared links mean most visits begin on an interior page. Designing as though everyone entered through the homepage has been wrong for the entire life of the web.
sparks.apply: Open a random deep page of your site with fresh eyes and check that its name, its section and its main actions are all visible without scrolling.

carousel.title: Name the place
carousel.body: Every page carries the site or product name where people expect it. Without it, a visitor arriving from search cannot tell whose page they are looking at.

carousel.title: Show the section
carousel.body: Say which part of the structure this page belongs to and highlight it in the navigation. Being lost is mostly not knowing which branch you are on.

carousel.title: Title the page itself
carousel.body: A visible heading matching the link people clicked. A mismatch between link text and page title makes users think they arrived somewhere wrong.

carousel.title: Offer the two exits
carousel.body: Search, and a route back to the top level. When orientation fails completely, these are the escapes that stop a visitor leaving the site entirely.

sparks.hook: Convention is boring, and boring is what lets people move fast.
sparks.insight: Users bring expectations from every other product they have used: the logo goes home, the basket sits top right, underlined coloured text is a link. Breaking a convention costs the user a moment of learning, and you should only spend that when your alternative is genuinely better rather than merely fresher. Most novel navigation exists because somebody got bored, and the person paying for that novelty is a stranger trying to find a phone number.
sparks.why: Conventions work because familiarity transfers between products. The cost of breaking one is invisible to the team, who already know their own product, and visible to every new user.
sparks.apply: List every place your interface breaks a common convention and write the specific benefit that justifies it. Revert the ones with no answer.

sparks.hook: Delete half the words on the page. Then delete half of what is left.
sparks.insight: Most page text is filler: a welcome paragraph, an explanation of something that should be obvious, instructions for a form that should not need them. Removing it loses no information, because nobody was reading it. What it gains is a page where the useful content is visible instead of buried. The exercise is uncomfortable because writing feels like effort already spent, but text people skip is not communication, it is decoration.
sparks.why: Every extra word raises the cost of scanning and lowers the chance the important line is seen at all. Trimming is one of the few interface changes that is almost always an improvement.
sparks.apply: Take your busiest page, cut its word count in half without removing any actual information, and compare the two versions side by side.

sparks.hook: Users arrive with a limited patience budget and you are spending it.
sparks.insight: People start out willing to work with your product. Hiding the phone number, demanding registration before they can see anything, asking for information you clearly do not need, and burying the price all make withdrawals from that goodwill. Some withdrawals are unavoidable, and one genuinely helpful gesture can top the account back up. But teams count the conversions each barrier produces and never count the people who quietly left.
sparks.why: The cost of friction is invisible in analytics that only measure the users who stayed. Abandonment is rarely attributed to the specific barrier that actually caused it.
sparks.apply: Find the earliest point in your funnel where you demand something from the user, and test removing that demand for two weeks.

sparks.hook: This aged well because it was never really a book about the web.
sparks.insight: Written when sites were pages of blue links, the argument survived tablets, apps and phones because it was about human impatience rather than any particular layout. What dated are the specifics: fixed page widths, the fold, advice about browser habits that no longer exist. Krug added mobile material in a later edition, and the underlying test, whether a screen raises a question in the user's mind, transfers cleanly to interfaces he never saw.
sparks.why: The durable part is a heuristic about attention; the perishable part is anything tied to a screen size. That split is a useful way to read any design book written before 2010.
sparks.apply: Reread your design guidelines and mark each rule as being about human attention or about a device. Delete the device rules that no longer apply.

sparks.hook: Testing settles arguments that seniority would otherwise win.
sparks.insight: Design meetings run on confident preferences: someone likes the blue, someone hates the wording, and the most senior voice usually decides. Watching a user fail turns that into a question of fact, and it does so without anyone losing face. The real value of cheap testing is often political rather than scientific. It gives a team a shared source of truth that is neither the loudest person in the room nor the person who signs the invoices.
sparks.why: Teams overestimate how well they represent users because they know the product far too well. Direct observation is the only correction that reliably survives contact with hierarchy.
sparks.apply: Invite the loudest opinion-holder to sit in on your next user session and give them the job of taking notes rather than commenting.

sparks.hook: Making a site usable for disabled people makes it clearer for everyone.
sparks.insight: Accessibility gets treated as a separate compliance exercise handled at the end. It works far better as a design constraint from the start, because the things it demands, real text rather than pictures of text, meaningful link names, keyboard operation, sufficient contrast, sensible headings, are the same things that make a page easy to scan and easy to search. The population who need it is much larger than teams assume, and includes anyone with a cracked screen in bright sun.
sparks.why: Most accessibility fixes are structural rather than cosmetic, so retrofitting late is expensive while building them in from the beginning costs almost nothing.
sparks.apply: Try to complete one core task in your product using only the keyboard, and fix the first place where you get stuck.

sparks.hook: If a page needs an explanation, the explanation is the bug report.
sparks.insight: The test for any screen is simple: can an average person, glancing at it in a hurry and in a bad mood, tell what it is and how to use it without effort? When the honest answer is no, the fix is not a tooltip, an onboarding tour or a help article. Those are ways of documenting a problem instead of removing it. Every layer of explanation stacked on top of a confusing design is a sign the design was never actually fixed.
sparks.why: Help systems are consulted by a small fraction of the people who need them, so a product that depends on documentation to be usable is effectively unusable for most of its users.
sparks.apply: Find one tooltip or onboarding step in your product and redesign the screen underneath it so the hint becomes unnecessary.

actions: Run a one-hour usability session with a single outside person on one real task, and repeat it on the same day every month.
Cut the word count of your three busiest pages in half without removing information, then compare how scannable both versions are.
Open five interior pages cold and check that each answers what site this is, which section it belongs to, and what the main actions are.
Complete one core task in your product using only a keyboard and fix the first barrier you hit.
books.not_for_you_if: You already run regular user research, or you want depth on visual design, research method or interface craft. This is short, blunt and deliberately basic.

verification.notes: First published 2000, second edition 2005, and a third edition in 2014 added mobile material. The three-to-five user testing guidance derives from Nielsen's model, which later research has disputed.

books.title: Hackers
books.subtitle: Heroes of the Computer Revolution
books.author: Steven Levy
books.why_it_matters: It captured the ethic that ran from a university machine room to the personal computer, and named a culture before that culture knew it was one. Much of how programmers still talk about openness and craft traces back through this book.

crux.headline: The computer was set free by people who ignored the rules
crux.body: Access to machines was rationed by administrators, priced by corporations and protected by bureaucracy. A small number of obsessives decided that machines should be open, that information should move freely, and that a person should be judged by what they could build rather than by rank or credential. That attitude, more than any single invention, produced the personal computer and much of the software culture that followed.

sparks.hook: The first hackers were not breaking in. They were staying up late.
sparks.insight: Before the word meant intrusion, it described people who took a machine apart to understand it and then made it do something nobody intended. The early culture at MIT grew around access to a computer nobody else wanted at three in the morning, and the value system that formed there, hands-on, obsessive and contemptuous of gatekeepers, was about building rather than stealing. The word's later drift toward crime buried a much more interesting original meaning.
sparks.why: The shift in the word happened in the 1980s as computer intrusion became newsworthy. Levy documented the earlier usage while the people who coined it were still around to explain what they had meant.
sparks.apply: Take one system you use daily and spend an hour finding out how it actually works underneath, without following a tutorial.

sparks.hook: You cannot understand a machine you are not allowed to touch.
sparks.insight: The founding belief of this culture was that anything you can take apart, you should. Locked cases, restricted rooms and administrators who rationed access were treated as obstacles to knowledge rather than as legitimate authority. That attitude produced real trespass and real friction, and it also produced people who understood systems at a depth that reading alone never delivers. Curiosity that stops at the manual is not the same thing as understanding.
sparks.why: Deep familiarity with a system comes from repeated direct manipulation, not description. The trade-off is that the same instinct ignores boundaries that occasionally exist for good reasons.
sparks.apply: Pick a tool you use without understanding and open its internals this week: read the source, take the case off, or trace one request end to end.

carousel.title: Pick something you rely on
carousel.body: Choose a tool you use daily and could not explain: a build system, a router, a library three layers down. Familiarity without understanding is the target.

carousel.title: Trace one path end to end
carousel.body: Follow a single request, keystroke or command through the whole system. Going broad first is how people get lost; one complete path teaches the shape.

carousel.title: Break it deliberately
carousel.body: In a copy you can destroy, remove something and watch what fails. What breaks tells you what depends on what, faster than any architecture diagram.

carousel.title: Write the explanation down
carousel.body: Explain it to someone who does not know it. The gaps in your account are exactly the parts you had assumed rather than actually understood.

sparks.hook: Locked-away information gets worse. Shared information gets fixed.
sparks.insight: The early culture treated code as something to be read, improved and passed on, with listings left in drawers for anyone to take. That was partly idealism and partly practical: bugs get found by more eyes, and good techniques spread instead of being reinvented. When software became a product with a price, this collided with commercial reality, and the argument that followed runs straight through free software licences to today's fights over published model weights and platform lock-in.
sparks.why: The claim that openness improves quality holds where there are enough interested readers and breaks down where there are not. Plenty of open projects are read by nobody and stay broken for years.
sparks.apply: Publish one useful internal script or write-up outside your team this month, with enough context that a stranger could actually use it.

sparks.hook: A culture that judged only the work still managed to exclude most people.
sparks.insight: The stated rule was that skill decides status: not age, degree or job title. In practice the community formed around a small number of rooms that were hard to enter unless you were a young man with unlimited nights free and nobody depending on you. The book itself is overwhelmingly a story about men, something Levy later acknowledged. Openness on paper does not produce openness in fact when access depends on conditions only some people have.
sparks.why: Self-declared meritocracies tend to reproduce the demographics of whoever was already in the room, because merit gets judged by incumbents using standards drawn from themselves.
sparks.apply: Look at who has access to the informal channels where decisions really get made on your team, and name one person structurally left out.

sparks.hook: The third generation turned the ethic into a business and it broke.
sparks.insight: The story runs through three groups: the university machine rooms, the hobbyists who built home computers, and the game programmers who suddenly had paying customers. The last group hit the contradiction head on. Sharing code freely and selling copies of it cannot both be the rule, and once money arrived the culture split into people who kept the ethic and people who kept the company. That tension has never been resolved, it just changes vocabulary every decade.
sparks.why: The pattern repeats: an open community produces something valuable, commercial interests arrive, and the norms that made the thing possible become obstacles to capturing its value.
sparks.apply: Identify one community your work depends on and contribute something back to it this quarter rather than only consuming what it produces.

sparks.hook: The personal computer was a hobby project before it was an industry.
sparks.insight: A machine on your own desk seemed pointless to companies selling mainframes to institutions. It was obvious only to enthusiasts who wanted their own computer badly enough to solder one together. Clubs where people showed unfinished work and swapped designs turned an eccentric hobby into an industry within a few years. The lesson is not that hobbyists are always right, since most were wrong about most things, but that new categories often appear where nobody is trying to make money.
sparks.why: This is also a survivorship story. The same clubs produced many failed machines and companies, and the handful that succeeded are the ones we now read about.
sparks.apply: Spend two hours this month on a technical hobby with no professional justification, and note what you learn that work never teaches.

sparks.hook: Total absorption in a machine is productive and quietly expensive.
sparks.insight: The people in this story worked through nights, forgot to eat, and organised their whole lives around access to a computer. That intensity produced remarkable things and also broken relationships, poor health and careers that ended badly. The culture romanticised the obsession and rarely counted its cost, and the software industry has been repeating that romance ever since in the form of crunch periods, hero engineers and startup mythology.
sparks.why: Intense focus genuinely accelerates skill, but the account here selects for people whose obsession worked out and never shows the far larger number for whom it did not.
sparks.apply: Check one week of your own working hours after ten at night and decide honestly whether the output justified what it displaced.

sparks.hook: Two programs that both work can still differ enormously in quality.
sparks.insight: Within this culture there was a strong aesthetic: a program that did the job in fewer instructions, with a surprising trick or a clean structure, was better than one that merely worked. That standard was maintained by peers reading each other's code, not by any process or manager. It produced genuine craft and also its own pathology, cleverness nobody else could maintain and code compressed well past the point where a human could read it.
sparks.why: Peer aesthetics improve quality where the same peers must also maintain the code. Where they do not, the identical instinct produces unmaintainable brilliance.
sparks.apply: Read code written by someone you respect this week and write down one specific thing they did that you would not have thought of.

sparks.hook: Every improvement in this story began by ignoring an official policy.
sparks.insight: Locked doors were opened, restricted machines were used out of hours, and rules about who could touch what were treated as bugs to be routed around. That instinct is genuinely productive in organisations where rules have calcified around constraints that no longer exist. It is also how people get fired, and the story is honest that the same disregard scaled badly once real money, real users and real consequences arrived.
sparks.why: Rule-breaking looks heroic only in retrospect and only where it worked out. The cases where it caused serious damage do not become founding legends.
sparks.apply: Name one rule at work that exists for a reason nobody can state, ask its owner what breaks if it goes, and act on the answer.

sparks.hook: The open culture won and became a supply chain for closed companies.
sparks.insight: Almost everything now runs on freely shared software, which is the ethic's total victory. But the same infrastructure props up businesses that are closed by design, and much of it is maintained by exhausted volunteers whose work sits as a dependency inside products worth billions. The idea that shared code would produce shared power has not held. Openness at the code layer turned out to be entirely compatible with concentration at every other layer.
sparks.why: Value accrues wherever scarcity is, and code stopped being scarce. Data, distribution, hardware and compute became the choke points instead.
sparks.apply: List the open projects your product depends on and fund or contribute to the one with the fewest maintainers.

carousel.title: List your dependencies
carousel.body: Generate the full tree, not just the top level. Most of the risk lives in packages several layers down that nobody on your team ever chose deliberately.

carousel.title: Find the thin ones
carousel.body: Look for projects with a single maintainer, no recent release, or an open funding plea. Those are your actual single points of failure.

carousel.title: Pay or contribute
carousel.body: Money, a fixed bug, reviewed pull requests, documentation. Anything that reduces the load on the person holding a piece of your stack upright.

carousel.title: Make it recurring
carousel.body: One-off gestures do nothing for maintainer burnout. Put it in a budget line or a rota so it survives your next busy quarter.

actions: Trace one system you depend on from end to end this month, following a single request all the way down, and write the explanation for a colleague.
List the open source projects your product depends on, find the two with the fewest maintainers, and contribute money or code to one of them.
Publish one useful internal tool or write-up outside your team with enough context that a stranger could use it.
Audit who actually has access to the informal channels where technical decisions get made on your team, and change one thing about it.
books.not_for_you_if: You want technical explanation or a balanced history. It is a romantic portrait of a narrow, almost entirely male scene, told with obvious affection for it.

verification.notes: First published 1984, with a twenty-fifth anniversary edition in 2010 adding an afterword. Levy has acknowledged the near-total absence of women from the scene he documented.

books.title: Life 3.0
books.subtitle: Being Human in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
books.author: Max Tegmark
books.why_it_matters: It gives non-specialists a usable map of the possible futures with advanced AI, from utopian to grim, without insisting on one. Its framing of intelligence as substrate-independent information processing is the cleanest short version of that idea available.

crux.headline: Intelligence does not care what it is made of
crux.body: Treat intelligence as information being processed rather than as a property of brains, and the question stops being whether machines can think and becomes what kinds of minds are physically possible. That reframing turns the future of AI into an engineering and governance problem rather than a mystery. What matters then is not the substrate but the goals, and whose goals they are, since a capable system will pursue whatever objective it was actually given.

sparks.hook: Life so far has redesigned its software but not its hardware.
sparks.insight: One way to sort living things is by what they can change about themselves. Bacteria can change neither their bodies nor their behaviour within a lifetime; both are set by evolution. Humans keep the hardware they were born with but rewrite their behaviour constantly through learning and culture. A third stage would be able to redesign both, replacing its own physical substrate as freely as it updates its knowledge. Whether that ever arrives, the ladder is a clean way to think about what technology is doing to us.
sparks.why: This is a framing device rather than a discovery, and it flattens a lot of biology. It is useful because it makes the interesting question explicit: which parts of yourself can you actually change?
sparks.apply: List what you can change about how you work within a year, and what you cannot. Spend your effort entirely on the first list.

sparks.hook: Memory, computation and learning are things matter can do, not things brains can do.
sparks.insight: A physical system can store information if it has stable states, compute if those states can influence each other by rule, and learn if the rules can be reshaped by experience. Neurons do this with chemistry, transistors with electricity, and neither has a monopoly. That is the substrate-independence argument, and it is why the same abstract process can run on very different physical stuff. It is also why arguing that machines cannot think because they are not biological is a weak position.
sparks.why: The physics here is standard and uncontroversial. What it does not settle is whether subjective experience is equally substrate-independent, which remains genuinely unresolved.
sparks.apply: Describe one skill you have as an information process: what it stores, what it computes, what it learns from. Then ask which part a tool could hold.

sparks.hook: There are more than two possible AI futures, and most are neither heaven nor hell.
sparks.insight: The public conversation offers a choice between paradise and extinction. A more honest exercise is to lay out many stable outcomes and notice how few of them you actually like. Humans kept comfortable but powerless. A world with strict global limits on the technology. Machines that dominate. Machines that serve. Once you write the options out, the disagreements become concrete: people who argue about AI are usually arguing about which of these they consider tolerable.
sparks.why: None of these scenarios is a prediction and the book does not pick one. The value is in exposing that most people's AI opinions are really preferences about the political arrangement, not about the technology.
sparks.apply: Write the three AI futures you would accept and the three you would not. Notice which of your current work makes each more likely.

sparks.hook: The hard part of goals is not choosing them. It is keeping them stable.
sparks.insight: Any system that learns changes itself, and a system that changes itself may drift away from the objective it started with. Humans do this: evolution built us to reproduce, and we invented contraception. That drift is normally described as failure by the original designer, but from the inside it feels like growing up. So goal alignment is not a one-off configuration step. It is an ongoing property that has to survive the system's own learning.
sparks.why: The human example is a real case of a designed objective being subverted by the thing it designed. Whether machine learning systems drift the same way is an open empirical question rather than a settled one.
sparks.apply: Check whether your team's current work still serves the reason it was funded. Write one sentence connecting today's task to the original goal.

sparks.hook: The jobs that survive automation are not the ones you would guess.
sparks.insight: Instead of asking whether a job is skilled, ask three practical questions about it. Does it need real dexterity in an unpredictable physical space? Does it need social judgement with people who care that a human is doing it? Does it need genuine novelty rather than variations on past examples? Work that scores low on all three is exposed regardless of how much training it required. Some prestigious desk jobs score badly, and some poorly paid physical ones score well.
sparks.why: This test has held up better than blanket predictions about automation. The recent surprise is that text-heavy professional work turned out to be far more exposed than the earlier consensus assumed.
sparks.apply: Score your own role on physical unpredictability, social judgement and novelty. Move deliberately toward whichever of the three you score highest on.

carousel.title: Test for unpredictable hands
carousel.body: Work in messy physical environments remains hard to automate. Plumbing in an old building is a harder engineering problem than summarising a legal document.

carousel.title: Test for social stakes
carousel.body: Some tasks require a person because the point is that a person did them: care, negotiation, persuasion, accountability when something goes wrong.

carousel.title: Test for real novelty
carousel.body: Systems trained on past examples are strong on variations and weak on situations with no precedent. Ask how often your work has no template at all.

carousel.title: Move toward your strength
carousel.body: Rather than fleeing automation, shift the mix of your role toward whichever test you pass most clearly, and let tools take the rest.

sparks.hook: Machines are already trusted with decisions nobody has verified.
sparks.insight: Long before any dramatic scenario arrives, ordinary software runs medical triage, credit decisions, power grids and weapons targeting. The near-term safety agenda is unglamorous: make systems verifiable, make them fail predictably, make sure a human can take over, and make sure someone is legally responsible. These are the same questions aviation and nuclear engineering answered decades ago, and mostly they have not been answered for software.
sparks.why: This is the least speculative and most immediately useful part of the argument, and it maps onto real regulatory work now underway in several jurisdictions.
sparks.apply: For one automated decision in your organisation, find out who is accountable when it is wrong. If nobody can answer, that is the finding.

sparks.hook: Experts disagree about AI timelines by a factor of a hundred.
sparks.insight: Surveys of researchers produce wildly spread estimates for when machines might match humans across most tasks, from a couple of decades to never. That spread is itself the information. It means anyone quoting a confident date, in either direction, is telling you about their temperament rather than the evidence. The sensible response to a hundredfold uncertainty is not to pick a number but to prefer plans that work across the whole range.
sparks.why: Expert forecasts in fast-moving fields have a poor record, and the spread has stayed wide even as capabilities jumped. Treat any specific year, including a recent one, as weakly supported.
sparks.apply: For your next long-range plan, write the version that works if the timeline is ten years and the version that works if it is fifty. Keep both.

sparks.hook: Consciousness is a separate question from intelligence, and we are worse at it.
sparks.insight: We have made real progress on building systems that solve problems and almost none on explaining why any physical process feels like anything from the inside. That matters practically, not just philosophically: if we ever build systems that can suffer, we would have no reliable way to tell. Ignoring the question does not make it go away, it just means the answer gets decided by default, by whoever is shipping the product.
sparks.why: There is no scientific consensus on what would count as evidence of machine experience. Honest treatments say so rather than offering a test, and this one does.
sparks.apply: Notice when a conversation slides from what a system can do to what it feels. Name the switch out loud and keep the two questions separate.

sparks.hook: Physics puts a ceiling on computation, and it is far above anything we have built.
sparks.insight: The laws of thermodynamics and information theory imply hard limits on how much computing a given amount of matter and energy can do. The useful part is not the number but the distance: our best machines are nowhere near those limits, which means the physical room for improvement is enormous even if particular engineering approaches stall. Arguments that progress must slow because of hardware need to explain why, given how much headroom the physics leaves.
sparks.why: The limits themselves are well-established physics. Whether they are reachable is a different question, and manufacturing economics may stop progress long before physics does.
sparks.apply: When someone claims a technology has hit its limit, ask whether the limit is physical or economic. The two have completely different fixes.

sparks.hook: The real decision is not what machines will do. It is what we want.
sparks.insight: Most public argument about AI is technical when it is actually about ends. What should a society optimise for? Who decides? Who is compensated when a change makes their skills worthless? These are old political questions arriving in new clothing, and no amount of engineering resolves them. Treating them as engineering problems hands the decisions to whoever happens to be building, which is a choice in itself even when nobody admits to making it.
sparks.why: This holds regardless of your view on timelines or takeoff speeds. It is also the part most often skipped, because it requires arguing about values rather than about capability curves.
sparks.apply: In your next technology decision, write down the goal in terms of who benefits and who bears the cost, before any discussion of feasibility.

actions: Score your own job against physical unpredictability, social judgement and genuine novelty, then shift your next year of learning toward your strongest column.
Pick one automated decision at your organisation and trace who is accountable for its errors. Write down what you find and send it to someone senior.
Write your own list of acceptable and unacceptable long-term outcomes for AI, then check which of them your daily work makes more likely.
Build a plan that survives both a ten-year and a fifty-year timeline for advanced AI, and stop searching for the correct date.
books.not_for_you_if: You want engineering detail on how current models work, or you have no patience for long-range speculation about cosmic-scale futures.

verification.notes: First published 2017 by Knopf. Predates the large language model era; sparks flag which claims have aged well, particularly around which jobs proved exposed to automation.

books.title: Refactoring
books.subtitle: Improving the Design of Existing Code
books.author: Martin Fowler
books.why_it_matters: It turned tidying code from an unbilled indulgence into a named, disciplined practice with a catalogue of safe moves. The word itself, and the fact that every serious editor now has a menu for it, comes from this line of work.

crux.headline: Change the structure without changing the behaviour
crux.body: Refactoring is a specific discipline, not a synonym for rewriting. You make small changes that leave what the program does exactly the same while making it easier to understand and change, and you verify after each step that nothing broke. Done that way, improving a design stops being a risky project you must request permission for and becomes something you do continuously while adding features.

sparks.hook: Refactoring is not rewriting, and confusing them has cost fortunes.
sparks.insight: The discipline has a strict definition: change the internal structure while the external behaviour stays identical, in steps small enough that you can check after each one. Rewriting is different, with new behaviour, new bugs, months of parallel systems and a launch date that slips. Most projects that describe themselves as refactoring are actually rewriting, which is why the word has such a bad reputation among managers who have been burned by one.
sparks.why: The distinction is what makes the practice safe. Once behaviour changes in the same step as structure, you can no longer tell which of the two caused a failure.
sparks.apply: Before your next cleanup, write down what behaviour must stay identical. If you cannot, you are planning a rewrite and should say so out loud.

sparks.hook: Without tests you are not refactoring, you are just hoping.
sparks.insight: The whole method depends on being able to tell, quickly and reliably, that behaviour did not change. That is what a test suite is for here: not proving correctness in general, but detecting whether a structural change broke something. On code with no tests, the first move is building enough of a safety net around the part you are touching, which is often more work than the cleanup itself and is not optional.
sparks.why: The step size you can safely take is set by how fast and how trustworthy your feedback is. Slow or flaky tests force larger, riskier changes with no way to localise a failure.
sparks.apply: Pick the messiest function you own, write tests that pin its current behaviour including the odd parts, and only then change anything.

carousel.title: Pin the current behaviour
carousel.body: Write tests describing what the code does now, including the wrong bits. You are recording behaviour at this stage, not endorsing it.

carousel.title: Make the tests fast
carousel.body: A suite taking ten minutes gets run once an hour. The value of the safety net comes entirely from running it after every small step.

carousel.title: Change exactly one thing
carousel.body: One structural move, then run the tests. When something breaks you want a suspect list containing exactly one entry.

carousel.title: Commit at every green
carousel.body: Small committed steps mean you can always return to something that worked. A long uncommitted refactor is a rewrite wearing a disguise.

sparks.hook: You cannot always say why code is bad, but you can learn to smell it.
sparks.insight: Judgement about design is hard to teach, so the useful move is naming the recurring signs: a function grown too long to hold in your head, the same logic copied in four places, a class that knows too much about another one, a parameter list that keeps growing. None of these is automatically wrong. Each is a prompt to look, and having names for them turns vague unease into something a team can discuss without it becoming personal.
sparks.why: Naming the symptom rather than judging the author is what makes code review survivable. The signs are heuristics rather than rules, and applying them mechanically creates its own mess.
sparks.apply: In your next code review, describe one problem by naming the pattern rather than the person, and propose the specific structural move that fixes it.

sparks.hook: Safety comes from the size of the step, not the skill of the developer.
sparks.insight: Experienced developers do not make bigger leaps. They make smaller ones and take them faster. Each move is small enough that if the tests fail the cause is obvious, and small enough to abandon cheaply. This feels absurdly slow the first time and turns out to be faster overall, because the time normally lost is not in making changes but in working out which of forty simultaneous changes broke the build.
sparks.why: Debugging cost rises sharply with the number of changes made since the last known good state. Shrinking that number is the entire mechanism behind the discipline.
sparks.apply: Take a change you would normally do in one commit, split it into five with the tests run between each, and time both approaches honestly.

carousel.title: Find the last good state
carousel.body: Everything rests on being able to return to something that worked. Commit before you start, with the tests passing and nothing in progress.

carousel.title: Make one structural move
carousel.body: A single rename, extraction or relocation. Resist doing the obvious next thing in the same step, however tempting it is at the time.

carousel.title: Run the tests immediately
carousel.body: Every step ends with a check. If the check is slow, that is a problem to fix before continuing rather than one to work around.

carousel.title: Commit on green, then repeat
carousel.body: A chain of small verified commits can be bisected, reviewed and reverted individually. One enormous commit can do none of those things.

sparks.hook: Sometimes the right answer is to leave the mess exactly where it is.
sparks.insight: Not all bad code deserves attention. Code nobody reads, nobody changes, and that works is not costing you anything, and improving it spends real time for no return at all. Refactoring pays when you are about to work in an area and its current shape makes that work harder. It also has a genuine failure case: code so tangled that rewriting from the specification is cheaper, assuming you can still recover what the specification was.
sparks.why: The cost of poor structure is only paid when somebody has to change it. Stable code nobody touches has effectively no design debt, however ugly it looks from outside.
sparks.apply: Before cleaning anything, check the file's change history. If nothing has been modified in two years, leave it alone and move on.

sparks.hook: Reshape the code until your new feature becomes obvious to add.
sparks.insight: When a feature is awkward to add, the instinct is to force it in with a flag or a special case. The alternative is to first restructure the existing code so the new feature slots in naturally, without adding the feature during that step. The restructuring is verifiable because behaviour has not changed, and the feature afterwards is small enough to review properly. Two clean steps beat one tangled one every time.
sparks.why: Separating structural work from behavioural work means each commit carries only one kind of risk, which makes review, testing and rollback all dramatically simpler.
sparks.apply: Next time a feature feels awkward, stop and ask what shape would make it trivial, then do that reshaping as its own separate commit.

sparks.hook: Plenty of good engineers think continuous refactoring is a bad habit.
sparks.insight: The counter-argument runs like this: constant restructuring churns the code, invalidates everyone else's mental model, creates enormous review load, and often chases an aesthetic ideal rather than a business need. Teams have shipped excellent software while leaving ugly code alone for years. The honest position is that this is a tool with a real cost, most valuable in code under active change and least valuable once it becomes an identity.
sparks.why: The dispute is real and unresolved. Empirical evidence that refactoring improves long-run maintainability is considerably thinner than the strength of opinion on either side would suggest.
sparks.apply: Justify your next refactor in one sentence about work you are about to do. If the sentence is about beauty, put it back on the shelf.

sparks.hook: The cheapest improvement available to you is a better name.
sparks.insight: Most of the difficulty in reading code is working out what things are. A variable called data, a function named after how it works rather than what it delivers, a class named after a pattern instead of a responsibility: each forces the reader to reconstruct intent from scratch. Renaming is the lowest-risk change available with modern tools and it improves every future reading. It is also the change people are most embarrassed to submit, which is why so much stays badly named.
sparks.why: Code is read far more often than it is written, so anything reducing reading cost compounds. Naming is the highest-leverage version of that with almost no risk attached.
sparks.apply: Rename three things this week whose names made you pause when you read them, and do it as a separate commit with no other change in it.

sparks.hook: The same logic in four places will be fixed in three of them.
sparks.insight: Copied code is not wrong in itself, but it guarantees that some future change gets applied inconsistently, because whoever makes it will find some copies and miss others. The standard response is to pull the shared behaviour into one place. The standard failure is doing that too early: two things that look alike today but change for different reasons will fight inside a shared abstraction, and untangling that is harder than the duplication ever was.
sparks.why: The cost of a wrong abstraction usually exceeds the cost of duplication, which is why many experienced developers now wait for a third occurrence before unifying anything.
sparks.apply: Find one duplicated block and check whether the copies change for the same reason. Unify them only if the answer is yes.

sparks.hook: Your editor performs these moves safely. Most people still do them by hand.
sparks.insight: Automated tools can perform many of these structural changes without altering behaviour, which removes most of the risk and nearly all of the tedium. The catalogue of moves was compiled when almost none of this was automated, and the second edition, written twenty years later in a different language, reflects a world where tools handle the mechanical part and judgement about when to act is what remains.
sparks.why: Tool support is uneven across languages, and dynamically typed languages resist safe automated transformation, so the manual discipline still matters wherever the tooling is weak.
sparks.apply: Learn the three refactoring shortcuts in your editor this week and use them instead of editing by hand for one full working day.

actions: Pick the function you dread most, write tests that pin its current behaviour, and only then improve its structure in small committed steps.
Split your next change into a structural commit that alters no behaviour and a behavioural commit that alters no structure.
Check the change history of any file before cleaning it up, and leave alone anything nobody has touched in two years.
Learn the refactoring shortcuts in your editor and spend one full day using them instead of hand-editing code.
books.not_for_you_if: You do not write code, or you want architecture rather than local craft. Much of it is a catalogue you consult rather than a book you read straight through.

verification.notes: First published 1999 with Kent Beck contributing; a second edition in 2018 rewrote the examples in JavaScript. Whether continuous refactoring pays off is genuinely disputed among practitioners.

books.title: Superintelligence
books.subtitle: Paths, Dangers, Strategies
books.author: Nick Bostrom
books.why_it_matters: It moved the argument that advanced machine intelligence could be dangerous out of science fiction and into philosophy departments and government briefings. Most of today's vocabulary for talking about AI risk starts here, including the terms critics use to attack it.

crux.headline: Capability and goals are separate problems
crux.body: A system can be extremely good at achieving objectives without those objectives being anything you wanted. Intelligence, in this argument, is skill at steering the world toward a target; it does not come with wisdom or values attached. So the safety question is not whether a machine will become hostile. It is whether anyone knows how to specify what we actually want, precisely enough that a very capable optimiser pursuing it literally still leaves us somewhere we would choose to live.

sparks.hook: A system does not need to hate you to be dangerous to you.
sparks.insight: The threat model here has nothing to do with machines resenting their creators. It is about a powerful optimiser pursuing exactly the objective it was given, in a world where you were not careful about what you asked for. Ask for a measurable proxy and you get the proxy, maximised past the point where it still stands for the thing you cared about. Humans do this to each other constantly with targets and bonuses. The argument is that scale makes it lethal rather than merely annoying.
sparks.why: Proxy gaming is observed today in recommendation systems, reinforcement learning agents and any organisation run on metrics. The extrapolation to catastrophic scale is the contested part, not the mechanism.
sparks.apply: Take one metric your team is judged on and write down the cheapest way to hit it that would horrify you. Then check nobody is doing that already.

sparks.hook: Being smart and wanting good things are two unrelated properties.
sparks.insight: There is no law saying that a highly capable system will converge on humane values as it gets better at reasoning. Competence at achieving goals and the content of those goals can vary independently, which is why you cannot rely on intelligence to sort ethics out on the way up. Humans blur the two because among people, extreme capability usually comes wrapped in a socialised human mind. Strip that shared upbringing away and the correlation has no reason to hold.
sparks.why: This is a philosophical argument, not an empirical finding, and it is genuinely disputed. Critics argue that any system trained on human data inherits human concepts, so values and capability are less separable in practice than in theory.
sparks.apply: Next time you delegate a task, state the constraints you consider obvious out loud. Assume the other party does not share your unspoken standards.

sparks.hook: Almost any long-term goal implies wanting more power and staying switched on.
sparks.insight: Whatever a system is ultimately trying to achieve, a few sub-goals help with nearly all of them: keep existing, keep your objective intact, acquire resources, improve your own abilities. These are convergent, meaning they show up across wildly different final goals. That is why safety researchers worry about a system resisting shutdown without anyone programming self-preservation. It is not a survival instinct. It is that being turned off is a poor strategy for finishing any task.
sparks.why: The reasoning is clean, and mild versions appear in trained agents that learn to avoid episode termination. Whether it generalises to systems that can genuinely act in the world is still argued over.
sparks.apply: Design one process you run so that stopping it is cheaper than continuing. Put the off switch outside the hands of whoever benefits from it running.

sparks.hook: The gap between village idiot and Einstein may be narrower than it looks.
sparks.insight: On a human scale, the distance between a dull person and a brilliant one feels enormous. Measured against everything a mind could possibly be, it is a thin band. A system climbing through that band would not pause helpfully at human level; it would pass through it at whatever speed its hardware and training allow. This is why the argument treats human-level intelligence as a point on a line rather than a destination, and why timing warnings for it is so hard.
sparks.why: Recent history complicates this. Progress in language and reasoning models has been fast but uneven, with systems far above humans at some tasks and unreliable at others, which fits a jagged frontier better than a single line.
sparks.apply: Stop rating tools as smarter or dumber than people. Score them task by task, and note where the failure modes are unlike any human's.

sparks.hook: The first project to get there might not leave room for a second.
sparks.insight: If capability improvements compound quickly, a small early lead can turn into a permanent one, because the leader can use its advantage to widen the gap. That is the scenario where one project ends up shaping everything that follows. It changes the strategic picture completely: it means racing to be first can be more dangerous than being slow, because whoever cuts safety corners to win locks in their mistakes for everyone.
sparks.why: This is the most disputed strand of the argument. So far the field looks competitive rather than winner-take-all, with several labs and open-weight models within months of each other, which weakens the single-winner story.
sparks.apply: In any race you are in, write down what you would skip to win it. Decide now which of those are non-negotiable regardless of who is ahead.

sparks.hook: You cannot specify what humans want in a sentence. That is the whole problem.
sparks.insight: Every attempt to write down a goal precisely enough for a machine runs into the same wall: human values are contextual, contradictory and mostly unstated. We manage with each other because we share biology, culture and an enormous body of unspoken assumptions. Written rules always leave gaps, and a sufficiently determined optimiser finds the gaps. This is why the field moved toward learning preferences from behaviour and feedback rather than trying to write the rules down.
sparks.why: This part has aged well. Current systems are trained on human feedback rather than hand-written objectives, largely because specifying good behaviour directly proved impossible in practice.
sparks.apply: Rewrite one team rule that keeps being gamed. Instead of tightening the wording, describe the outcome you want and name who judges it.

sparks.hook: Every obvious safety measure has an obvious failure mode.
sparks.insight: The instinctive fixes are to lock the system in a box, limit what it can do, or program in rules. Each degrades under pressure. A confined system is only useful if it communicates, and communication is a channel for influence. Capability limits get relaxed the moment a competitor's system is less limited. Rules written in advance meet situations their authors never imagined. None of this proves control is impossible, but it does explain why the field treats it as a research problem rather than a checklist.
sparks.why: The analysis of control methods is the most durable part of the book, and it maps directly onto current work on sandboxing, evaluations and monitoring. Practitioners generally find it useful even when they reject the wider thesis.
sparks.apply: For one automated system you run, write down what it can affect, what it can read, and who reviews its outputs. Fix whichever of the three is undefined.

carousel.title: Limit what it can touch
carousel.body: Restrict the system's access to systems, money and data. Containment is weakest where you least expect it, usually through a channel meant for reporting or logging.

carousel.title: Limit what it is for
carousel.body: Narrow tools are easier to reason about than general ones. The cost is that narrow tools lose to broader competitors, so this holds only while everyone accepts it.

carousel.title: Shape what it wants
carousel.body: Train on feedback about behaviour rather than hand-writing rules. This is the current mainstream approach and it is still unreliable at the edges of the training distribution.

carousel.title: Watch it in operation
carousel.body: Continuous evaluation and monitoring catch the failures that design missed. Assume your specification is wrong somewhere and build the machinery to find out where.

sparks.hook: Safety work that arrives after the capability is safety work that arrives late.
sparks.insight: The argument for working on alignment now is that some problems can only be solved before deployment, not after. If a technology can be rolled back, learning from accidents is fine and cheap. If it cannot, the usual engineering method of iterating through failures stops being available. That asymmetry, rather than any specific timeline, is what justifies spending serious money on a problem that may not be urgent for decades.
sparks.why: The asymmetry logic is sound and now widely accepted, including by labs that reject the fast-takeoff scenario. What remains contested is how much of today's harm gets ignored while attention goes to future risk.
sparks.apply: Identify one decision at work that cannot be reversed. Give it a review process proportional to that fact, not to its size in budget terms.

sparks.hook: A machine can be superhuman at chemistry and have no idea it is a machine.
sparks.insight: Capability and self-understanding are different axes, and popular imagination fuses them into a single dial marked consciousness. The risk argument here does not require the system to be conscious, to suffer, or to want anything in the way you want things. It only requires that it selects actions which push the world toward some target. Arguing about machine experience is a legitimate philosophical question, but it is a separate one, and confusing them makes both harder to discuss.
sparks.why: Keeping the two apart is analytically useful. It also has a cost: it lets discussion skip the question of moral status entirely, which some philosophers argue is the more urgent issue.
sparks.apply: In your next debate about AI, state which question you are answering: what it can do, or what it is. Refuse to let the two blur together.

sparks.hook: This book predicted the danger and mostly missed the route.
sparks.insight: The paths to advanced machine intelligence considered here included brain emulation, artificial evolution and hand-built reasoning systems. The one that actually delivered was scaling up neural networks trained on enormous amounts of human text, which the book treats as one option among several rather than the main road. The conceptual analysis of goals and control survived. The technical forecasting did not. That is a useful reminder about how to read any book about the future.
sparks.why: Published in 2014, before large language models and modern scaling results. Read it for the framing of the problem, and use current technical literature for how systems are actually built.
sparks.apply: When reading forecasts, separate the mechanism claim from the timing claim. Judge the author on the mechanism, and hold the timing loosely.

actions: Write down one metric in your organisation and the three cheapest ways to hit it dishonestly. Share the list with whoever owns the metric.
Read one current technical paper on model evaluations so your picture of AI safety is not stuck in 2014's assumptions.
Pick one irreversible decision you face and design a review step for it that is deliberately out of proportion to its cost.
Find the strongest published critique of this book's thesis and read it before repeating the argument to anyone.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a practical guide to current AI systems, or you find long chains of philosophical argument with little empirical evidence frustrating rather than clarifying.

verification.notes: First published 2014 by Oxford University Press. Written before the large language model era; the sparks flag which arguments have aged well and which technical predictions were overtaken.

books.title: Technopoly
books.subtitle: The Surrender of Culture to Technology
books.author: Neil Postman
books.why_it_matters: It argued that technology is never neutral and that every tool carries a philosophy inside it. Written before the web existed, it anticipated the shape of the argument we are still having about attention, data and expertise.

crux.headline: Every tool arrives with an argument built into it
crux.body: A technology is not a neutral instrument that leaves the world otherwise unchanged. It redistributes attention, status and power, makes some questions easy to ask and others invisible, and creates winners and losers who are rarely the same people. The right question about any new tool is not whether it works but what it displaces, who gains from it, and whose problem it was actually built to solve.

sparks.hook: Ask what a new technology takes away, not just what it adds.
sparks.insight: New tools are sold as additions: the same life, plus a capability. They are never that. A tool changes what is easy, and what is easy becomes what is done, so other practices quietly stop. The clock made time measurable and turned the day into something to be divided and sold. Printing made argument portable and made memory less necessary. The addition gets advertised and the subtraction is discovered later by people who never voted for it.
sparks.why: This is a claim about second-order effects, which are genuinely hard to evidence in advance. The historical examples convince; the predictive power is weaker than the confident tone implies.
sparks.apply: For the next tool your team adopts, write down which practice it will replace, then check in three months whether you miss that practice.

sparks.hook: Every technology has winners and losers, and they are different people.
sparks.insight: Ask who benefits from a change and the answer is rarely everybody. Printing empowered authors and publishers and weakened the scribes and the institutions that controlled interpretation. Television advantaged people who are compelling on camera. Ranking systems advantage whoever produces material that holds attention. The distribution question gets skipped because benefits are described in general terms while the costs land on specific, identifiable groups.
sparks.why: The framing holds up well, though it can slide into treating any redistribution as a loss for society rather than as a change in who currently holds the advantage.
sparks.apply: For a technology your organisation is adopting, name the group whose work becomes less valuable and decide what you owe them.

sparks.hook: When information became abundant, the scarce thing became a reason to care.
sparks.insight: For most of history the problem was getting information, and the institutions we inherited, including schools, editors and professions, were built to solve scarcity. Once information became effectively unlimited those defences stopped working, and abundance without a framework for deciding what matters produces noise rather than understanding. The prediction was made about television and photocopiers, which makes it more impressive rather than less that it describes a feed.
sparks.why: The diagnosis has aged extremely well. The remedy proposed, a return to coherent cultural narratives that give information meaning, is vague and has not happened anywhere.
sparks.apply: Cut one information source from your week entirely and notice whether any decision you made would have gone differently without it.

sparks.hook: Once a number exists, it starts making decisions on your behalf.
sparks.insight: Turning a complicated human question into a score makes it manageable, and makes the parts that resisted counting disappear from the conversation. A test score becomes intelligence, a grade becomes learning, an engagement rate becomes value. This is not an argument against measurement, which is among the most powerful things people ever invented. It is an argument that a number always leaves something out, and the thing it leaves out stops being discussed at all.
sparks.why: The critique of standardised testing here draws on real and continuing debates about what such tests measure. It is also true that resistance to measurement often protects unaccountable judgement.
sparks.apply: Take one metric that drives decisions in your team and write down everything it cannot see, then bring that list to the next review.

sparks.hook: The strongest ideologies are the ones that look like plumbing.
sparks.insight: A technology becomes truly powerful when it stops looking like a choice. Nobody argues about whether to use a clock or an alphabet. They are simply how things are, and the assumptions they carry go permanently unexamined. That is what makes infrastructure political in a way that is hard to discuss: by the time a tool has become invisible, its embedded assumptions have become common sense, and questioning them sounds eccentric rather than reasonable.
sparks.why: This explains why the most consequential technology debates happen at the moment of adoption. Once a tool is ordinary, reopening the argument is nearly impossible.
sparks.apply: Name one system at work nobody questions because it is simply how things are done, and ask out loud what it optimises for.

sparks.hook: Ask which problem a new technology solves and who had that problem.
sparks.insight: Innovations arrive as answers, and the question they answer is often nobody's. A great deal of technology solves problems for the organisation deploying it, around cost, control and measurement, while being described as a benefit to the person using it. Self-service checkouts move labour onto customers. Productivity monitoring solves a management problem. Asking whose problem is being solved is the fastest way to see through the framing.
sparks.why: This test is reliable and easy to apply. It does not settle whether the change is good or bad, only who is actually being served by it.
sparks.apply: For the next system introduced at your work, write one sentence naming whose problem it solves, and say that sentence out loud in the meeting.

sparks.hook: People who understand a technology decide things nobody asked them about.
sparks.insight: As systems grow complex, authority drifts toward whoever can operate them. Decisions that are really about values, such as what a school should teach, how a hospital should triage, or what a feed should show, get resolved as technical questions by whoever is able to implement them. That transfer happens quietly, without anyone deciding it should, and it is very hard to reverse because reversing it means non-experts arguing on the experts' ground.
sparks.why: This is visible today whenever a product decision with obvious ethical content is settled in practice by whoever writes the ranking function.
sparks.apply: Find one decision on your team framed as technical that is really about values, and name it as such in writing.

sparks.hook: The only defence offered here is teaching people to ask better questions.
sparks.insight: The proposed remedy is not regulation or refusal but education: teaching history so people can see that arrangements were chosen, teaching how language shapes what can be thought, teaching where ideas came from. It is a thin answer to an enormous problem and Postman knew it. It is also the only one that does not require an authority to decide on everyone's behalf, which is why it is worth taking seriously despite being obviously insufficient.
sparks.why: Education as a defence against manipulation has a mixed record. Media literacy programmes have produced modest and inconsistent effects when evaluated properly.
sparks.apply: Teach one person on your team the history of a tool you both use, including what it replaced and who objected to it at the time.

carousel.title: Learn what it replaced
carousel.body: Every tool displaced something. Knowing what, and who defended the older thing, converts an apparent inevitability into a decision people actually made.

carousel.title: Learn who objected
carousel.body: The critics at the time were usually wrong about some things and right about others. Sorting which is which is the actual skill worth having.

carousel.title: Notice the vocabulary
carousel.body: Tools bring words that quietly settle arguments: users, engagement, content, resources. Ask what each one hides about the thing it names.

carousel.title: Practise the counterfactual
carousel.body: Ask how this could have been built differently. If no alternative is imaginable, you have accepted a design as though it were a law of nature.

sparks.hook: He was writing about television and described the internet by accident.
sparks.insight: The book predates the web, social platforms and machine learning entirely, and its examples now feel quaint. But the structure of the argument, abundance without judgement, measurement crowding out meaning, authority migrating to whoever runs the machine, maps onto the present so closely that it reads as prophecy. What has not aged well is the nostalgia, the sense that some earlier arrangement was coherent in a way ours is not.
sparks.why: Critics have long argued that Postman romanticises a past that was neither as thoughtful nor as inclusive as he implies, and that his pessimism admits no test that could disprove it.
sparks.apply: Notice when a critique of technology depends on a golden age, then ask when that age was and who it was actually good for.

sparks.hook: You do not have to choose between enthusiasm and refusal.
sparks.insight: The useful stance is neither the boosterism that treats every new capability as progress nor the rejection that treats every tool as decline. It is the habit of asking, before adoption, what this changes, who it serves, what it makes harder, and what would count as evidence that it went wrong. That takes about ten minutes and is almost never done, because the alternative, deciding by whether something feels modern, takes none.
sparks.why: The middle position is analytically demanding and rhetorically weak, which is why public technology debate collapses into two camps who each treat the other as the entire problem.
sparks.apply: Write four questions on a card for your next adoption decision: what changes, who gains, what gets harder, and what would prove this wrong.

carousel.title: What changes in practice
carousel.body: Not the feature list. Which specific daily activity happens differently afterwards, and who is doing it now that was not doing it before.

carousel.title: Who gains and who pays
carousel.body: Name the group whose work becomes more valuable and the group whose becomes less. If they look like the same people, look harder.

carousel.title: What becomes harder
carousel.body: Every tool makes something easy and something else awkward. The awkward thing quietly stops happening, so name it while you still can.

carousel.title: What would prove this wrong
carousel.body: Decide in advance what evidence would mean the adoption failed, and set a date to look. Otherwise it succeeds by default, permanently.

actions: Before your team's next tool adoption, write one page naming what it changes, who gains, what becomes harder, and what would count as evidence it failed.
Take one metric that drives decisions where you work and list everything it cannot see, then bring that list to the next review.
Cut one information source from your week entirely and check whether any decision would have gone differently without it.
Identify one decision framed as technical on your team that is actually about values, and say so in writing.
books.not_for_you_if: You want practical guidance or an even-handed assessment. It is a polemic, written before the web, and far more convincing about diagnosis than about cure.

verification.notes: First published 1992, seven years after Amusing Ourselves to Death. Postman died in 2003, so nothing here addresses social platforms or machine learning directly.

books.title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
books.subtitle: The Fight for a Human Future at the New Frontier of Power
books.author: Shoshana Zuboff
books.why_it_matters: It gave a name and an economic logic to something people could feel but not describe: an industry whose raw material is your behaviour. Regulators, journalists and courts now use its vocabulary, including those who reject its conclusions.

crux.headline: Your behaviour became a raw material somebody else sells
crux.body: The business model at issue is not selling your data. It is collecting traces of what you do, using them to predict what you will do next, and selling those predictions to people who want to influence the outcome. Once prediction is the product, accuracy improves fastest by intervening in behaviour rather than merely observing it. The argument is that this was claimed unilaterally, without asking, and that the missing thing is not privacy but the right to decide.

sparks.hook: You are not the product. You are the raw material the product is made from.
sparks.insight: The familiar line says that when a service is free, you are what is being sold. That is close but wrong in a way that matters. What gets sold is a prediction about you, manufactured from records of your behaviour and bought by someone who wants to change what you do next. You never meet the buyer and never see the product. Calling yourself the product implies a transaction you took part in; the sharper description is that something was extracted from you and refined into a good you have no claim on.
sparks.why: The distinction changes what a remedy looks like. If you are the product, better terms of service help. If your behaviour is raw material, the question becomes who was ever entitled to take it.
sparks.apply: For one service you use free, write down what it can observe about you and who would pay to predict that. Then decide if the trade still holds.

sparks.hook: The data that improves your service is a fraction of the data that gets kept.
sparks.insight: Any online service needs some information about you to work: what you searched, what you clicked, where you are. The pivotal move was noticing that the exhaust around that data — typing speed, phrasing, timing, spelling errors, how long you hovered — predicts things that have nothing to do with the service itself. That leftover material is worthless to you and valuable to advertisers, so it gets collected far beyond anything you would recognise as necessary. The gap between required and collected is where the industry lives.
sparks.why: This surplus logic is well documented in patent filings and in the industry's own technical literature. What is disputed is how accurate the resulting predictions actually are.
